records.description: Dominik Bochenski, founder /CD at Tantrum Studio in Toronto: "The production company approached us about the feasibility of digitally recreating Canadian cancer research activist Terry Fox's face and seamlessly compositing it onto an actor. "Initially, there was discussion about a more traditional multi-angle, cut-heavy edit that would gradually reveal Terry's face. "But as the concept developed, it became clear that the spot would be a single, continuous take – meaning there would be no room to hide imperfections. "Because there were only a handful of grainy photos of Terry Fox, an AI-driven face swap would not deliver the level of realism required for the film. "After extensive research and conversations, it became clear that the only viable approach was a fully CG solution. "We needed to model, texture, shade, track, animate, light, render, and composite Terry's face from scratch. "The biggest creative challenge was twofold. First, making a believable CG human is still one of the hardest things to do in VFX. The tiniest imperfections in proportions, skin texture, or lighting can break the illusion. "The second major challenge was staying true to Terry's likeness. As Canadians, we all have a mental image of him, but even real photos of him sometimes felt inconsistent. "On top of that, we were sharing our work with the Terry Fox Foundation and his family, which made the stakes even higher. It had to feel like Terry, not just a CG version of him. The first technical challenge was that without a scan of Terry's head, determining his true shape was a guessing game. "We sculpted in ZBrush using key reference images, and at times, we felt confident that we were on the right track. "But as soon as we moved the model into our Maya scene with the correct lens and lighting, everything changed. "He would look completely different – sometimes shockingly so. We had to rely on trial, error, and pure intuition, often making intentional exaggerations just to have it feel right in-camera. "The second technical challenge was matching the CG Terry to the real actors standing all around him. "This wasn't just about making the CG head look real – it had to integrate seamlessly with the live-action footage, where the lighting and skin response were naturally perfect. "Our actor served as a strong reference for integration, but he looked nothing like Terry and was noticeably older, which affected the way light interacted with his face. "We had to constantly tweak the shading, rendering and compositing, often by gut instinct, to ensure the CG Terry didn't feel separate from the scene. "Tracking was another major hurdle. We brought in a specialist to refine the tracking, but Adam's facial proportions were different from Terry's, so we also had to subtly warp the footage to make everything align properly. "Rendering also became a challenge due to the length of the shot. Running full renders often took an entire day, and evaluating only partial sections didn't give us the full picture. "To judge realism, we needed to process the entire sequence properly, play it back, and then assess what was working and what wasn't. It was an exhausting but necessary process. "In the end, we did incorporate AI-based face swapping, but only as a fine-tuning tool, which was trained not on top of the footage but rather on our intermediate CG composite. "The face swap systems that provided any sort of usable results looked very fake, but we found that mixing these in just around the eyes helped refine the likeness. It wasn't a replacement for our CG work, but rather an enhancement. "This project was a reality check for anyone who thinks AI is a magic bullet. While AI-generated imagery can be effective in some contexts, it often falls apart under real production demands. "We experimented heavily with deepfake approaches, but they simply weren't robust enough to hold up in a high-end cinematic setting. The moment you need full creative control, you quickly realize that traditional VFX techniques are still the backbone of this kind of work."

records.description: Le Truc Studio, whose Bell & Ross film we featured in Stash 166, returns with another luxury product in this work for French audio brand Devialet and the Opéra de Paris edition of their Astra integrated amplifier. records.description: The motion crew at London's Form Films constructs a full-CG reveal film for the XP electric motorcycle, a collaboration between vehicle designer Hugo Eccles at UNTLD MOTO and American manufacturer Zero Motorcycles. Dan Preston-George, producer at Form Films: "Inspired by the XP's radical design and UNTLD MOTO's meticulous process, we structured the film around the concept of completely rebuilding the motorcycle piece by piece. "These shots echo the designer's attention to detail and are interwoven with high-energy riding sequences (also built in CG) that showcase the motorcycle's beauty and rideability. "This approach allowed us to showcase Eccles' visionary design and served as a fitting way to announce ‘a new era in motorcycling'. "The challenge was to create a compelling brand film that showcased the XP's groundbreaking design while speaking to motorcycle enthusiasts, as well as a broader audience interested in the future of transportation. "To achieve this, we brought the concept of ‘Genesis' to life in the physical sense (how materials and components come together) and in the conceptual sense (the evolution of motorcycle design). "The story structure not only mirrors the design process, but represents the fundamental shift from combustion to electric power and XP's position as a vanguard of that transformation."

records.description: Colle Ignacio Godoy, EP at BUDA.tv in Buenos Aires: "The idea was to bring Vear, a character created by Japanese artist Verdy, to life for the Beats headphones. "The result was a series of pieces in which Beats and Verdy join forces in a collaboration that seamlessly blends music, urban culture, and avant-garde design. A perfect expression of the Beats spirit. "One of the biggest challenges we faced was translating Vear, a 2D character full of Verdy's signature gestures, attitude and street energy, into a 3D being that could exist convincingly in a rich, tangible world. "It wasn't just about modeling or texturing. It was about preserving his essence, the looseness of the line, the emotion in each pose and making sure that once he stepped into three dimensions, he still felt alive, touchable and undeniably Verdy. "Every detail, from his proportions to the way light interacts with his materials, was crafted to keep that balance between animation and reality, design and soul. "The production timeline spanned 12 weeks, covering the development of both the teaser and the first spot. "The response from Verdy's team was overwhelmingly positive. They embraced the character, the story and the visual style from the very beginning. "That enthusiasm fueled the entire process, keeping the energy high and pushing everyone involved to keep raising the bar until we reached the finish line. "The overall production was handled in Blender, which served as the backbone for layout, modeling, and rendering. Maya was used for animation. Meanwhile, all graphic design and compositing were developed within Adobe Creative Suite."

records.description: Simon Ravet, director at I-REEL in Paris: "We have collaborated for over eight years with the Ulysse Nardin team, and each project is a really creative time, always inspiring and innovative, offering lots of freedom for creativity. "They wanted to introduce their new product, the Diver [AIR], and its major features: high technology, high horology, high performance. "The brief was to create a link with the Watches & Wonders trade show booth scenography already engaged when we started, so we imagined a scientific experimentation laboratory located in the Swiss mountains. "To echo the watch that weighs only 52g, we focused on evoking a sense of lightness and aimed to convey this notion throughout the film. "We drew inspiration from inflatable architecture for the design of the laboratory, which brings up a sense of protection and shock resistance, mirroring the watch's features and creating a harmonious blend of form and function. "This inflated laboratory is a white, minimalist, and futuristic place whose organic shapes blend into the snowy natural landscape of the Swiss Jura. "To add a human dimension, we incorporated AI-generated sequences showing athletes undergoing tests, pushing their watches to the same limits as themselves. "These animations required a lot of reworking within our traditional VFX pipeline to achieve the level of quality we were aiming for. "As usual, the schedule was quite tight since we had less than two months between the brief and the delivery. "We spent two weeks developing the creative concept and finally proposed two different directions. When one was approved by the client, we spent two weeks working on the animatic and around three weeks on CGI texturing and rendering."

records.description: Paul Copeland, VFX Supervisor at The Embassy in Vancouver: "We were tasked with having CG snowmen terrorize the city as a metaphor for harsh winter conditions that the Nissan Kicks can overcome with ease. "We were also asked to make these characters feel menacing and mischievous with a touch of humor. "One of the main challenges was to convert a sunny fall Toronto day to feel like it's in the grips of a major snowstorm. "The art department did a great job dressing the street around the car to feel like winter, but we had the task of adding snow and ice to the rest of the city. We did this by using matte paintings and 2.5D compositing techniques. "Another challenge was the large number of snowmen to animate, with each one needing a separate FX pass of interactive snow to help integrate them into the scene. "There is a sequence at the end of the spot where the snowmen build a huge wall blocking the street to try and keep the Nissan Kicks from passing. "When the car breaks through, we had to collapse the wall and all the snowmen with it. To achieve this required many passes of snow simulations and a keen eye to composite it all together to get the final result." Schedule: Seven weeks (after the edit was locked).

records.description: Shane Griffin, director at GRIF. in New York: "Our task was to design an ‘Atelier of Wonder' for Nespresso that felt like a mix between a magical factory line, a rube goldberg machine, and a high-end luxury store. "The purpose of the atelier was to show how all of the flavors, accessories, and a wide array of products get created, packed, and shipped in time for the festive season. "The creative challenge was to design a series of little technical machines that actually worked together to transport our products through the atelier in a whimsical & surprising way. "These machines had to be functional, yet charming, while also adding a sense of premium quality, exuding a warm, festive feeling. "It felt more akin to engineering than a motion design project, as every little decision had a knock-on effect further down the conveyor belt. "There was a heavy modeling and look development period, specifically getting the foams of the various different types of coffees correct – each recipe has a different ratio of coffee to milk, and different preparation, so the crema (or foam) changes color, density, and height. "We rendered with Redshift, and used mostly a blend between an SSS shader (for any milky coffee or foam) and a standard liquid shader (for transparent coffee). "But that was just the static assets; the coffee pours themselves needed a new approach entirely. "Let's take the milk pouring into the glass, and then the coffee pouring into the milk, that is an extremely difficult sim to begin with, now pair that with the action of it dynamically moving on a conveyor belt with mechanical arms that pick it up and swing it around, and let's add some ice cubes on top of that! "It was very tricky. We used a blend of Phoenix, Embergen, TyFlow, After Effects, and Redshift procedural shaders to pull off that shot. "Then came the machinery. Some of it relied on physics, some of it relied on kinematic systems, and some relied on good old-fashioned keyframes. "There really was no blueprint or reference point here; we blocked out the action using simple geometry, but when it came to building them out, we made a concerted effort to architect them in a way that could physically work in the real world. "For the most part, all the cogs, wheels, and levers were rigged up to work correctly, so if you look closely, everything makes sense." Schedule: Five months.

"Let's take the milk pouring into the glass, and then the coffee pouring into the milk, that is an extremely difficult sim to begin with, now pair that with the action of it dynamically moving on a conveyor belt with mechanical arms that pick it up and swing it around, and let's add some ice cubes on top of that! "It was very tricky. We used a blend of Phoenix, Embergen, TyFlow, After Effects, and Redshift procedural shaders to pull off that shot. "Then came the machinery. Some of it relied on physics, some of it relied on kinematic systems, and some relied on good old-fashioned keyframes. "There really was no blueprint or reference point here; we blocked out the action using simple geometry, but when it came to building them out, we made a concerted effort to architect them in a way that could physically work in the real world. "For the most part, all the cogs, wheels, and levers were rigged up to work correctly, so if you look closely, everything makes sense." Schedule: Five months.

records.description: Fx Goby, director at Nexus Studios in London: "These three films for Lemonade turn complexity into charm, like showing how filing a claim can feel as easy as ordering a sweater online. "The innovation here lies in making the complex feel simple, and doing so with warmth and whimsy. Each film is crafted to feel handmade, even when powered by cutting-edge tech. "The project spans live-action, stop-motion, 3D, motion design, and even some 2D flourishes to keep things surprising. "Each film has its own tone, whimsical, epic, or quirky, but they all feel cohesive through a shared sense of craft, playfulness, and imagination. It helps position Lemonade as both innovative and human. "In ‘Purchase Online', I love the texture that comes from combining the stop-motion sweater with the 2D backgrounds. "The blend of stop-motion and 2D gave the film a tactile richness. I wanted viewers to feel the texture, like the fibres of wool, and make each frame visually irresistible. The contrast with illustration made those textures pop. "The ‘That One Song' film plays with the scale of an infinite music library, from massive soundscape cities to the grooves of a single record. We used texture and shifting perspectives to take viewers on a journey from the cosmic to the intimate. "In ‘Money', I wanted to avoid anything dry when talking about data/money transfer, so we filled the world with strange, surprising characters and objects loosely tied to money. The goal is to keep the viewer guessing and grinning. "These films celebrate the beauty of instantaneity, how tech can shrink time, while keeping things deeply human. We brought warmth, texture, and craft to powerful algorithms."

records.description: Guto Terni, co-founder/director at ROOF Studio in New York: "These animated vignettes are part of a brand campaign created by MullenLowe Design Studio for the ADC Annual Awards around the theme ‘Be Seen by the Best Eyes.' "We started with several initial vignette ideas, choosing the final selection based on our timeframe and their visual potential – all aimed at embracing this concept. "The eye is always the main character, appearing in completely different scenarios. There's always a dreamlike quality, with the eyes interacting with the camera throughout, reinforcing the sense that we are constantly being watched. "I opted for hyperrealism to bring this vision to life, packing every render with intricate details. "The same attention is applied to the animations, which feature complex movements and simulated extra motions to enhance realism. Together, these elements enrich the bizarre, hallucinatory style of the vignettes. "I truly enjoy working on projects that are as curious as they are engaging. This one is both weird and fun, inviting you to watch it repeatedly to capture every detail. "There's something extraordinary about a process without limitations. Our partnership with MullenLowe Design Studio was pure gold. "We aimed for something visually rich with eye-catching animation. "Even though they all had their complexities, the biggest challenge was the ‘Chinese Takeout' video. "Animating a realistic eyeball emerging from a box of yakisoba noodles in 3D is very hard. We began by animating the chopsticks picking up the eyeball from the box. "Once that was convincing, we started simulating the noodles, which was the first big challenge, especially when some of them had to hang from the eyeball as it was lifted. It took a lot of work and many tries. "However, the hardest challenge was simulating the sauce. It needed to coat the noodles convincingly and maintain a fluid consistency to drip naturally from the eyeball as it opened at the end of the sequence. "Finally, we added finer details like sesame seeds and parsley to enhance realism. Each element had to work in harmony, making this project a true test of technical and creative problem-solving. "In addition to the films, the package included 40 poster executions, 275 unique jury posts (each with the jurors' eyeballs), and social and digital assets, combining humor, surrealism, and nostalgia."

records.description: Following up on 2023's IGA holiday spot "Mr. Beaver" (Stash 163), Montreal's Tonic DNA studio delivers another ambitious character-driven tale capturing the power of cooking to transcend family conflicts. Quentin Fachon: "Our goal was to stay true to the IGA look and feel, and also differentiate this year from the two previous tales Tonic DNA and Sid Lee have done together. "So we played a lot with the grammar of the cameras. Adding split screens, crash zooms, and strong angles. "Another goal was to create a narrative through the use of light and color. We needed to color code the movie to add to the symbolism and clarity, but also to guide the viewer through the quick pacing." Marta Grasso, art director at Tonic DNA: "When the sisters fight, we're in a gray and de-saturated world, everything is super cold. "When Gabrielle discovers the first dish on her porch, we started to add a bit of saturation to the scene. "From there we gradually bring in more and more color until the sisters finally put their past aside and reunite. "The sisters are identical twins so we needed the audience to recognize their differences and ensure they were equally interesting. "Audrey is more eccentric, she's an artist and wears green. Gabrielle is more traditional, always perfect with her nails done, and wears red."

records.description: Adam Droy, CD at Untold Studios in London: "As with some of the best briefs we receive, it was very simple: Create an octopus that befriends a boy at Christmas. "As soon as we heard that we were unbelievably excited about the project and couldn't wait to get stuck in. "One huge challenge was BlubBlub the octopus' performance. How do we show his range of emotions without the key facial features we are used to? "We relied heavily on overall body shape along with expressive eyes to do a lot of the heavy lifting. "We looked at subtle pupil dilations or head tilts to help portray how BlubBlub felt in a particular scene. We had a whole team working on just the look of his eyes. "Crafting the exact level of reflection and highlights could really bring life into the performance. "It's safe to say this was one of our most complex and challenging creatures to date. "Our biggest ‘how do we do that?' moment was related to integrating the octopus onto the head and hair of the boy. "We created three unique grooms of hair, wet, dry, and under the hat, based on a full 360 scan. "Once we had this, BlubBlub could move anywhere on the boy's head and we could realistically simulate all the hairs he interacted with. "One feature that makes BlubBlub unique is that he has a thin film that covers his entire body inspired by what is found in nature with real octopuses. We named this the ‘clear coat'. "It's a secondary layer of super thin skin that covers his whole body and bridges gaps in his underlying body giving really detailed and delicate reflections over him. "This technique gave us a huge range of control allowing us to dial in exactly how wet or dry Blub Blub might feel in certain situations. "We created the model for BlubBlub in Zbrush and Maya with all the lighting and rendering work, along with creature FX (simulations) done in Houdini and rendered in Arnold. Composited was handled in Nuke. "Unusually, in this case, we used Houdini to create a fully procedural skin system that allowed us full dynamic and procedural control to change the color, pattern, and shape of the cells of BlubBlub's skin – mimicking that of a real octopus."

records.description: Shane Griffin, Director at GRIF studio in New York: "The agency MullenLowe approached us with an ambitious idea to craft a journey for the new Acura ADX through multiple surrealist worlds, each one reflecting a selling point of the car, referencing Culture, Fun, Technology, and Performance. "Each world had its unique mood and treatment of the car, so from a motion design perspective this was a great challenge and required us to think about unique lighting, movements, fx, and environments for each section, while also having that cohesively sit together as a final piece with a distinct color palette. "Because there was a request to keep the car static, we needed to establish a sense of scale and depth with the environments, and also design them so they framed the car as the center of attention. "The look development process was a ton of fun, and the client encouraged us to go wild with the ideas. "The main technical challenge was with the density and detail of the CAD model of the ADX vehicle, and adapting that for all the fun FX we developed. "From VDB sims, to tech blowaparts, to wind tunnels and pyro sims, each sim involved using the CAD data, so we had to invent new workflows as we're adapting and experimenting. "For example, we loaded the entire CAD data model into TyFlow to achieve the blow-apart effect, so no proxies or reference models could be used, this was time intensive, with huge file sizes, but ultimately worth it. "We also used a combo of different pyro techniques to achieve the wind tunnel and turn burnout. "For the wind tunnel, we settled on using Embergen to simulate the wind, as it gave us near real-time feedback to craft and art direct the fine details of exactly how the aerodynamics would work." Schedule: Seven weeks.

raw_source.description: Shane Griffin, Director at GRIF studio in New York: "The agency MullenLowe approached us with an ambitious idea to craft a journey for the new Acura ADX through multiple surrealist worlds, each one reflecting a selling point of the car, referencing Culture, Fun, Technology, and Performance. "Each world had its unique mood and treatment of the car, so from a motion design perspective this was a great challenge and required us to think about unique lighting, movements, fx, and environments for each section, while also having that cohesively sit together as a final piece with a distinct color palette. "Because there was a request to keep the car static, we needed to establish a sense of scale and depth with the environments, and also design them so they framed the car as the center of attention. "The look development process was a ton of fun, and the client encouraged us to go wild with the ideas. "The main technical challenge was with the density and detail of the CAD model of the ADX vehicle, and adapting that for all the fun FX we developed. "From VDB sims, to tech blowaparts, to wind tunnels and pyro sims, each sim involved using the CAD data, so we had to invent new workflows as we're adapting and experimenting. "For example, we loaded the entire CAD data model into TyFlow to achieve the blow-apart effect, so no proxies or reference models could be used, this was time intensive, with huge file sizes, but ultimately worth it. "We also used a combo of different pyro techniques to achieve the wind tunnel and turn burnout. "For the wind tunnel, we settled on using Embergen to simulate the wind, as it gave us near real-time feedback to craft and art direct the fine details of exactly how the aerodynamics would work." Schedule: Seven weeks.

records.description: ManvsMachine's visual adventures with website building platform Squarespace continue with a masterclass in shiny pneumatics touting the brand's collab with artist Jeff Koons. From the team at MvsM: "The brief was very concise; dive into the mind of Jeff Koons. Following a re-imagined awakening of his most iconic balloon sculptures, enjoy their complex affirming reflections, as we breathe life into these contemporary monoliths. "It was key for us to represent Jeff's artwork as he intended. His iconic balloon sculptures convey a positive permanent optimism, which contradicts a real balloon's temporary fragility, this was the crux of the campaign. "Balancing the playfulness of balloon animals with the immaculate, imposing nature of Jeff's large-scale finished sculptures presented a real challenge. "A lengthy R&D phase was used to explore inflation in-depth – iteratively honing the weight, thickness, stiffness, and pressure of our metallic material to create simulations which felt both engaging and realistic."

records.description: The latest 3D motion work from Rimantas Lukavicius and the KORB team for Nike finds the Lithuania-based studio crushing symbols and icons from LeBron Jame's career in a spot for the LeBron XXII shoes releasing this week. "The technical goal was to make the film look as real as those viral crushing videos circulating online while also elevating the aesthetic side. "A lot of experimentation and physics simulations were involved, applying pressure to objects with different properties, such as crushing, squeezing, pushing, fracturing, etc. "Overall, the product's slogan ‘Pressure Tested. Pressure Ready.' makes perfect sense and truly reflects the process behind the spot it as well."

records.description: Blinkink director Sam Gainsborough reteams with acclaimed animator Andy Biddle on this innovative spot for British retailer Co-op, printing 900 2D frames onto individual shop receipts and then animating them in stop-motion. Sam Gainsborough: "It was a fun starting point to think, how would it look if we animated with receipt paper? Receipt printers use thermal paper, rather than ink. "This led me to look at lots of black-and-white ink animation techniques to find inspiration for the animation style. "We also knew text, numbers, and symbols would play a huge part in the aesthetic, so we created many tests to see how the typography could play a big part in the visual storytelling. "We had a wonderful printing team, who would print and cut each frame of the film through the receipt printer, then they would shoot all the frames in stop-motion animation. "It's always lovely working with a new process/technique – and it was a joy to discover that receipt printers naturally create such lovely errors, textures, and details. "The film looks very simple, but a huge amount of work went into creating it. "We were lucky to work with an incredible team of animators – led by Reg Isaac, whose naturalistic approach gave the characters in the film real authenticity. "I love the character designs which were based on initial sketches by Stephen McNally. To me, the world feels very true and real – although it all exists within the tiny, slightly glitchy print on the receipt paper." Schedule: 11 weeks.

records.description: Using a heartwarming mix of felt puppetry and CG animation, director Stephane Berla and Paris prodco Eddy fight loneliness in the Belgian city of Bruges this holiday season on behalf of charity De Warmste Week and broadcaster VRT. From the team at Eddy: "The most exciting challenge for this campaign was visually interpreting the inner flame – a symbol of the flame everyone carries within as well as the logo for the event. "Everyone's flame is different: some burn big and strong, while others are small and desperately kept alight. "One of the agency's and the client's warnings was that the flame in the hand can seem dangerous. So solutions had to be found to make the flames resolutely friendly, harmless, and capable of pure kindness. "We did this by humanizing them, using felt textures that make you want to snuggle up to them. "The production challenges lay in realistically integrating the 3D flame animation into the live-action environment. "There were technical constraints linked to tracking and post-production, mastering complex reflections (particularly on wet ground), and implementing a 3D scan of surfaces before shooting to ensure lighting consistency. "Each shot required multiple passes with luminous objects to capture natural reflections and provide precise data for the composition of the flames while avoiding these objects being visible in the image."

records.description: In their second project for The Woolmark Company (see Stash 156 for the first spot), Studio Birthplace directors Sil van der Woerd and Jorik Dozy stage a clothing-zombie apocalypse in the style of World War Z with Amsterdam's Dead Pixel handling VFX. Sil van der Woerd & Jorik Dozy: "‘Wear Wool, Not Waste' aims to educate consumers on the lifespan of their synthetic clothes. Whether in landfills or manifesting as microplastics, synthetics are omnipresent globally. "In this film, we visualize this unnaturally long lifespan as a zombie horror and showcase pure wool products as a more sustainable alternative. "Each empty shell of clothing is designed to resemble human figures, creating a haunting visual as they race through the streets, embodying the idea that discarded garments continue to affect our world long after they've been thrown away. ‍"The main challenge of the film was crafting a believable stampede of hollow, synthetic clothes invading a city. Our approach was to combine practical effects with digital enhancements. "We used air cannons to launch real synthetic clothes onto the set, then blended those shots with visual effects to create a seamless and lifelike invasion. "We started with motion capture, recording the actions of an actor, which were then translated into the digital realm and mapped onto a generic human model. "The CG synthetic clothes needed to behave with realistic physics as the invisible digital dummies ran through the streets. "For instance, when the CG clothes hit an object – like a car – they had to seamlessly snap off their invisible dummy character and become lifeless clothes. "To achieve this, we developed a system that randomized the clothes while still allowing for manual control when needed. "This randomization made each agent in the crowd unique. We used over 50 individual clothing pieces, each with at least five variations in color, texture, and shape, resulting in over 10,000 possible outfit combinations. "The 3D artists spent three months building this fully procedural, system allowing us to adjust parameters like color, fabric stiffness, reflectivity, and translucency in real-time. "For he crowd's motion and interaction, we built a system in Houdini that used the motion capture as a foundation for crowd behavior. "Most agents were programmed to avoid each other, but in cases where they did collide, we used motion capture data to generate realistic interaction physics. "When the agents collided with the terrain, or objects such as cars or signposts, the model would fall down realistically and only clothing would remain."

records.description: Ben Cronin, CD at Untold Studios in London: "This is the TVC for this year's Virgin Media campaign regarding the speed and consistency of their broadband service. "We partnered on the last two Virgin Media projects, "Highland Cow" and "Goat Glider" (Stash 161) and worked closely with the agency creatives to help search for the next brief, creating some visuals of potential animal/vehicle combos. "They came back with the idea of a walrus on a speedboat, and we could all immediately envision how good this was going to look – such a weighty animal that moves like a ballet dancer underwater but becomes ungainly and quite funny on land. "From the previous projects, the rules were always very clear: This is a photorealistic animal that never strays into anthropomorphic performance and we let the audience interpret as much as possible. "The creative challenges were about the discipline in crafting the beast and the animation. "With animation, there is always the discipline of finding and referring to real-world references, but the creative challenge here was to push it just the right amount to aid the narrative without breaking reality. "There were also several technical challenges. For instance, the walrus is a short-fur animal, which can be more challenging than long fur. Shorter hair is not very forgiving with regards to flow, density, bald patches, scars, and lookdev. "The team also had to deal with a groom and lookdev transition, from wet to dry, as the walrus leaves the water and the water drains off its fur. And of course, we also had to create the water surface and interactions for the first three shots. "One of our favorite parts of this project, and a technically challenging one, was the Blubber Shudder of our walrus. "From the very first meeting we all knew this would be TV gold; we just didn't know how much vibration and jiggle we could get away with before it looked fake. "Luckily, the speed boat had to deal with some choppy water on the live shoot in Sweden, and the bouncing and vibrations gave us ample reason to dial up the blubber shudder. "There were plenty of other deliverables beyond this spot, including creating an entire walrus, speedboat, and environment in Unreal to allow the agency to produce their own social content." Schedule: Four weeks of prep and previz plus eight weeks of post.

records.description: Ant Baena, ECD at FutureDeluxe in London: "Sonos challenged us to visualize immersive sound in a fresh and exciting way for the relaunch of their high-end sound bar, the Arc Ultra. "We collaborated with Warner Brothers and Legendary Entertainment to bring the world of ‘Dune' into the home. "The project's most challenging aspect was creating simulations and effects that felt unique and ownable to us as a studio and our client and also lived alongside the visual world of the movie that took years to perfect and develop. "The film is so visually rich we weren't short of inspiration but building a world that tied the film in with a high-end CG living space and sand simulations took some trial and error. "We work with artists all over the globe, so one technical challenge was moving the large complicated simulations and setups between artists, which is never as quick and seamless as you'd like it to be. "We also spent a lot of time remapping, which strains the technical setups within Houdini, especially when we're changing things, creating a lot of back and forth. "This piece was part of a wider product launch of Arc Ultra and Sub 4. FutureDeluxe collaborated with Sonos to create a wealth of product assets to be used online and on social media to help reinforce the new engineering and technology within the products." Schedule: Six weeks.

records.description: Fx Goby, director at Nexus Studios in London: "The BBC came up with a very simple but clear brief: Paris is the city of love, they wanted to subvert expectations around sports films and focus on the love athletes have for their sports. "So I decided to make a film drawing a parallel between romantic love and the relationship between athletes and their discipline. "We wanted to make a very warm, cozy, soft, and elegant film, breaking the codes, but still appealing to sports lovers. Finding the right balance was challenging. "I decided to have a very tight edit with many shots in a short period of time in order to create the energy of a sports film and counter that with a very gentle, delicate art direction. "We were very ambitious, 54 shots, 36 athletes, all unique designs, to squeeze into 60 seconds. But I think this film needed us to aim high. "The style of animation although looking simple and almost naive is very complex. "It ended up being labor-intensive manual work to match the original designs to the final animation and retain that gorgeous illustrative quality throughout the many steps of 2D animation. "Once we had a process, it still needed to be bespokely adapted to each single shot that had its own sets of challenges. "There is nothing that we usually use in 2D animation like outlines, flat colors, etc. It's all silhouettes with subtle gradients to create the faces and bodies of numerous diverse athletes. It was intense but we managed to keep the bar as high as we hoped. "As for the schedule, we had a bit more time than usual for a :60, with 3.5 months. "So we took the first three weeks to explore and define the look of the film with the art director, Callum Strachan and the character designer, Antoine Bonnet, two artists that I love. "We also spent many hours checking references and had sports experts confirming that our athletes and their sports were accurate, as much in the athlete's morphology than the gear they use or the movements they make."
records.campaign_title: BBC "WELCOME TO THE CITY OF LOVE"

records.description: Bryant Nichols, CD and Maria Hanafy, Managing Director at FutureDeluxe in Los Angeles: "The initial project brief was quite different from where we landed. "Originally, the client wanted to see their shoe enlarged and traveling through a NYC city street. "We went back and forth on the concept after realizing the initial idea wasn't working. "We landed on something called 'shape deform' where we start on the shoe and it warps and contorts into different shapes. "We went through Unreal Engine testing, decks of references, etc, which led us to the honor and rare luxury of a client who is asking for their shoe to be distorted. To pin down the client's idea of weirdness we went through several rounds of ideation. "The team started animation testing with all manner of odd and hilarious deformations with the art direction crafting a bright and punchy palette to really hero the black and white shoe. "The product is always such an important piece of the puzzle, shoes are always a tricky one, we reached out to our Sydney studio to give us a hand. "They were able to quickly provide us with a shoe that looked photo-real. Not to mention the knowledge they provided in the scanning process. "Creating the morphed shapes in Houdini and then bringing them into Cinema 4D to be used in a pose morph allowed us to utilize the power of Houdini but with the speed and simplicity of C4D for animation and rendering."

records.description: Continuing its quest to raise awareness of global issues, Studio Birthplace leverages its narrative and VFX talents to help environmental non-profit Canopy sound the alarm that 3.1 billion trees are cut each year for paper packaging. Directors Sil van der Woerd and Jorik Dozy at Studio Birthplace: "In the face of our climate crisis, every industry must transition towards zero-impact, sustainable solutions. "Making packaging from agricultural residues and discarded food waste instead of living trees, is a perfect example. What does the volume of 3.1 billion trees look like? "When considering how to best visualize this, we felt it was crucial to depict trees not as mere trunks that look like resources, but as living beings that are part of complex ecosystems, providing habitats for animals, producing clean water, and generating the oxygen we breathe. "To emphasize their role as living entities, we visualized the various types of CGI trees seen in the film, complete with branches and leaves. "Together, they form a slow, elegant avalanche creeping through the streets of London, overwhelming yet graceful."

records.description: A smart mix of humor and urgency from London's Blue Zoo Animation and GOOD Agency makes an entertaining and effective case for the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), the UK's largest nature conservation charity. Blue Zoo director Dane Winn: "Our goal was to create an emotional connection with the audience; making them laugh, reflect, and act. "The charismatic characters we've introduced carry the weight of their message with a hopeful note, encouraging viewers to support the RSPB's mission. "The four films aim for a tactile, miniature set look inspired by the works of Wes Anderson, an influence that also extended into the cinematography. "The characters were designed for efficient modeling, rigging, and precise performance without over-complicating the assets. "This project marked our first use of Blender rigging by our in-house team as we continue integrating Blender into our pipeline leveraging its geometry nodes system to create the intricate groom for all characters and environments. "We optimized our workflow by designing everything to frame, creating fast 3D blockouts of the scenes followed by paint-over designs that the CG team closely matched. "We utilized various techniques to achieve specific effects. For example, the plastic bag hitting the hedgehog combined a cloth simulation with shape keys for the comedic nose poke effect. "Unable to simulate the rubbish falling timing perfectly, we keyframed each piece manually. The sewage splash involved a Blender liquid simulation with additional dripping geometry for the animation resolve."

records.description: ECD Martin Schurmann and the animation team at Vascolo in Buenos Aires transport viewers back to historic Rickwood Field in Birmingham, Alabama, in this promo for a special MLB game honoring the Negro Leagues and their greatest players. Martin Schurmann, ECD/Founder at Váscolo in Buenos Aires: "Rickwood Field, the oldest ballpark in America, boasts over 100 years of rich history. "Our animation pays homage to the baseball legends and this iconic venue where much of baseball's storied past was written. "A major challenge was designing the players to match the style of the short film while ensuring that their likenesses were captured accurately, as each sketch required approval from the players' families. "We also had to accurately replicate the players' movements. To achieve this, we studied original footage of them playing and crafted the animations to reflect their signature moves." "Each player is depicted wearing their team jersey, representing either the period they played in the Leagues or the most iconic moment of their career. "For each legend's introduction moments, we used a typographic design inspired by two classic styles from the league's golden era: the typeface used in the players' locker room and a more script-like font that directly references how team names were written on the players' jerseys." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: Marcel Hita, CD at Trizz Studio in Barcelona: "The project brief was to create an animation piece that visually conveys concepts such as soothing, smoothness, and relief using a visual language inspired by the key ingredients of the product: caramel, honey, and Swiss herbs. "Our primary challenge was to craft a compelling narrative using only these three ingredients to develop a visual language that captures the product's deliciousness through a dynamic and artistic lens. "You know you're facing a challenge when you aim to blend fluid simulations with controlled and dynamic animation and all the elements need to look photo-realistic. "To achieve this balance, we established a general structure to define timings and motion intentions. From there, we created various simulations that interacted with hand-animated elements like typography and the Ricola product. "Finally, we fine-tuned and refined the motion and lighting of the piece, highlighting every detail characteristic of the Ricola ingredients. "With elements like refractions, subsurface scattering, and complex simulations, the renders were certainly heavy! "With Ricola, we were blessed to have the time in the initial stages of production to dedicate to exploring look development and animation to capture the message and feel we wanted to portray."

records.description: Gus Karam, co-founder at Le Cube in Buenos Aires/São Paulo: "The project brief from NEC was to create a promotional spot that highlights the journey of two heroes as they prepare for a major boxing fight. "The aim was to capture the inner struggles and aspirations of the fighters on the eve of this significant event for the boxing community. "The event in question was the historic fight where Oleksandr Usyk edged Tyson Fury to become the undisputed heavyweight champion of the world. "The main creative challenge was to seamlessly integrate the diverse narrative elements and visual styles into a cohesive story. "The film had to balance the excitement and heightened expectations of the fans, the inner dreams and fears of the fighters, and the climactic moment in the ring. "This required a carefully structured three-act narrative and a mixed-style visual approach, particularly in the second act, to reflect the emotional and psychological landscapes of the fighters. "The biggest technical challenge was blending different animation styles seamlessly. Each piece of artwork needed to be meticulously planned to fit into the overall animation, with key transition points identified to ensure smooth transitions between styles. "Maintaining consistency in style and fluidity throughout the piece required extensive communication within the team and precise execution of the mixed-style technique. "The production schedule was 11 weeks, we did a super fast three-week preproduction and then jumped right into the production of style frames and layouts for animation. "It was a really fast turnaround so we divided the whole video into three acts, and the second and middle acts were divided into different styles, so we could work on those at the same time as individual segments with their own prepro and production "A notable highlight of the project was the second act, where a mixed-style technique was used to enhance the psychedelic journey of the fighters. "This segment involved collaboration with top talents in animation from around the world, resulting in a rich and intricate piece filled with Easter eggs for the boxing community. "The project exemplifies the beauty of collaboration and the ability to blend storytelling with visual artistry, creating a historic and emotionally resonant piece that celebrates the fighters' journeys and their place in the history of boxing."

records.description: Chad Howitt, CD at ManvsMachine in Los Angeles: "Primarily known for their Dewars White Label, the brand wanted to reinforce the Double Double as their luxury product line. "Focusing on craft and substance over style, they wanted to use a room's interior design to redefine what a good scotch whiskey is and break the old and overly traditional perceptions. "Our biggest artistic challenge was the interior design of the rooms and establishing visuals that everyone could agree on. "When creating the ‘traditional ornate room', how far is too far? When does filigree become too much for anybody? "There are wonderful Baroque and Rococo-era designs that are breathtaking, but we needed to embrace it with more of an outlandish approach – like someone with money, but no taste. "On the opposite side, the ‘clean white room' needed to feel like an improvement on the gold room. "Modern aesthetics push design boundaries and room functionality, which often, can be too avant-garde for everyone's tastes. So finding those borders was difficult. "Art directing FLIP and Vellum sims is always a heavy lift that takes lots of time. It's also never a one-and-done process. As revisions and feedback come in, we repeat the process. "Thankfully, our team was able to take complex setups and adjust to the agency's notes to ensure the clients were happy with the final product.

records.description: Matt Taylor, animation director at Titmouse in Los Angeles: "There wasn't a brief or instructions, per se. Will Carsola of Liquid Death and I were hanging out at the Titmouse 2023 Christmas Party and I got my first glimpse at the Murder Man storyboards that he had put together. "They were hilarious and his vision was clear as could be. I told him this and he said Liquid Death only had one note: ‘to make it crappier,' which we set out to deliver on. "One challenge was how much blood would be okay to show. When it comes to posting on social media there is a visual limit that, when pushed too far, would result in the post being taken down. "So, we had to walk a fine line of showing just enough. But, I've grown to appreciate challenges like this that can open up a project to a wider audience. "Adobe Animate was used for all the backgrounds and animation and we spent a lot of time wrestling with line weights. "All the art could be looking great and then a character symbol was placed with a background. Some layout and scaling would take place and suddenly the background linework was thicker than the character line. "Or, the character linework looked too thick when scaled up. I was hoping to discover some kind of universal line weight adjustment. Some function to take every line in such-and-such a symbol that was size 1 and make them .75 would save a lot of time. "Another technical challenge was character symbols having different stage/scale orientations than others. "So, for instance, we needed to add detail to a close-up of Murder Man's nipple, but somewhere along the way, inside that nipple symbol, the stage got blown out of proportion, likely equal to the size of a two-story building. "When it's orientated to a massive scale like that, you'll know because Animate will only draw either straight lines or the most jagged vector brush lines you've seen in your life. "The best solution I know of is to break every symbol apart until you get back to the main stage, but you likely run the risk of a lot of different problems such as layers getting mixed up or mashed together, so it's not easy. "Getting into the weeds here just to say 'hi' to Adobe and ask if they'll please implement a function to reset the stage size/orientation in a symbol. "The schedule was ideal. There was time built in for character layout, which was great to have. "Layout eliminates the need for animators to have to build out their scenes, hunt for a background, pull in a character design, import audio, etc. "Instead, the scene is all set up, and at times even posed out so an animator can jump right in and do their magic. "I would meet with the animators and compositor twice a week to review scenes. As more animation was completed, those meet-ups transitioned into edit sessions. Then the schedule concluded in late March with a sound mix and final watch down."

"To maintain authenticity we engaged traditional 2D animators and comic book illustrators throughout the production to influence our animation or add human-made elements into the scenes. "This approach allowed us to bridge the worlds of legitimate comic book art and high-end CGI. "With so many different styles and looks for the characters, we had to create a bespoke system for each one that enabled them to maintain their unique stylization but also feel integrated into the light and shadow of the live-action world. "This meant each character had a different VFX ‘recipe' which was a tricky thing for the team to juggle. "Our VFX workflow involves several in-house tools but the backbone of the software toolset is Maya / Zbrush for modeling, rigging, and animation, and Houdini / Arnold for lookdev, lighting, and FX, with Nuke for compositing. We also used Blender for some of the 2D face animation. "We worked extremely closely with director Antoine Bardou-Jacquet throughout the process. He sat side-by-side with the animation team to refine the previs so we had a plan in place for every shot (in terms of action and framing) before the shoot began. "During production, Antoine ensured that we stuck closely to the previs and also enabled us to film loads of in-camera references (figurines, materials, bottles) which were often puppeteered by Antoine himself. They were enormously helpful during the creation of the film." Schedule: Five months.

records.description: Rich Webber, director at Aardman in Bristol, UK: "The BBC asked us to produce six 30-second shorts as part of their ‘Things We Love' campaign. The objective was to hear people's genuine thoughts about the BBC shows they love. "So, using the real voices of the great British public, we interviewed over a hundred people from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, then whittled our selection down to 15 people from each region across the six films. "With this way of working, you have no script, so starting from scratch you tailor some questions as discussion points and hope you get something back in the recordings that you can pick at and form into short pieces, that then evolve as you move forward with the edit. "The creative challenges for us were picking the right voices and setting them to the right characters and scenario. Sometimes the idea leaps out at you, other times you must work a little more on making the edit work for what you have in mind. "The family of foxes, for instance, jumped out instantly with their love of MasterChef and what they'd cook if they were on the show, so foxes rummaging in bins to make a culinary delight felt right for them. "Our interviewer was very skilled in making people feel relaxed and getting the best from them. The people he interviewed made this project so much fun, with their warm, natural, humorous responses and discussions. "This enabled us to explore a little world of wonderful clay animals and scenarios. The whole project was a joy to work on." Schedule: Six months.

records.description: Tim Fox, Director at The Mill in London: "The Coca-Cola Caravan has been synonymous with holiday seasons for over 30 years, delivering moments of Real Magic to millions around the world. "Ramadan is a period of solidarity, self-reflection, and shared experiences through the ritual of fasting, and the Coca-Cola red trucks have once again become vessels of togetherness to deliver an unprecedented Iftar moment, through the ritual of breaking fast together. "The animation team was set the task of bringing the characters to life using a ‘stepped' keys approach, animating on two's, threes and sometimes fours. "This is more in line with the approach used in traditional 2D or stop motion animation. As well as creating a strong visual style, it also helped connect the 3D characters to the stylized backgrounds. "With this approach creating strong key poses and strong in-between's is vital to help convey the weight, fluidity, and intention of each character. "We wanted the animation to feel vibrant, full of life, and capture the feeling of celebration. To achieve this, we worked on the performance of each character to bring a feeling of anticipation and excitement that culminated with them all coming together at the end of the film. "The aim was to have a collection of more intimate moments between characters that when combined to create a world full of life. "Each character was designed as a piece of concept art, then modeled and textured in ZBrush, rigged and animated in Maya, and rendered in Houdini with Arnold using reduced shading to emphasize the painted textures. "The best part of the film for me was the use of broad color palettes to get across the idea that the town is in full event mode. When it came to the skies and sunsets, our use of color and light played an integral part in making the sky a character. "Iftar and Ramadan centre around the sun setting, so there is always a sense of anticipation that every Muslim feels when they see the sun edging towards the horizon."

records.description: German post and VFX house ACHT backs up English director Joshua Vii as he takes a bee's eye view in this mix of motion-control and CG exploring the exterior and interior of the new Skoda Kodiaq crossover SUV. Produced through Film Deluxe GmbH for agency FCB London to air in Czechia and the UK, the film was shot in Prague and finished at ACHT on what the director calls "the tightest of postproduction schedules." Joshua Vii: "Rarely does a camera have a reason to move in the manner we do in this film. Usually, it's a purely stylistic choice, but here we had an opportunity to embody the point of view of a small bumble bee, adding a narrative touch to each camera move as the bee discovers and explores Skoda's latest SUV. "It was a very technical piece to pull off, combining seamless CGI together with precisely designed motion control shots, some of which were taken directly from FBX files output and mimicked from cinema 4D, while other shots were handcrafted on set due to needing to adapt the path of the camera to the geometry of the set and car. "In order to pull this off, every shot in the film was intricately pre-visualized, beginning by flying an iPhone around my own car to get a sense of where we wanted to be on our journey." "It was important to have the right post-production partner for this and ACHT Studio really pulled off the impossible with our time frame of just 2.5 weeks to edit, grade, animate, light and render CGI, composite, and compose the sound design and music. "Txo pull this off, every shot in the film was intricately pre-visualized, beginning by flying an iPhone around my own car to get a sense of where we wanted to be on our journey, and then crafting the curves and pace of the camera in Cinema 4D which were then handed over to ACHT to be perfected and embedded into their workflow. "It meant that before we shot the film we had a good sense of the edit and pace, and allowed us to overlay mattes of the car interior when shooting the exterior plates which would be composited afterwards. "ACHT did an incredible job bringing everything together and were amazing partners throughout the process, with a true creative understanding of what would help to elevate the film, from bumps and creases in the interior leather, to refining the design of our bumble bee. "FCB London oversaw the creative of the project and brought a solid creative vision of the piece, backing us through a complex process to create a bold visual piece."

records.description: Alon Isocianu, director for Impossible and CD at Reactiv in Toronto: "The initial brief was from the ad agency Juliet Creative who have worked with the Canadian Cancer Society on several campaigns. "The concept revolved around a series of striking vignettes, set in a black studio environment, that highlight the notion that it takes a society of people and programs to help fight cancer and provide resources to those who need it. "The ask was to find a way to showcase the Daffodil as a symbol for hope, and show it blooming throughout each scene. "The main creative challenge was how to depict the Daffodil as an organic, real, and tactile flower, while also giving it a hopeful, magical and graceful feel. "During early calls on the project, the client would affectionately refer to the flower as needing to be Exquisite. "We decided on an approach that meant designing and simulating a Daffodil digitally instead of capturing or sourcing timelapse footage. "Traditionally when you see timelapse footage of flowers blooming they seem jittery or jumpy because the footage is sped up to compress time. By creating a ‘realtime' blooming animation we could exude a sense of gracefulness and wonder. "For the design of the flower, we brought on Buenos Aires-based Houdini artist José Molfino. After several RnD passes we landed on a beautiful, graceful simulation that felt both tactile and dreamlike. "We then worked to integrate the rig/simulation into the rest of our pipeline which involved creating variations of that daffodils and different interactions with our live-action props. "In terms of the integration, we did a lot of work on set to set us up for success. Our VFX supervisor Jake Doforno 3D scanned all the props which were later used to create dynamic interactions with the CG daffodils. "He also captured 360 HDRI images of our practical lighting set up on set so that we could replicate the lighting in the CG space. "Our production designer Karlyn Koeser sourced real daffodils that we used on set to capture reference shots. This meant shooting every shot twice, once with the real daffodils for reference, and once without (which ended up being the plate shot we used in the VFX). "In post our matchmover Eddy Habib would track each shot and pass it to our animator Ben Carmeli who would re-simulate and animate the daffodils onto the different live-action elements as well as light and render the shots. "The most challenging shot ended up being the two hands clasping together – it involved scanning the hands on set and using that as a guide for where the flowers would grow. "We had to do some compositing trickery to get the stems to line up perfectly with the grooves in the fingers, as the scans and real hands couldn't be matched 100%. "This 30-second spot was a part of a larger campaign that also featured the Daffodil as a symbol for hope. The campaign was used to promote the Canadian Cancer Society's annual donation drive in April for ‘Daffodil Month'. Schedule: Four weeks of post-production.

records.description: Somei Sun, director in Singapore: "Due to iQOO being our long-term client, they told me about their new product plans very early on. This includes a combination of a phone and watch accessories. "The biggest selling point of the phone is its dual-core processor which emphasizes gaming capabilities. "In previous advertising projects, we would create characters and scene concepts based on product needs. "However, these were all one-time use only. Once the ad was over, people wouldn't think about it anymore and the assets created would be wasted. "This time the client said, ‘Can we create a world and protagonist that runs through all the ads?' So we decided to create a digital spokesperson named NEO, as well as an entire worldview. "We didn't have much time, but we needed to shape the entire world and lay the groundwork for a series of upcoming products, which is extremely challenging. "Based on the dual-core needs of our customers, I was reminded of very detailed animated works from the past: ‘KILL la KILL' and ‘FLCL'. I really liked this combination of an electronic device that can speak and a cute protagonist. So here's the story: "iQOO is a top-tier electronic beast with a monster soul hidden within it. It chose NEO, a 21-year-old boy who is not good at expressing himself, as its host – to be its brand spokesperson. "Once the boy finishes the advertising slogan, iQOO can lift its seal and unleash a powerful energy. "They work together, operating while tackling the evil electronic beasts that bring chaos to the world. However, things do not seem to be that simple, as iQOO also hides other secrets. "The biggest challenge in this project was to make the characters both realistic and maintain the stylized features of Japanese animation. "We want the characters to be believable because the film uses a lot of live footage. "To avoid falling into the uncanny valley, we wanted to maintain the stylization of animation. "At the same time, the performance of the characters also needs to be natural and believable, especially in the first half, where the character need to have a lot of emotional performances, such as misspeaking. "We originally planned to use a professional camera to shoot models similar to Neo's physique, and then replace the head. "But when we composited the CG head, it felt very strange, so in the end we chose to use full CG to complete all character performance shots. "This is the first time I've tried to control a character's facial expressions and speech, and surprisingly the effect is not bad. "During the test editing, we found that these shots did not stand out when edited together with other live footage, which gave us more confidence in dealing with the remaining shots. "In addition, we also used AI to assist in the creation of the monster set and director set. " And in a small section of the monster flashback in the film, we tried to generate content directly with Runway. To some extent, it has played an efficiency-enhancing role. "I found that mixing Japanese 2D FX with realistic rendering is also a good way to blend reality and stylization. "Therefore, I adopted this style in the climax part and tried to make the character's actions and camera movements more dynamic. "The hope was that it would form a strong contrast with the realistic film style presented earlier." Schedule: Three months.

"We want the characters to be believable because the film uses a lot of live footage. "To avoid falling into the uncanny valley, we wanted to maintain the stylization of animation. "At the same time, the performance of the characters also needs to be natural and believable, especially in the first half, where the character need to have a lot of emotional performances, such as misspeaking. "We originally planned to use a professional camera to shoot models similar to Neo's physique, and then replace the head. "But when we composited the CG head, it felt very strange, so in the end we chose to use full CG to complete all character performance shots. "This is the first time I've tried to control a character's facial expressions and speech, and surprisingly the effect is not bad. "During the test editing, we found that these shots did not stand out when edited together with other live footage, which gave us more confidence in dealing with the remaining shots. "In addition, we also used AI to assist in the creation of the monster set and director set. " And in a small section of the monster flashback in the film, we tried to generate content directly with Runway. To some extent, it has played an efficiency-enhancing role. "I found that mixing Japanese 2D FX with realistic rendering is also a good way to blend reality and stylization. "Therefore, I adopted this style in the climax part and tried to make the character's actions and camera movements more dynamic. "The hope was that it would form a strong contrast with the realistic film style presented earlier." Schedule: Three months.

records.description: Monika Kurek, ECD at BluBlu Studios in Warsaw, Poland: "WWF wanted to create a PSA for general brand awareness as part of a larger existing campaign called ‘Love it or lose it' but in general, we had a lot of creative freedom when it came to the visual language of the piece. "We had worked together with WFF a couple of times already, and they liked the work we had done but they also liked our approach to fluid transitions and organic shapes in some of our other projects. "The animation had to be universal, not too concrete or specific about a particular place. We had to think broadly and include places and animals from all around the world. "Also, the animation was supposed to show the effects of climate change, but not scare the viewer. On the contrary, its goal was to convince people to take action. "I believe we found the right balance, not only through deliberate design but also with the composition of beautiful music specifically for the piece. "The animation was based on a poem, which shifts from topic to topic very quickly, so we had to find a solution for seamlessly transitioning from scene to scene. Also, combining After Effects animation with frame-by-frame is always a challenge so it looks right." Schedule: Three months.

records.description: ManvsMachine laid aside their usual digital toolkit to celebrate Samsung's semiconductor development, creating a fully in-camera process using a scanning electron microscope to film nanoscopic 3D-printed models. From the team at ManvsMachine: "The task was to create a series of dioramas, depicting different uses of semiconductors. "They were to range from the ordinary to the extraordinary, but all needed to be physically produced in incredible, super miniature detail. "The result is a ground-breaking live-action film featuring 3D-printed models on a nanoscopic scale and captured using a one-of-a-kind scanning electron microscope (SEM). "Together with microfabrication pioneers Nanoscribe, we used a cutting edge 2GL® 3D printing technique, based on Two-Photon Polymerisation, to fabricate a series of microscopic sculptures depicting various applications of semiconductors. "From everyday moments like making a video call, or playing a video game, to life-saving inventions and space exploration; every microscopic model depicts a different incredible technology that wouldn't be possible without the ‘micro-miracles' that are semiconductors. "The models were so small they could not be captured with a traditional film camera. "So, we enlisted the help of scientific photographer Stefan Diller who used his pioneering Nanoflight® system to painstakingly recreate the camera moves from our animatic, frame-by-frame, at a nanoscopic level. "The result was giving the microscopic world a sense of cinematic style that has never been seen before in commercial filmmaking."

records.description: Alexandra Kotova, Producer at Media.Work in Los Angeles: "Proclaiming its mission to improve skin health backed by science, SkinCeuticals invited us to create a series of visualizations showcasing the brand's core message. "Our task was to integrate the unique benefits of the products and communicate the essential tenets based on research and innovation. "Talking about the creative challenges of the project, we aimed to connect the power points of medical procedure, science, and the product's advantages. "In drawing a strong visual thread between these components, we developed a set of metaphors to demonstrate a clear commitment to research and evidence-based validity. "With the formulas of the brand's primary products in our arsenal, we dedicated ourselves to an extensive visual exploration to highlight the uniqueness and active action of each of them but staying within a consistent visual language of the entire series. "We used Houdini and Redshift which allowed us to build our working tools and move our imagination into digital reality. Regarding the hardware, we used our own render farm which includes more than twenty machines." Schedule: Two months.

records.description: Mike Wigart, Senior Producer and Brian Burke, CG supervisor at JAMM Visual in Culver City, CA: "JAMM has a long history of CG creature work with agency David&Goliath dating back to the Kia Hamster commercials (Stash XXX). "This script called for photorealistic Raccoons in a live-action setting, but animated and anthropomorphized to feel and emote like humans. Ultimately, the client wanted to retain as much ‘sweetness' between the two characters as possible. "Working with director Chris Balmond, we put extra emphasis on capturing human stand-in characters to nail the raccoon performances. "We worked hard in animation to strike a balance between the stand-in and animated character performance while pushing the render quality towards realism at every step. "The nature of finding the look of the male and female heroes of the spot meant that they had to be developed in parallel, so each incremental improvement would apply to both characters while their fundamentally different nature of appearance would also be preserved. "This led to a large amount of complexity in the fur grooming, that we needed to separate from the lighting scenes to maximize performance and keep our lighting scenes from grinding to a halt. "Using Houdini's node-based grooming tools, keeping every aspect of the grooming procedural, including the fur texturing, and caching the results down to geometry files before passing to lighting helped to manage that complexity and avoid slow iteration times or maddeningly complex lighting files. "Post-production can be a grind (as many Stash readers know) but sometimes a project comes along that's a joy from start to finish, reminding us why we got into this business in the first place. This is one of those projects." Schedule: Three months.

records.description: Dan Marsh, director at Hornet in New York: "FCB's brief was a story about two Christmas ornaments in love. When they're hung on the tree and separated, they go to great lengths to get back together. "They also wanted an animation style that stood out from the sea of CG holiday films. "We were packing a lot of story in a short time frame. The film balances patiently creating an emotional connection with the audience while also getting across the many attempts and rising stakes of their tries to reconnect. "And of course, it all has to be told with pure visuals. Additionally, our style meant rethinking a traditional production pipeline. Our characters are all hand-animated in 2D, with varying frame rates to mimic the hand-crafted feel. "But these two-dimensional characters were then placed in a 3D cinematic space with much grander camera moves. "There's a balance of classic 2D approaches to communicate perspective or depth, as well as realistic 3D approaches with real-world lensing and lighting. "Each shot almost had to have a bespoke approach, and we had to have our environment painters, animators, and CG lighters working in parallel to meet the timeline. "In a spot like this, the creative and the technical are really in sync. "Our goal was to create a process that allowed for the hand of artists to be felt in the work, so our communication and pipeline became the technical backbone to make that process work. "Our pipeline team had to create a fluid connection to get multilayered, hand-animated assets into Maya so they could be lit as if existing in dimensional sets. "And with so many moving pieces and unique hands in each shot (from painting ornaments to tree branches, to characters, to camera work, and finally compositing) everybody on the team had to remain in sync to make the final result come together. "What makes this spot a triumph is its perfect imperfection. "Our great tools let us work faster and (sometimes) smarter, but the real story is having an inkling of an idea, crafting a visual story around that, and then getting amazing artists and allowing them to work the way they do. "This is a film made by people working together, and you can see their hands in the end result." Schedule: Four months.

records.description: Led by directors Kun Chang and Fabien Fulchiron, Tonic DNA in Montreal re-teams with grocery retailer IGA and agency Sid Lee to conjure a grandfather's magical story of Mr. Beaver and how he came to share his favorite holiday dessert. "Other challenges included creating the characters and balancing how they feel real but also like they could be the girl's stuffed animals. "Also, creating the stop-motion look to really create a difference between the tale and the reality took a lot of time and brain power. "Everyone was invited to imagine the backstories of the characters and the directors let everyone on the team embrace the project and bring something to the table." Schedule: Five months.

records.description: Eddie van Rensburg, ECD at Wicked Pixels in Cape Town, South Africa: "The brief was to construct an extremely cold testing facility in the South Pole where outlandish yet logical experiments highlight the ‘More Than Warmth' benefits of Nike's winter jackets. "Each section of the film had to showcase specific tests for jacket attributes including being warm, breathable, waterproof, and lightweight. records.description: Jorge Montiel Meurer, animation director at The Mill in London: "At the heart of this campaign lies our protagonist, a photo-realistic CG pig asking the question that tugs at our ethical compasses: ‘Do you think that I think?' "This simple yet profound query is the gateway to an exploration of the abilities and intelligence possessed by pigs. "Our journey began with an extensive research phase. We delved into the lives and behavior of real pigs to understand their movements, expressions, and anatomy. We closely observed various pig breeds to ensure accuracy and realism. "The first step in bringing our CG pig to life was creating a 3D model. This involved sculpting the pig's digital form and paying meticulous attention to anatomical details. "We crafted two different looks; a young, healthy appearance for the first part of the film and a dirty, sad look for the final reveal. "Animating our hero pig was one of the most challenging aspects. We had to convey complex emotions and thoughts while maintaining realism. "We used reference videos of real pigs to replicate their movements, and our animators spent countless hours fine-tuning the character's gestures, expressions, and eye movements. "In the end, the creation of our pig was a labor of love, driven by our passion for storytelling and our commitment to raising awareness about animal cruelty."

records.description: Sil van der Woerd and Jorik Dozy, directors/founders at Studio Birthplace in The Netherlands: "The goal with this film was to expose the criminal attitude of fossil fuel companies like TotalEnergies who greenwash their dirty business by sponsoring major sporting events like the Rugby World Cup 2023. "We also had to connect with rugby fans and Rugby World Cup spectators and reach them as a new audience. Don't crash their party. Ease them into the message. Use rugby codes and lingo. "Speaking to a broad range of audiences was important, such as Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, France, UK, Argentina, etc. while potentially using the stadium as an inspiration for an animated video. "We had made the film "Wasteminster" (Stash 148) for Greenpeace UK two years earlier and we felt that film established a very effective visual language – visualizing big data dropped onto mannequin dummies combined with a humorous voice over. "When we read this brief for TotalPollution, we immediately felt it was an opportunity to continue that language. "So, we decided to re-create the Stade de France, fill it up with over 80,000 mannequin dummies and rugby players, and unleash a stadium full of crude oil onto them. "The biggest challenge was to create the massive oil simulations that had to dynamically interact with the crowd and the players. "Some of the simulations contained North of 1.5 billion voxels (3D pixels), which required lots of computing power and patience. "Through precise planning, being smart about recycling simulations, and digital storyboarding, the team was able to complete these massive simulations within the deadline and with a very minimal crew. "The film was leaked before its official release and spotted by both The Rugby World Cup and TotalEnergies, who threatened legal action and a ‘cease and desist'. "This fueled the story to the press. The film hit local television in Australia, New Zealand, France, and the UK (BBC). International media in over 25 countries covered the film."
