records.description: Aurélien Thomas, director/animator in Lyon, France: "The main goal of this video was to promote the launch of the product on the client's pre-order website and social media. "There were three main challenges. The first was to explain the concept of a modular kitchen which is new to most people. "The second was that the client wanted very ‘high end' visuals, inspired by luxury brands and fashion campaigns. "The last and I think the biggest challenge, is there was not really any storyline or storyboard at the beginning of the project which led to many big changes to the story and visuals before settling on the version you see here. "The biggest technical challenge was to be efficient with my time because the client's budget was pretty small and the deadlines were tight. "Most of the time on the project was spent on visual research (about a week, part-time). "The animation was pretty quick (around two days). Then post-production/editing and sound design went pretty smoothly in about two days. "This project was very interesting because I had a lot of creative freedom. The idea of combining two different films in one (orange and natural/cold) color came when I saw that the client had a hard time deciding between the two options during the research phase. "Even if this kind of project with smaller clients has a reduced budget, I tend to always accept them because this is how you can attract bigger clients and more profitable projects in the long run."

records.description: Director Shane Griffin in New York City: "The core concept was to visualize the birth and construction of the new Mercedes GLC, using the fundamental elements that make up the car; glass, chrome, electricity, etc. "These elements, densely packed together, burst out like the Big Bang that started the universe. "We've seen a lot of very technical constructions of cars and products as of late, so creatively we were searching for a novel approach to build the car, at a pace that felt natural, not overly technical, and not rushed. "It's a fine balance when you're trying to fit the entire thing into 30 seconds, so we did a lot of R&D on effects to find the right pacing. "We also worked hard establishing a very bespoke palette for all the shots, so the live action and CG shots melted together with the same romanced lighting. "We established a look for this prior to the shoot and created a scene in Unreal Engine to use as the backplate for our virtual production shoot, which, luckily we got a near-perfect match for on our location day. "We developed a couple of different approaches for the fluid look of the car paint surface, such as VDB, Pyro, and opacity-based techniques. "During the shoot, we actually did strip a car down entirely to just the exoskeleton and the wheels, the Mercedes engineer who was driving it sat on an apple box. "The schedule was roughly eight weeks, including the two-day shoot in LA – one location on an old missile silo site, and another on the Orbital virtual stage."

records.description: With a wink to Pixar's groundbreaking 1986 short film Luxo Jr., the VFX team at The Mill in Paris and Bangalore create a curious CCTV camera character for this Peugeot E-308 spot directed by Mark Jenkinson at Movie Magic. Michael Girod, CG supervisor at The Mill: "Our mission was to tell a love story between the camera and the new Peugeot. "We treated it like a short animated film with a sympathetic story including 32 shots to rig and a unique and endearing character to create from scratch. A pleasure for a CG enthusiast! "Very quickly our inspiration turned to Pixar classics that spoke to us. We created several CG asset mock-ups to validate the modeling, rigging, textures, and shading. "We wanted a friendly, emotive camera with a slightly weathered look without it looking dirty or obsolete. We managed to give the camera life and personality without creating a cartoony asset. "During the shoot, the idea of printing the camera model in 3D quickly became obvious and enabled us to work more efficiently. "Added to this work on the camera were many environmental details that served the script, such as rain, water on the camera, reflections, etc."

records.description: Lightening up cancer-related projects is always a tricky balance to strike but director Kristian Andrews and the Studio AKA animation team nail it for the Scottish DCE program with this gaggle of eccentric yet empathetic avians. records.description: With a combination of CG and macro cinematography, Paris creative digital agency I-réel expands its portfolio of luxury product films with this intimate and intricate work for venerable Swiss watchmaker Baume & Mercier. ​​​​​​​ Simon Ravet, director and lead motion designer at I-réel: "The Riviera watch is inspired by the French Riviera mood: sea, sun, and the art of living on the Côte d'Azur. "In addition, each collection of the brand uses its own design. Our objective for this film was to link those two universes, one from the maritime world and the other astronomical, with different textures. "This project is completely post-produced in 4K resolution. The Moonphase images were shot with our RED 8K camera in our in-house studio, coupled with our motion-control robot. CGI sequences were created with 3ds Max and V-Ray. "The film is divided into four parts, where each texture highlights a specific detail of the watch. For the opening we created small pebbles, reminding us of the lunar surface, pushed back by an invisible object, emitting light, and recalling the different moon phases. "In the second part, we focus on the dial, which is encircled by a thin blue disc. Closer, blue streaks stand for the movement of the waves. It took us lots of experiments to create this texture, associated with a ripple animation to represent the sea. "The rendering is of a subtle softness, and the light hangs perfectly on the fringe waves. "You can't talk about the Riviera without mentioning water. For this part, we created a transparent outer dial but kept the indexes (the hour indication markers) in steel. Then we poured water into this cylinder. "The idea was to see the liquid bouncing in that shape and create a structure halfway between an art installation and science fiction, where gravity would not exist."

records.description: Salvatore Giunta, founder/CD and Claudio Gasparollo, senior designer at Ditroit in Milan, Italy: "Hublot asked our studio to highlight the new Big Bang Meca-10 Black Magic 45mm through bold and minimalistic imagery, dark tones, neat lighting, and contrasty images. "They also suggested introducing a clean industrial environment as the ideal setting for the watch. Red lasers and neon lights could be another touch to allow for more evocative and engaging storytelling. "We really wanted to lead the company into embracing a more editorial kind of aesthetics, where 3D photorealistic renders could blend seamlessly with flat colors and silhouettes – typical elements of an illustrative approach. "This was a bit different compared to the usual Hublot communication style, but somehow we managed to get the right balance between the different elements. "This was the first time for us using very complex 3D watch CAD models so it took a significant amount of time to organize and learn how to manage the endless number of pieces. "Even nowadays, flexibility and updatability are still touchy topics, an ongoing and ever-learning process. Moreover, the overall render time was very long, since the required output quality forced us to crank up the render settings quite a bit. "The production schedule lasted approximately three months, spread between the concept adjustments, an initial R&D phase, a more advanced production period, and the very last finalization."

records.description: Ambassadors ECD Justin Blyth in Amsterdam: "The BMW XM is a high-performance hybrid SUV that breaks from tradition, so it's only fitting that its launch commercial is equally as daring. "The film is narrated by, composed by, and features six-time Grammy-nominated musician Christian Scott, also known professionally as Chief Xian aTunde Adjuah. "All visual symbols such as the throne of trumpets, piano tied by balloons, clouds, lightning, crown, and breaking mirror were designed and created by the Ambassadors design, animation, VFX & 3D teams. "I particularly love the crown, which was built by unfolding and rearranging parts of the BMW rim". "VFX supervisor Bas Moonen led the team in ensuring the CG was as hyper-realistic and beautifully lit as possible. He also helped ensure there were easter eggs of details throughout. "While on set, Bas noticed that Chief's trumpet had a unique engraving. So we asked if he'd be up for seeing this in his trumpet throne, and when he was, so we captured as much reference imagery on set as possible to incorporate it into the CG. "Other details include the mirror break, which splinters into the pattern of the uniquely sculptural BMW XM roof liner. This was about a fine balance between keeping to this geometric pattern design and also keeping the glass break believable. "Shaping the clouds was also a challenge, as we had to ensure they had the right sense of scale. There's a fine line where it can become too much like thick smoke, or lose too much detail if it becomes transparent. But we feel like we achieved that dreamlike, ‘in the clouds feeling. "The process with the whole team involved was about as collaborative and inspiring as it can get. In the end, a thousand little choices and tweaks multiplied exponentially to create this film."

records.description: Jack Seymour, creative lead at Found in London: "The product range is a collaboration between Devialet and The Palais Garnier Paris, so our brief was to combine the luxury of the Opéra de Paris with the contemporary forms of the Devialet speaker range. "Materiality and color were to be used to add cues from the interior of the Palais Garnier opera house which we could use to build a world that suggested architectural form, rather than an explicit rebuild of the venue. "Premium is the keyword here. Premium materials add up to a premium product that delivers a premium audio experience. "Ensuring the high-end aesthetic of the Devialet product range came across without being able to showcase its primary feature, the amazing sound quality was certainly a challenge. "Visually, we wanted to showcase the product's elegance and class, while hinting that under that flawless surface, there's harmony between the many innovative parts, that are both functional and beautiful. "Building the mechanics of the product plinths to feel elegant, complex, and technical took time and effort. Each plinth has a unique way of moving, all based on time, to reveal the inner workings. "Additionally re-creating the unique PUSHPUSH mechanic of the woofers (placed on either side of the products) had to be matched accurately so we used the real products at high volume to observe the way in which audio physically affects the speaker." Schedule: Seven weeks.

As to the final result of this film, the feeling of scary and powerful are so close to each other that we made several tests on lighting, to avoid the feeling of scary. records.description: Nexus director Johnny Kelly melds stop-motion, 2D facial animation, and the talents of UK puppetmaster Andy Gent into a message advocating conscious consumption for renewed devices marketplace Back Market. Johnny Kelly: "The script was already very funny so my job was to not mess it up. "The first challenge was the monster itself, and the creatives at Back Market were open to ideas about how it could look, generously giving us full license to go odd. "Advertising is chockablock with furry monsters so we wanted to create something that stood apart. Given that our monster is the embodiment of tech over-consumption, it made sense to make him out of tech itself. "He started out as a pencil scribble with legs, then I did this initial sketch for the pitch [see images] and he didn't change much since. "Live-action puppetry felt like the right choice to capture the unstable energy our performance required. "The way Andy Gent and his team fabricated him – with all sorts of loose cabling – means you immediately get lots of ‘free' wobbly movement, compared to say CG or stop-motion animation. "This bubbling freneticism is an important part of his personality, so you feel like he might unravel at any moment, literally and figuratively. "In order to accentuate this effect, Andy made each cable out of light silicone tubing, with handmade weighted plugs hanging on the ends. "To do all the actions required, Monster needed a team of puppeteers. One to operate his eyes, another on his body and mouth, and one to move his arms. "This immediately dictated the scale of the character as he needed to be big enough that three pairs of arms could get around him. "The knock-on effect of this larger-than-expected-scale however, meant that his lair set would need to be gargantuan. "Thankfully our technical leads at Nexus devised a system whereby we could create the background sets at 50% scale, shoot them separately and drop them in behind our monster performance in post-production. "The production crew also hand-built 20+ puppets, including three versions of the Monster. "We used photogrammetry to capture the sets, puppets, and props to help with previsualization and develop faster turnarounds for compositing – enabling the animation team to quickly visualize in a 3D space how the 2D animation will track onto the real-life puppet's face."

records.description: NOMINT follows up their 2021 WWF stop-motion ice spot (Stash 151) with an even more improbable effort using fire in this global campaign designed to raise awareness about the danger of wildfires caused by climate change. NOMINT founder/CD Yannis Konstantinidis: "Launched during the 2022 COP27 climate change conference, the film was shot entirely in-camera and used traditional stop-motion techniques together with slow-motion, timelapse, and long-exposure to create the visuals. "We struggled for months to find a way to use the natural properties of real fire in a way that conveys the devastation of wildfires. Fire is destructive and remorseless, both in real life and on the stop-motion set. "We ended up walking a very thin line where the whole project was on the edge of literally going up in flames, creating a level of jeopardy that is hopefully conveyed in the story."

records.description: Dan Gregoras, CD at BUCK in New York: "Our frequent collaborators at Microsoft needed a campaign for their new Surface laptops and they approached us with the desire to evoke a sensorial journey. "This new iteration of the Surface is loaded with precise and thoughtful new design features, each requiring a chapter within the film. "So we conjured up some visual metaphors and packaged them into a smooth, ASMR-style film. "The goal was to capture the features touch, power, and sound of Microsoft's Surface through natural and organic elements that appeared as a mix of both technological and raw materials. "The blend of 3D and live-action gave us the freedom to explore this mix as we composed abstract, magical moments in the design process. This was an exciting reimagining of the product's main features. Eventually, we fused them together with a human perspective for the live-action sequences. "Some of the primary challenges were defining those metaphors to pack into the film. Figuring out the right combo of visuals required a huge lift from a squad of ace designers during the front end of the production. "There were a few technical challenges but the one that comes to mind immediately was solving for the foam keyboard sequence. "The new keyboard is super quiet and we knew we wanted to use the sensory feeling of pressing foam for the metaphor. It took almost one hundred iterations to get the material and texture to feel right. "Getting the light and color effect was quite a wormhole too. We explored a range of trippy vibes and ultimately landed on something subdued and elegant." Schedule: 10 Weeks.

records.description: Anders Schroder, CD/co-founder at Frame in Copenhagen, Denmark: "As time passes and we live our busy city lives, our skin ages prematurely due to the pollutants that it absorbs. "This line of Zhiben products contains antioxidant properties that protect the skin by neutralizing these free radicals before they get absorbed. This was the story the client wanted us to tell in a metaphorical way. "We wanted to visualize the concept of ‘protection' which inspired us to create the visual metaphor of letting the rose petals catch the bottles as they were falling from the sky. "Rose petals exude a sense of delicate serenity and beauty. They are velvety and lush so they were ideal for playing the role of the ‘protectors' as the rose extract is also a part of the actual product. "The light in the scene is hard and directional to symbolize the harshness of the environment that the Zhiben product is protecting us from. "The entire film feels as if it is in slow motion but the lights and the shadows that are being cast move unnaturally fast, again to illustrate time passing. "All of this is packaged into a gentle and soft expression that resonates with the brand's usual communication and attitude. "What sets this film apart in our view, is the graceful and evolving flow of the editing and animation and the overall soft and gentle feel of the film. "The shader of the rose petal was extremely difficult to nail. It could very easily look like human skin which made it quite gross. "It was extremely minor details such as tiny adjustments of the hue, making the edges of the petal ultra-thin, and more subtle veins in the leaf that shifted the expression dramatically from human skin to rose petal." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Helen Randall, producer at Builders Club in London: "We were brought on board to direct, shoot and produce the campaign with an objective to appeal to new runners or those looking for a suitable trainer to help them push to a new goal. "The Cloudgo is an affordable, comfortable, energy-boosting shoe that will help kick start any journey so Builders Club and On Running sought to create more than just another product film. "The idea was to merge the runners' urban journey with a gaming aesthetic and experience. This core idea struck our team as the ideal metaphor for showcasing the Cloudgo's unique technology and ability to level up and achieve your goals. "We really liked the idea to look at all the things that go wrong in video games and applying that to the real world in a stylized way. "Basically messing up our runner's environments to the point where it becomes an Escher-esque landscape where nothing makes much sense anymore. "What really excited us early on was our tests with 360 cameras and the seamless integration of CGI. "Playing with the typical 360 camera aesthetic and its possibilities and using the technology in a new context was one of the most challenging things in the whole process yet also one of the most rewarding ones. "On Running was a dream client to work with, we had a really dynamic, open brief to play with, incredible mutual trust, and a team of creative minds all eager and open to creative exploration – pushing outside of the usual brand approach to create a surreal depiction that is still rooted in reality."

"Playing with the typical 360 camera aesthetic and its possibilities and using the technology in a new context was one of the most challenging things in the whole process yet also one of the most rewarding ones. "On Running was a dream client to work with, we had a really dynamic, open brief to play with, incredible mutual trust, and a team of creative minds all eager and open to creative exploration – pushing outside of the usual brand approach to create a surreal depiction that is still rooted in reality."

records.description: Shane Griffin Director at AKKURAT Studios in New York: "What differentiated this brief from the run-of-the-mill commercial is that it was more of a question than a directive – What is Forwardism? "My role was to visualize a transformative art movement that defies convention, a metaphor for how BMW approached the engineering and design of the 7. "The main challenges from the creative side were re-thinking a series of classic artworks, transforming them into something completely unexpected, through this lens of Forwardism. "Each artwork's transformation had to be unique to them, amplifying their concept, construction, and composition. "With Mannerism (Vertumnus - Giuseppe Arcimboldo) I had this idea of transforming the fruit and veg depicted in the painting into a larger-than-life installation, where they cascade into the frame, allowing our talent to walk through the new dimensional composition. "With the sculpture (Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss - Antonio Canova) I employed a technique from a body of work I created last year, Reinterpretations, which remixed forms of classical sculptures. It felt like the perfect opportunity to reimagine this 3D form as a four-dimensional moving structure. "With Impressionism (Woman with a Parasol - Claude Monet), emphasizing the flowing form of this style of painting seemed like the perfect solution. "Impressionism paintings have these feelings of motion to them like a turbulent noise flow is driving the paint stroke direction, so I wanted to pop that off the canvas. "Impressionism was all about capturing ordinary subject matter, so my idea was to capture the museum-goers as little snippets of everyday life, and have these impressionist brush strokes swirl and flow around them. "With Dali, I knew we needed to end on a bang. And Dali being the master of surrealism, it had to be more than just an effect. So, I designed a room and modeled the Persistence of Memory as a sculptural form. "We built and painted this for real, and created the subtle melting effect in post, with a mix of mesh warps, and Houdini flip sims on photogrammetry. "For the BMW cars, we needed a futuristic backdrop that felt like it ignored conventional architecture, something with organic shapes, one that was minimal and had a dramatic wide shot. "I found the Champalimaud Foundation building in Lisbon, Portugal, and knew right away this was the backdrop for Forwardism. "Technically we had a lot to shoot. We had three camera units, Main, B, and Drone. Four cars, interiors, exteriors, detail shots, running shots, and multiple locations in a busy city. It was a complex jigsaw puzzle for production. "We shot over five days. Our post schedule for the main spot was eight weeks. Prior to the shoot, we did two weeks of previz and design exploration to visualize."

records.description: Directors Yves Geleyn and Michael Thurmeier at Hornet in New York: MICHAEL THURMEIER: "When I came on to the project, the agency had two ideas: in the first idea, an old dining table that had seen many family dinners was discarded by its original owners and then taken in by a new family. "The other idea was about a recipe book that could take a person back in time when they tasted the food. Yves and I gravitated toward the recipe book right away, and we agreed the best way to tell this story would be an emotional journey about how food brings a family together. "Early in the writing process, Jack's wife hadn't passed away, and he found the recipe book up in the attic while scrounging for holiday decorations. He then brought it down and they relived old memories together. "But it just didn't go far enough, and we thought it would be so much more powerful if Jack was on his own, missing his wife, and reveling in the opportunity to relive their time together. "At first some people thought it would be too sad for a Kroger spot, but in the end, that emotional thread is what makes it so heartwarming. "Through Jack and Isabela's story, we are reminded that as life goes on, we have special ways of keeping our loved ones with us." YVES GELEYN: Our goal was to find a sweet spot, emotionally. After iterating with different casts, more joyful scripts, and even more sad scripts, the final version struck a perfect balance. "We wanted to make it relatable to the viewer, emphasizing the importance of living the moment and placing the magic of family meals at the core. "Our biggest challenge was to hit so many different emotions in the run time we had, without anything feeling underdeveloped or over the top." MICHAEL THURMEIER: "After the story was established, the next big hurdle was getting this giant narrative into a 60-second film. "We realized that 60 seconds meant rushing through the acts too fast, and losing the connection to the characters, so we expanded the film to 78 seconds and tried to remain clean and efficient with the shots and performance. "But we also pushed for a high level of character performance, spending a lot of time nuancing the expressions and subtlety. "We really wanted the performance to be more elevated and cinematic than what Kroger has done in the past. "A huge challenge was finding a way to honor the original Kroji character designs while bringing their look to the next level. "To get the kind of expressiveness we were going for meant restructuring and adding new detail to the faces, hands, and bodies. "Everything from the rigs, the hair groom technology, and the details in skin texture was upgraded to push the overall quality of the characters. "The hair was a challenge, and right up until the last few days before we delivered, there were technical glitches in the eyebrows (which doesn't sound like much but it affected the expressions of Jack and Davi in their big emotional moment together)." YVES GELEYN: "Animation is about patience and bringing things to life over the course of many steps. We developed the script over a couple of weeks after receiving the brief, tightening the script, and making the story resonate. "Once we felt strongly about it, we dove into designing the world and timing out the story in a storyboard animatic. There was a lot to develop since we were recreating multiple time periods of the hero's house, and we wanted the changes to feel grounded in the design of each decade. "Mike Knapp, our art director, did a terrific job matching styles, from kitchen appliances to wallpaper designs, from each of the time periods. "Once the storyboard was locked, we dove into 3D previs, we set all the framing, the camera movement, and blocked some basic character poses to make sure everything worked. "In parallel, the team was modeling and texturing the approved character and environment designs. Our animation team took over the rigging of all our characters to get them ready for animation. "The next phase was to animate the spot and start updating all the models in the set. Once everything was in place, we started rendering the shots one by one with all the textures and details. The final phase was to comp all the shots and bring in the final touch of magic to the spot. "From the initial brief to delivering the final film, it took four months. Here's a breakdown: Story ~ 500 hours Animation ~ 1500 hours Model Look Dev ~ 2700 hours Lighting and Comp ~ 3500 hours Render ~ 50,000 hours."

records.description: Maldita, Directors at The Youth in Curitiba, Brazil: "We got a briefing from the agency with the mission of producing 12 spots that would show a bit of the brand's history and values in a lucid way. "We made each spot with a different theme like the brand origin, how it became a global brand, how it reached the fashion world, and its goal to spread the Brazilian way around the globe. "Along with the 12 films, we made this bigger version encompassing everything. "Also, we needed to show a bit of how the product is made, talking about sustainability and reuse of material. And with all the most symbolic theme's from the Havaianas universe, like football (soccer), beach, surf, and summer. "One challenge was passing along the sensations that Havaianas carries within it. It's an iconic Brazilian brand, and everyone here has a different feeling associated with it. "We chose a mixed media approach between 2D and 3D animation, giving a touch of reality while still having the freedom of passing some sensorial imagery to the viewer. "We needed to show the product up close with all its details in 3D while finding a way to make it fit the narrative and add to the 2D visuals that we were going for. Making both techniques fit into the same mood was by far the biggest challenge. "From the green light to final delivery we worked for six months on this project and there were times we were working at five spots at the same time."

records.description: From the team at BOL in Barcelona, Spain: "We teamed up with the MNSTR agency to create a special campaign for the launch of three new Adidas x Real Madrid official jerseys. "The result is an epic story about confidence, resilience, and fair play coming alive in full anime style. "Starting from the synopsis provided by the agency, we developed a script brimming with adventure, magic, action, and football. "We worked with director 2Veinte, a new addition to BOL's roster, to create a dynamic animated short film with a challenging length and a quick turnaround. "The narrative was based on a mystery-solving structure: our three main characters go through a magical journey into a parallel universe, trying to solve the mystery of their football rivals' disappearance. "The key elements connecting the two worlds? The three Real Madrid jerseys which represent the past, the present, and the future. "Story-wise, we wanted our main character to overcome a recent failure that made her feel insecure after letting her teammates down – a very relatable feeling that can easily go beyond the pitch. "Our three main characters would evolve inside our story with only dialogue and a strong narrative to rely upon, as there was no additional voice-over to guide us through the film. "Style-wise we followed the agency's direction, designing an exciting mix of anime aesthetics and real-life elements that would strike a chord with the public. "We aimed to recreate a young supporter's world, paying close attention to the dialogue, clothing, surroundings, and their quirks in order to design characters and situations that could appeal to the team's fans, while also supporting the brand's needs. "The anime style also fit the football action scenes to a T, allowing us to enhance and exaggerate them, using the extreme dynamism typical of the Japanese style. "We used mainly cel animation to match these aesthetics and animate the very complex actions across the film, focusing on quick transitions and epic movements to create an immersive universe. "With no voiceover to guide us, we relied much more on music and sound effects to create the perfect atmosphere and enhance each scene. "By successfully mixing all these elements, from the anime visuals to the epic narrative, from the short film cinematographic approach to all the real-life elements and the talents involved, we managed to create a unique campaign launch for the brand, while also telling a compelling story for the team's supporters."

records.description: Anders Schroder, CD/Co-founder at Frame in Copenhagen, Denmark: "TAG Heuer has been synonymous with Formula 1 motor racing since 1971 so the creative challenge was to capture the thrilling suspense of F1 racing, depicted through the key features of the F1 Colours timepiece - all whilst celebrating the three distinct colorways. "First we needed to tackle the challenge of the device that was going to be the glue in the film. "We tried various ideas such as wind tunnel smoke, mechanical exploded views, and racing stripe patterns but quickly realized Tag Heuer had used most of these in earlier campaigns. "So, the only relevant idea left was using the idea of racing flags and banners. "We wanted to portray the race without being literal. We wanted to create something more sophisticated and conceptual so we identified iconic moments in F1 racing to serve as inspiration for the animation: pitstops, spin-outs, burnouts, collisions, finishing line crossings, cockpit POVs, etc. "At FRAME we always try to shave the idea down to its core essentials both conceptually and visually without unnecessary bells and whistles. "Therefore we decided to tell the story of an F1 race using only watches and flags in iconic racing situations. "For example, the scenario of a race car spinning out in the sandbox was told by having a watch twirl into a billowing flag which is much simpler and more elegant. We underlined these metaphorical shots with real-world F1 sounds. "The last step in creating the film was to string these metaphors together to form a rather linear narrative that would take the watches from the start lines, through various obstacles to the finishing line. "By far the biggest challenge was developing a sexy edit with its many ramped shots fitting together. "So we would time ramp in the editing and then once the edit was locked, we would go back into 3D and recreate these time ramps properly. The tricky thing was to combine this with all the cloth simulations in each scene." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Minna Griffiths, creative assistant at Optical Arts in London: "The agency Wonderhood Studios were launching a new brand platform for UK furniture maker MADE that focused on stepping away from the ordinary and embracing the distinctiveness and individualism of their customers. "One of the challenges of this project was combining the highly stylized set with the less rigid cinematic and narrative feel we were striving for – an atmosphere that was both playful and disconcerting without being too comedic or sinister. "We designed a series of bold and distinctive sets taking inspiration from modern showrooms and Memphis design as well as more traditional Victorian homes. "One of the biggest technical challenges was designing the fish head and bringing it to life as we had to make it fit on human shoulders and mimic the movements and facial expressions of the actor with our animation." Schedule: Six months.

"We designed a series of bold and distinctive sets taking inspiration from modern showrooms and Memphis design as well as more traditional Victorian homes. "One of the biggest technical challenges was designing the fish head and bringing it to life as we had to make it fit on human shoulders and mimic the movements and facial expressions of the actor with our animation." Schedule: Six months.

records.description: Julian Frost, director at Unlisted in Melbourne, Australia: "The spot is about making a kid's future hopes come alive for the viewer so that it's a bit of a gut punch at the end when you see that the kid may not have a future, and they know it. "We've all seen dying kid charity ads before, and although powerful they can sometimes feel a bit demoralizing. "We hoped that by showing the child's subjective interior reality we could tell a story with spirit and humor, and leave the viewer feeling motivated to save a life, rather than dispirited by loss. "The ad needed to feel genuinely childlike – to have the strangeness and naivety of a real kid's mind. If it felt like an adult putting a story in a child's mouth it would seem forced and/or maudlin, and the child would feel generic rather than a specific kid. "Of course, in reality, the ad was made by a bunch of craggy middle-aged guys, but we tried hard not to lose the spontaneity and weirdness of the earliest off-the-cuff drafts. "For instance, to get the right amount of looseness in the artwork I drew tiny designs on paper and enlarged them, wobbles and all. "Anything I tried drawing normal-size came out boring and right which was extremely annoying. "The spot is not complicated technically, but the choice was to begin rough animation almost from the beginning, and iterate a lot, rather than having distinct script/boards/design/animation phases. "That meant the animation could influence the script (which we continued workshopping well into animation), and the timing was locked before the design which helped me to judge the visual complexity required for different shots. "The animation was crummy Flash placeholder animation till the last stage, then I redrew all the assets in Procreate and replaced them. "I like to work this way but it requires 1) a trusting client because it all looks like a pile of junk right till near the end, and 2) Flash to not buckle under the weight of 100s of MBs of PNGs, which until a few years ago it was veeeerry prone to do." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: Taking inspiration from both surrealist and romantic artists, the BUCK crew mix painting, 3D, live-action, and a touch of machine learning into a series of reflective vignettes for wellness brand Thorne. From the team at BUCK: "Steering away from traditional supplement commercials' obsession with ‘anti-aging', we focused instead on an aspirational view of healthy aging that delivers a holistic lifestyle, rather than a cure. "Playing with scale and surrealism, we created a set of sublime environments for real people to inhabit as we told our story. The painterly textures and serene natural landscapes feel like a natural extension of the visual language that had been explored in our previous work for Thorne. "The paintings themselves set the tone for each of the scenes, meaning the 3D elements needed to feel integrated and embedded with each landscape. Matching lighting between the painted world and our 3D objects helped to unify each environment. "As well as modeling the products, we also used 3D to bring depth to landscape elements in scenes with dynamic cameras, adding parallax and a sense of depth where it was needed. We also used some cutting-edge machine learning (EBSynth) to apply our painted style to some complex elements, like clouds and water."

records.description: ManvsMachine's recent run of CG head-turners (see their Magnum "Remix" spot in Stash 154 and Mini "Elements" in Stash 153) continues with this spot for a portable speaker/handbag manufactured by luxury audio brand Bang & Olufsen and unveiled as a catwalk accessory at Balenciaga's 2022 couture show in Paris. records.description: Ellie Koepke, Marketing Manager at Found in London: "We were given initial storyboards from the client that loosely outlined what they wanted to achieve. This evolved during the initial previz phase, with additional concepts developed by our creative team. "One of the biggest challenges was translating the TV's complex technologies into an understandable and engaging film. "We used the natural world to relay the benefits of each technological feature, such as lightning for electrifying brightness, and a corolla of petals to symbolize its fast refresh rates. "We broke the film into chapters to retain the viewer's attention, with each chapter telling the story of a key technological feature in the TV; precision, brightness, quantum color, and refresh rates. "The original concept included a lot of organic growth, so dozens of bespoke flowers were needed. "We wanted to create these from scratch and so developed a system in Houdini to procedurally generate and grow the variations, ‘cross-breeding' coral and plants to create semi-sentient flowers." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.description: Renee Zhan, director at Blinkink in London: "Trolli wanted to make their ‘darkest ad yet' to celebrate the release of the new Sour Burstin Crawlers. "The film was to take place in a factory which ground up worms into goo to inject into the bodies of their wormy brothers. "We had so many ideas that we wanted to fit into this project. Narrowing them down so they would fit in the time constraints of two 15s was the most challenging part. "We really wanted to go big on this campaign, to make huge factory interiors and expansive worlds. We decided to use CG to create these huge sets, but we really wanted to maintain the handmade feel and texture of the previous ads. "We worked closely with Saurus, a brilliant Norwegian CG company, to replicate the look and feel of stop motion sets and puppets. "Trolli, Wieden+Kennedy, and Blink Ink have a long and beautiful history of collaboration. The first films were directed by Becky and Joe, then Sam Gainsborough. "The humor, irreverence, and craftsmanship in their films were so inspiring. Making a Trolli ad was a dream of mine since I first began in advertising. It was such a rich and fun universe to draw from and build upon." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: With help from Ponder director Tomas Jonsgarden, the creature VFX crew at Framestore, and Bonny Tyler, a pet reptile named Jeff goes walkabout (or vacuum-about) in this comic :60 for telco and internet provider Three Ireland. Framestore VFX Supervisor Jules Janaud in London: "It was a challenge to come up with something interesting that was real and comical. Jeff had to be believable but at the same time we needed to create something beyond the boundaries of realism." "On set, the team used a taxidermy bearded dragon for lighting references. In addition, they 3D-scanned each scene and captured as many references as possible to help reconstruct each shot environment. "Several shots were shot at high-speed, so it was tricky to ensure the animation felt real. Lizards move in a broken-up way and if you start slowing things down it doesn't always work well visually. "We had to find subtle elegant moves whilst ensuring Jeff remained looking like an authentic lizard, so we added some skin passes, such as rippled, deformation, and details on the spikes to move with the wind." "On set, the team used a taxidermy bearded dragon for lighting references. In addition, they 3D-scanned each scene and captured as many references as possible to help reconstruct each shot environment." Framestore lead animator Daniel Bielawski: "In order to illustrate Jeff's newfound lust for life, we built upon his generally relaxed posture and inserted some lizard-like head looks and eye darts to emphasize the comedy. "The parts that work best for me are when he's not in control – his entire body might lose grip on the slippery vacuum cleaner surface, but he still happily bumbles through the city streets!". "Alongside the creature work, the environment called for various digital matte paintings and backgrounds including some sky enhancement and adding buildings such as skyscrapers to heighten the vibrant city feel."

records.description: Nexus directors Alan Smith and Adam Foulkes return to Center Court at Wimbledon, following up their "Take On History" spot with an animated epic starring Emma Raducanu, Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer, and Serena Williams. Set to Summer Kennedy's track "Come Alive", the spot commemorates the 100th anniversary of the All England Lawn Tennis Club's relocation to its current Church Road venue. Smith & Foulkes: "This was the sort of creative brief that you dream of, taking a cherished national institution and completely re-imagining it as a vivid dream. "We looked at the iconic images of Wimbledon through a lens of surreal invention, packing every scene with unexpected twists, using a textural illustrative look and seamless transitions to create a fluid stream of consciousness. "It was a chance to paint a picture of Wimbledon that isn't all about the tennis, focussing as much on the iconic architecture and sense of social occasion, although there's obviously a fair sprinkling of the tennis greats along the way."

"CGI pasta fields and celestial bodies feature alongside real-life water and colorful clouds, all blended in with cosmic 2D backgrounds and 3D textures. "Colour, backgrounds, and lighting all had to be coherent in this abstract scenario. Lighting, for example, was carefully studied to achieve the right balance between space light (strong and directional) and flattering product light. "After skim-reading NASA's research on black holes and how light actually works in this phenomenon, we realized it wouldn't be possible to make a completely accurate physics model – cosmic pasta aside. "Therefore, to make it look realistic and to bridge the boundary between space and pasta, we had no option but to bend physics a little." Schedule: "The three months of pre-production, in which we were heavily involved, included a test shoot and allowed us to properly experiment with the creation of the visuals. The mix of 3D, 2D and in-camera work was fully developed and integrated in two months of post-production."

records.description: Albert Garcia, lead 2D artist at Glassworks in London: "The client wanted to present a friendly atmosphere with a good balance between the humor and the seriousness of a beer commercial. "The ad is therefore full of subtle comedic details that were incredibly fun to work on. For example, the friendly farmer robots, the angelical painting, or the David-like statue of Mads Mikkelsen. "Finding the right look for the robots was one of the main creative challenges for our team. "We needed to develop a farmer android that would look friendly and nonthreatening in a post-apocalyptic setting. So, we tested various expressions and looks until we found the one that suited the tone of the ad. "The ad features many different scenes and environments in a short period of time. They all had to be perfectly built and integrated, each one with different degrees of compositing and 3D. This meant that the on-set supervision and the VFX integration were a key part of the process "The Chamber scene was filmed in the impressive Rondel cellars in Barcelona. Our 2D and 3D teams built it up so that it would be reminiscent of the old Carlsberg brewery in Copenhagen. "The magnificent elephant sculptures frame the scene, and the Carlsberg logo and portraits subtly feature in the background."

records.description: Director Yves Geleyn and the CG animation team at Hornet carve out a timely and timeless story about a father and son, a homecoming, and the chance for new beginnings to mark the Chinese Lunar New Year. Yves Geleyn: "In Chinese culture, the Lunar New Year is the biggest, most important festival when the entire family comes together to reconnect, bond, and celebrate the beginning of the new year. "I thoroughly enjoyed getting lost in this project. Harmonizing the old with the new and surprising people with something at once familiar and completely unexpected. It was a fun journey." "I was ignited in my research by the wondrous and rich history of Chinese folk, art, sculpture, and culture and all of the different, yet recognizable ways they represent tigers. "Their shapes pushed into a more graphic world and their faces and stripes were made into complex patterns. Wooden marionettes and sculptures complemented the paint workings or differing wood grains." "One of the best aspects of this project is that almost everything was done in-house in Hornet's studio. It's always such a pleasure to have such a close-knit and talented team of artists working together. "And I'm very proud of the result — a nice mix of almost stop-motion style CG (led by Natalia Perez) and graphic and painterly texture."

records.description: Steve Mottershead, CD/owner at Artjail in New York: "The brief from the agency GS&P and Reset director Henry Scholfield was very ambitious. The concept was to show how trends come and go but Doritos has always been relevant and popular since it's been around. "The whole spot was planned to be a constant transition through all the fads and trends that have come and gone and some futuristic ones that haven't even happened yet. "So right from the get go we knew this one was gonna be both a creative and technically demanding project. "One of the biggest challenges was translating and executing the multitude of ideas that Henry was throwing our way. There are a staggering number of details packed into these 30 seconds, many which evolved and emerged along the way. Artjail head of 2D Lee Towndrow: "We love how many disparate cultural references Henry is able to tap and make them all fit. Aesthetics from the 70's, the 90's, 2000's on up to 2050 are in the mix and it all feels so natural. "The coda called for an entire future city which we built, replete with flying cars. "We referenced Bladerunner and Alita, two of our favorite films. "There were also a lot of additional details to finesse and pepper into this bonkers edit pulled off by the talented Sam Ostrove of Cabin Edit. Designer/CD Matt Greenwood:, "We kept pushing the motion graphics and adding lots of layers and it was a chance to be able to pull out all the stops." "There's so much visually going on throughout the spot, it was an interesting challenge to add to this look and it's fun for the viewer to catch all these crazy details. "Even though a lot of these crafted elements are only on screen for a quick moment, it adds a really rich overall feel to the piece. "The CG elements in the spot played a key role with the team providing a host of elements to help 2D and motion design blend certain shots together. "For example the blockbuster scene required a torrent of movies to fly up through the wormhole and a holographic transporter deck was also a CG lift. The goal was to help transform the final result into a better visual experience. Artjail lead CG artist Mark Ingle: "The creative workflow was unique in that it allowed many different interpretations of the glitch effects. A procedural approach in Houdini gave us the opportunity to quickly explore dozens of glitch styles in a short timeframe. "This was a true team effort and allowed us to use all the tools at our disposal; Creative and technical problem solving, 2D, CG, 360, motion design, matte painting, and color grading."

records.description: Miguel Wratten, 2D supervisor at Optical Arts in London: "Optical Arts worked with agency BBH to create this campaign for Refuge – a charity supporting victims of domestic abuse. "We were asked to create an unsettling campaign designed to raise awareness of how domestic abuse is evolving. We wanted to reveal how abusers are increasingly taking advantage of constant advances in technology. "The main creative challenge was making a film that appeared to be a simple tech advert but had a subtle sinister message behind it. "This required a clever and careful approach to the idea, tone, sound design, and visual details of the film. "Although the film references slick technology advertising, we wanted to have a realness, depth, and unsettling quality to the film. We did this by adding small imperfections which became more prominent as it progressed. "We added subtle marks, fingerprints, and scratches on the products to enhance the unsettling nature of the film. We also disrupted the camera moves by adding long pauses on single shots and stark lighting and color tints. "All these factors proved challenging to achieve but once complete, they created the uncomfortable feel to the film and drew attention to the danger of tech abuse – helping us get Refuge's message across. "We used Cinema 4D in the early product design stages. Once production started in CG, we moved to Maya to refine the CG models and the main package used was Houdini with Redshift. "For 2D we used Flame to composite followed by Da Vinci Resolve to bring all the shots together with color grading. "We designed the devices for both the print campaign and the film, taking care to create original pieces of technology; we then worked on elevating the lighting and camera movements in CG. For this we shot live-action references, to enhance the lighting in each CG shot."

"All these factors proved challenging to achieve but once complete, they created the uncomfortable feel to the film and drew attention to the danger of tech abuse – helping us get Refuge's message across. "We used Cinema 4D in the early product design stages. Once production started in CG, we moved to Maya to refine the CG models and the main package used was Houdini with Redshift. "For 2D we used Flame to composite followed by Da Vinci Resolve to bring all the shots together with color grading. "We designed the devices for both the print campaign and the film, taking care to create original pieces of technology; we then worked on elevating the lighting and camera movements in CG. For this we shot live-action references, to enhance the lighting in each CG shot."

records.description: With a labor-intensive mix of in-camera effects, 3D-printed stop-motion, and algorithmic CGI, Blinkink director Balázs Simon showcases "how Olympians push themselves to the extreme" for the BBC Winter Olympics coverage. Balázs Simon: "I really admire people having the will to push things to the limits. Especially the winter games where they compete in environments that are so different from our usual experiences. "When I got approached by this project, the biggest question for me was how to portray and live up to that dedication. A good way was to bring the film out to the real world. "Although most of my work is tied to digital animation, I'm most intrigued by the physical reality and the uncertainties that come with it. In a way, I wanted to find myself in a similar situation as the Olympians: in a foreign, unforgiving place that needs to be conquered. "This resonated well with our controlling idea: to be able to compete, these people must be made of something different. We wanted to portray them being born into ice and snow and eventually breaking out."

records.description: Sean Cochrane, VFX lead at The Vanity in Toronto: "Early in the project and before any footage was shot, director Mark Zibert engaged us to create a look for the 'darkness'. "Mark wasn't entirely sure what this should look like but he knew he didn't want it to feel VFX-y. He didn't want there to be any internal detail in the black. "So during our initial first rounds of look-dev we embraced an old school optical printer animation approach. In 2D perspective, we animated a reveal matte and filled it with pure black and overlaid it on the footage. "This was a conscious attempt to move away from super-slick fully integrated VFX utilizing fluid sims and other modern methods. "We liked how different this was and we also dug the throwback sensibility. It felt like something ILM would have done in the mid-eighties. "Unfortunately, even with foreground objects re-composited back over the animation, the resulting darkness effect always felt like it was happening on top of the plates and not inside the footage. "Although we liked the 2D flat quality, the lack of integration created a disconnect between the people and the impending darkness, which hurt the narrative. "We needed to find a way to integrate our 2D reveals of black into the footage while also retaining the pure black/lack of light idea. "Foreground roto helped sit the effect into the footage but the real eureka moment was having ambient light and flares spill around the darkness. We embraced the idea that light could leak around the edges of the darkness but it wouldn't ever reveal any detail. "In the end, we created a library of 2D 'creeping darkness' assets by utilizing shots of black ink flowing on white captured on an animation stand. "Although the ink comprised 85% of the elements used, there were times when it was just too ordinary and lacked a creepy alien quality we wanted. "So we did use a 3D fluid simulation but we rendered it flat on a 2D plane with no internal detail. This resulted in a strange milky tentacle-like quality that we pepped around in certain scenes. "Creating the darkness was definitely the biggest challenge but it wasn't our only one. When the kids fight the darkness, Mark wanted the kids to be holding these road flares as a weapon. "Mark shot the kids holding sparklers and we animated and rendered out the flares using Maya. We also gave them a smoke sim which really helped add a lot of believability and atmosphere. "We also had to create two huge crowds for a couple of overhead drone shots. For one we used a fully CG crowd with help from our friends at SHED in Montreal. For the other we utilized some shot footage of a few kids holding lights, rotoscoping, duplicating them, and composing them into an empty drone plate. "We created some Roman candle-style flares and ran a volume smoke simulation on these crowd shots to add atmosphere to them to give them some final touches. "The biggest challenge was the pure volume of shots. Initially, we scheduled the project anticipating finishing a 60-second spot with various cutdowns. Then we heard there will be a 90. "But when the edit settled in at 2.5 minutes we all called our significant others and told them we wouldn't be home for that month. "Each shot required a massive amount of work. The look we settled on was a complete 2D approach and required meticulously rotoscoping of each element. We layered in various ink elements at different scales and speeds to create an illusion of depth all while holding back every object in the shot and layering in their own ink elements. "Then we added the light leak look by hand to each element. In the end we had over 120 shots that all required a ton of work. "We had just under three weeks to finish the project. Which was just out and out crazy with the shot count sitting at around 120. "So simple math tells us we would only be able to dedicate 1-2 hours per shot, which of course is ridiculous with a project of this scope. In an effort to get ahead of this we sent out a massive amount of roto work and we had half of the shots camera-tracked to aid in layering in our 2D ink elements. "All of the people in these films are real. Every year doctors, nurses, hospital staff, parents and the kids all come out to be a part of these campaigns. "Being on set and watching Mark work with all of the people to create these films is like nothing else I've ever seen in my 20 plus years in this business. "I remember six years ago, Mark was setting up a wide shot depicting a line of kids and their parents running down a hill in a war charge with some actors dressed in full roman gladiator costumes. "It was very complicated, some kids were running with IV drip bags, some kids in crutches and in wheelchairs. This was the last shot of the day and they were losing light. "There were a couple of younger kids that were too sick to run and were really upset that they weren't able to participate. Mark didn't flinch, he stopped mid-setup and told these kids they weren't running because he needed them to stand with him behind the camera and say action and cut. "With one sentence Mark turned kids from feeling weak and sidelined to important and empowered."

records.description: Ten years after completing his culture-shifting stop-motion spot "Back to the Start" for Chipotle, Nexus director Johnny Kelly helms a sequel - updating and extending the conversation around sustainable farming for a more complex time. Johnny Kelly: "It's a rare opportunity to be handed the keys to a stop motion epic, so I was delighted to be able to get the band back together for a sequel. "I still love the simplicity of 'Back to the Start' but 10 years on the world is a more complicated place (to put it mildly) and it would have felt reductive to remake the last film. "In order to work in 2021 this needed further complexity and scale. More nuanced performance. More geographic authenticity. And more dog. At their heart however, the two stories complement each other; the last one was about animal welfare and the thrust of this story is human welfare." Set to a Coldplay cover by American Grammy-winner Kacey Musgraves, the two-and-a-half-minute spot includes 10 sets and 82 hand-made puppets.

records.description: Channeling the feel of classic stop-motion holiday specials, Nexus director Conor Finnegan crafts the warm and fuzzy tale of Tiptoe, a reindeer who overcomes a fear of flying when friends teach her to believe in herself. Conor Finnegan: "It was a pleasure to tell this Christmas tale for Macy's. I was lucky to collaborate with the best people working in stop-motion animation, from model and puppet makers to lighting, camera, and animators. "We went for a 'get as much in-camera as possible' approach and the results are something I'm really proud of. We've made a rich, warm, nostalgic - and hopefully - uplifting Christmas film." A giant inflatable version of Tiptoe will also feature in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on November 25 in New York.

records.description: The creative and production teams behind IGA's standout 2019 holiday film "Inseparables" (Stash 139) regroup for another animated heartwarmer for the grocery chain, this time fusing food, family, and hockey into a very Canadian tale. Animated by the CG crew at Mathematic, the 90-second film was directed by Bertrand Bey and Marie-Julie Dallaire through agency Sid Lee in Montreal. Sid Lee copywriter Mathieu Bouillon: "IGA's Holiday story is not only a long-awaited tradition but also an opportunity to produce a large-scale creation that's halfway between advertising and film. "Every time the story is shared on social media, IGA will contribute $1 in support of the Montreal edition of Scotiabank Girls HockeyFest, an event designed to make hockey more accessible to young girls and teach them valuable skills that will serve them well both on and off the ice."

records.description: Jon Hurst, managing director at nineteentwenty in London: "The brief was to enhance and help build a truly stunning cinematic piece of work; to work closely with the director and agency to bring the script to life. "In the early stages of the project, we worked closely with director Mark Molloy and a number of concept artists to design the spacecraft. "Once we had the ship designed, we then began building the craft in CGI, adding texture, finer details, and wear-and-tear. "A grey, full-sized physical version of the craft was then built and placed in the position that it would finally come to rest in the forest. This was a great practical prop for the Actors to interact with, climb on, shelter under and make their temporary home. "We also had to be mindful that the design of the spacecraft did not distract from our lead characters and their performances. "One of the biggest challenges for us was to make the forest feel like early evening in late December when, in fact, the shoot was done during the early afternoon in the middle of September. "This was done through a combination of digital matte paintings, color grading, and compositing. "It meant that we had to augment a large number of shots in the forest and treat them to look like December, reducing the amount of green and adding snow for the latter part of the film. "Our DMP artists provided matte paintings to our compositing teams that were then seamlessly integrated into the original live-action plates. "As the spacecraft has crashed on earth, another of our challenges was to create an entry path for the ship through the forest; again, we achieved this through a combination of CG, DMP, and compositing. "Due to the design process and the flexibility we wanted to maintain after the shoot, the practical craft that was on-set was grey and not textured like our final designs. That meant that we had to track and light and render a CG craft into every shot. "When compositing these shots, we added additional environmental elements like smoke and snow to help with realism; every shot featuring the ship was crafted and touched in post in some way. "Similarly, the shot of the boy looking out of the window was filmed in a studio. As such, we added Christmas lights, decorations, and houses in the distance, as well as general atmospheric snow to help the wintery feeling of the shot. "The schedule consisted of a nine-day shoot followed by four weeks for the concept and build of the ship as well as four weeks from the date of approval for all VFX and post. "Whilst on set, we Lidar-scanned the forest so that openings for entry, landing, and take-off sites could be created. And for the environments, we worked closely with the director and creatives to create DMPs and set extensions."

records.description: Working with Object & Animal directing duo Bert & Bertie, the Framestore creature crew ramp up the furry charm of an imaginary friend named Iggy in this holiday tear-trigger for McDonald's UK thru Leo Burnett. Framestore VFX supervisor Jules Janaud: "We had to create something that looks physical and not cartoonish, but at the same time find ways in the animation to bring out emotion and to communicate well with the girl at different ages. "Once the concept was locked, the team could start to pre-visualize scenes and design a life-size puppet of Iggy to be used on set, enabling actors to interact with the character and start to embed Iggy into the world. "The challenge was to create a character which performs enough to emote but doesn't stretch too much like a cartoon character. It had to have a lot of physicality, and this brought demanding technical work in the groom process and the creature effects area. "The character looks very naive and simple but on the other hand you want to feel that it could almost be someone in a costume, but you are not too sure. "One of the interesting things about the technicality of this job is that it's a very simple character but it has a lot of highly technical stuff going into it. "His fur is quite long and fluffy like mohair, his socks and horns are hand-knitted, his scales made of felt and he even has a tinsel tail. "All of these materials had to be meticulously designed and groomed using our own custom hair system generated in Houdini and all of these features had to be simulated individually to make Iggy physically believable."

records.description: André Osna, marketing manager at Final Frontier in Buenos Aires, Argentina: "We had a very open brief, calling for the use of Dia De Los Muertos celebrations as a backdrop for an acceptance and pride story, where it's never too late to be who you really are. "Working with CGI characters is always demanding, but in this particular case, finding a natural and intimate tone for the storytelling was our first objective. We knew we had to be as warm, empathic, and inviting as possible, but avoid it becoming childish. "We had to pay close attention to every line in the script, to be sure that not only was the character acting working perfectly but the lip-sync as well. "The film was released for the Mexican market as part of Doritos' #PrideAllYear campaign, created by agency Slap Global. "The push began with a Christmas spot last year, continued in a Mother's Day film and now makes its way to this sweet story for Dia De Los Muertos, the holiday celebrated in Mexican and Latin American communities to honor deceased loved ones." Schedule: 12 weeks.

records.description: Director Pete Candeland, his team from Partizan Studio, and new Bordeaux-based animation and VFX house LIGHT take a painterly approach to highlight the planet's wonders and Sky's pledge to be carbon-neutral by 2030. The anchor of a campaign by agency Engine Creative, the film was inspired by the Overview Effect, the profound experience astronauts have when they see the earth from space for the first time. Pete Candeland: "I had no trouble finding inspiration for this film, the world we live in is, of course, an inspiration above all else, and the beauty of our home is best enjoyed in person. "So without traveling all over the world to enjoy each location, we found the next best lens to view the world through; landscape painting. We brought the painter's point of view to this film, taking careful consideration of light, atmosphere, and color. "It was an absolute pleasure to be involved and put my mind to something of such significance." "We wanted to do something timeless and create a poem through our visual storytelling and landscape painting that also felt fitting as an applicable message to our current situation. It was an absolute pleasure to be involved and put my mind to something of such significance." Antoine Moulineau, LIGHT founder and VFX supervisor: "I was moved by this project from the very first brief and can't express how excited we were at LIGHT to take this on, especially within months of opening our studio's doors. "This project was also an opportunity for me to reunite creatively with Pete Candeland. I'm very proud of the work and dedication from our artists, particularly toward a project with such a crucial message to express."

records.description: Framestore Pictures' director Murray Butler and the Framestore creature VFX team resurrect a 70 million-year-old Utahraptor (voiced by Jack Black) to deliver a message about the dangers of fossil fuel subsidies and their contribution to our own extinction. Murray Butler, director at Framestore: "We studied the way great speeches were delivered in film and TV and approached this project with the same cinematic language. "We opted to use two cameras, which enabled us to covertly capture spontaneous reactions and cover action from a variety of levels and angles throughout the Hall. "The stirring musical score, our computer-generated dinosaur hero, and the UN staff members and delegates who volunteered their time to play the role of the audience each brought this incredible film to life for an important cause." Timed to air ahead of the COP26 climate change conference in Glasgow and driving viewers to dontchooseextinction.com, the spot was created for the United Nations Development Programme thru Activista in Los Angeles. From the UN release: "The world spends an astounding US$423 billion annually to subsidize fossil fuels. This is four times the amount being called for to help poor countries tackle the climate crisis. "UNDP is the leading United Nations organization fighting to end the injustice of poverty, inequality, and climate change. Working with our broad network of experts and partners in 170 countries, we help nations to build integrated, lasting solutions for people and planet."

records.description: Vincenzo Lodigiani, director at Dress Code in New York: "The client was looking for someone that could develop a series of films with a fresh and sophisticated aesthetic. "An approach that would combine minimalism and graphic compositions with a cinematic twist, given by the use of cameras and clever transitions. "With the unconventional choice of using animation, Porsche was aiming to enhance its own identity and to appeal to a younger demographic, with particular attention to the female audience. "Some of the creative choices we found in the brief gave us an indication of the world of references. Like the title of one of the 30', Gestalt, a word used both in psychology and in art to indicate the capacity of the human brain to recognize patterns and make associations. "From the beginning, we focused on finding interesting relations between elements, and the perception of space and depth from flat illustrated assets. "We used motion to achieve that, playing with transitions, negative space, and optical illusions. The result is a very dynamic piece, with a lot of flow and big shifts in scale. "We wanted the viewer's eye to be connected seamlessly and continuously from the beautiful design and details of the car to very dramatic shots of the landscapes, always playing on the edge between the physical world and the abstract and surreal. "Animating a beautiful car driving recklessly through abstract scenarios is basically my dream task as a director, but definitely not a walk in the park. It was very hard to maintain that smoothness, dynamism, and fluidity in the motion throughout all the sequences. "The other difficult aspect has been the integration between 3D and 2D assets, both from a motion and a visual standpoint. Every element in the scene needed to feel perfectly integrated within the same style of illustration. "We really tried to bring that quality to every single frame, thinking like we could pause at any point in the timeline and still see beautiful artwork. "It has been an amazing ride. It's rare to get the opportunity to work on something so beautiful and to be given the trust and flexibility to bring it to the next level."

"It's a nostalgic look towards a new era of agriculture, with beautifully crafted backgrounds, delicate animation, and a completely unique score by long-time Ghibli composer (and absolute legend) Joe Hisaishi. (Yeah, we can't believe this happened either). "We love the aspiration in Chobani's vision of the future and hope it will sow the seeds of optimism and feed our imagination for what the future could be. "It's a vision we can totally get behind. We couldn't be happier to be part of this campaign."

records.description: Senior producer Zoe Coleman and creative director Duncan Patterson at Linetest in Vancouver: "We were briefed to create a multi-deliverable campaign for The Home Depot Canada Foundation to launch their TradeWorx Program. "This initiative helps end youth homelessness in Canada and provides a more sturdy and stable living for those at risk and on the streets. "Creatively, the animation needed to complement the script and guide the viewer's eye through the story. "The FCB team wanted to explore animation and not live-action for this piece because they didn't want to be constricted to realism, and instead, we could explore abstract transitions and pushed proportions in this illustrated world. "Frame by frame animation by nature has its own challenges both in terms of time and execution. The lengthy process of cel animation however felt like the right choice for this particular project to ensure a tactile and authentic feeling, which compliments the narrative and art direction. "The use of colour as a vehicle to convey emotion within the narrative was very important to our team and client combined. "By establishing the TradeWorx world with darker tones, and then progressively utilizing brighter notes with just splashes of The Home Depot orange as the story progressed, we were able to add glimmers of hope just when we needed them. "From the start, we knew numerous deliverables would be required so we were able to work smart and put technical processes in place to ensure we were able to deliver multiple ratios, durations, and languages within a short timeframe. "Creating single-style frames that worked at multiple ratios using our custom framework was key in saving time, while also retaining the highest quality. "A framework which then our animators also worked within, alleviating the need to re-animate for other ratios. "Planning for the 30-second and 15-second cut downs right from the start of the project was another key decision. It meant we molded the hero 60-second animation to strategically place cuts where we knew it would not negatively impact the flow of the story. "The project took us nine weeks to complete, from initial style concepts and storyboards to final character animation and compositing. We spent roughly 30% of the production time storyboarding and developing the art direction, collaborating with agency and client to ensure complete alignment on creative vision, brand enforcement, and narrative. "For the final scene, we reveal Taye, our hero homeless-youth character but now shown in work clothing as she continues her journey to success as a trade worker. "We tried multiple creative solutions to achieve this shot, the main challenge being the combined rotation of the work truck, characters, and background/foreground elements. "At first, cell animation appeared to be the best option for the entire shot, however, as we started to add more detail it became far too complex and time-consuming to rely solely on hand-drawn techniques. "In the end, we used a combination of 2D, 3D, and cell animation to achieve the result we were aiming for. "The background elements were handled within After Effects. The work truck was modeled, animated, and rendered in 3D but with a flat illustrated look to match the overall style, and finally, the characters were animated in cell using the 3D animation pass as reference. "Utilizing and combining these techniques is a process we as a studio have been doing for a long time. "We know that failure is often part of the creative process and that most problems have multiple solutions. But by staying positive and surrounding ourselves with others that challenge and amplify innovation, we can continue to create work we are proud of."

records.description: Director Sam Gainsborough at Blinkink in London: "The agency wanted to make a heartfelt animated film that pulled on the heartstrings of the audience. "They knew they wanted the main character to be ushered into action by a living house, with magical moments peppered throughout. The story itself was open for development, and it was a fantastic opportunity for me to shape a unique story. "It was a really collaborative process, which meant I had a huge amount of freedom to explore different versions of the narrative. "From the beginning, I wanted to focus on the main character and bring his struggle and triumph to the forefront of the film. "When developing the story, there were many ideas that didn't make it into the final film. I loved the idea of animating dust, sanding wood in stop motion, and animating the stitched patterns of rugs and curtains to create magical moments from everyday DIY processes. "We also designed a son character who would be struggling to ride a tricycle which had been encased in rock-like everything else in the world. Through a long process of editing and reworking the animatic, we boiled everything down to just include what was needed for the main character's story. I loved a lot of these ideas, and it was a challenge refining the film to its essence. "There were so many technical challenges in this production, as it was a hugely ambitious stop-motion film. It's important to me to capture as much as possible in-camera to create an authentic world. "In order to create glowing cracks shooting away from the main character Nigel, the entire floor of the set was made of plasticine which sat on a layer of perspex which was lit from below. "Another hugely complex shot was when Nigel breaks free of the chair, the dog also breaks free and jumps around while twenty rolls of wallpaper magically unravel in the background, and many lights lower from above. "This shot took ten hours to set up and another six hours to animate with three animators on set working simultaneously. It was a huge amount of work for a four-second shot! "Another challenging shot was where Nigel is lifted up by a magical tower of DIY products. This tower was made from 200+ handmade miniature items and the animator had to stand on a platform to reach the top. "A particularly nifty creative solution was created to achieve the wallpaper magically unraveling. Each roll of miniature wallpaper was suspended by fishing wire, each attached to a separate fishing reel. "This meant for every frame, the animators had to reach above the set and gradually wind 20 fishing reels to gradually pull them up." Schedule: 12 weeks.
