records.description: This brave mixed-media film directed by Golden Globe-winner Nisha Ganatra and punctuated with animated sequences from Framestore aims to "dispel myths, encourage a positive conversation, and address the life-changing moments in a woman's life". Framestore CD Sharon Lock worked with AMV BBDO ECDs Nadja Lossgott and Nicholas Hulley to select the styles of animation including 2D cel, stop-motion, and oil paint on glass. Sharon Lock: "It was important the animations produced for this film not only looked as good as possible but also made an emotional impact on audiences because of the nature of the film. "We worked with animators who had wonderful storytelling abilities and whose work was unique and handmade and could communicate a range of tone and emotion to audiences in a short amount of time on-screen. Framestore senior producer Niamh O'Donohoe: "We were telling real stories about the experiences of being a woman so having the [predominantly female] team we did meant we had something of a shorthand. "We could easily communicate what we needed because there was a mutual understanding of how these stories had to be presented, something that I feel beautifully reflects the messages that Libresse/Bodyform is always communicating."

records.description: Working with Oscar-nominees Shawn Levy (Stranger Things, Night at the Museum) and Will Gluck (Peter Rabbit), the MPC crew populates an all-night party at DICK'S Sporting Goods with 46 CG characters including the star Nike Air Max 270. MPC Creative Director Ashley Bernes: "The inherent challenge was to take a photo-realistic inanimate object, place it in a live-action setting, and make it behave in a way that's not natural. "While there is an aspect of creative license when you're working with a character such as a robot or a mythical creature when it comes to an everyday object such as a shoe, we needed to make it look like it's walking on its own – not like someone is walking in it. "Levy and Gluck brought an incredible wealth of experience in both live-action and animation which proved critical in defining the rules of this film." "We needed to create an emotional connection with these characters, and as they don't have faces, we had to convey the emotion through motion and behavior. "Research was carried out on the movement of animals that have similar proportions as the objects, for example, incorporating the elegant movement of a flamingo's long neck into the behavior of the golf clubs and making the hockey stick's gliding movements similar to that of a dolphin. "The main character is a new shoe in the store, so there was a very fine line between giving it a young, curious childlike personality, and making sure it didn't seem too scared or timid." "We used Maxine's laces as arms in one sequence so she could join hands with another character, so we had to balance the behavior of an arm with the behavior of a piece of string, which was a challenge."

records.description: Executive producers Richard Cureton and Luc Frappier at Revolver Films in Toronto: "Saatchi and Saatchi LA's brief was to shoot the commercial in Rome, but Rune Milton, our director, chose to pitch Kyiv, Ukraine instead. "We were strongly inspired by the locations we had seen in Kyiv, they turned out to be a much more spectacular than what we could have had in Rome. "Additionally, Kyiv ended up being a win-win situation budget-wise as well - money goes much further in Ukraine than in Italy. "One of the main creative challenges was the size of the art department. We build a lot of set pieces; the concrete skate park, the partial ramp on which Lily does her flip, 12 massive pillars (about two stories high), plus the stadium seating. "The use of VFX was another challenge. With our amazing team at TGBVFX in Copenhagen we painted out the entire center pillar in the hero location, there were literally thousands of buses housed in the location (it's a bus graveyard, not a station, as we found out on arrival). "We dragged two-thirds of them out and the post crew had to clean up the rest, they also had to convert the location to a full-size Olympic venue for the final sequence. "The biggest technical challenge was figuring out how to move the camera in a dynamic way. We had to improvise on the spot, and create a new filming technique. "The spot has been seen in more than 50 countries and translated in many languages. It is part of the wide international Toyota Olympics campaign 'Start Your Impossible'. "We actually had issues finding the perfect hardware for the skating footage. We tried using a Russian arm and a techno crane, but after looking at the dailies we decided the footage was just not dynamic enough so we had to improvise. "Our DOP suggested creating something very low-fi and we went to the hardware store. We ended up the camera screwed to a small piece of wood with plastic wheels. "The footage we got from that rig was much more dynamic since it put you in the perspective of Lily's wheelchair… who knew that would be the best way for capturing the action? "Overall, it was a very intense and arduous shoot. A couple of days before filming, we spent a day in Rome scouting the Toyota wheel park. We were scheduled to go back to Kyiv that night. "As we were sitting down for dinner at the hotel, we heard on the news the Russian military had seized Ukrainian naval ships. "The threat of a Russian invasion was escalating and tension in Ukraine was increasing just as our talent and crew were about to fly to Kyiv to start shooting our spot. "It was OK in the end but it did create a slightly ominous backdrop for an already challenging shoot."

records.description: Creative directors Guido Lambertini, Rodier Kidmann, and Carmen Angelillo at Niceshit Studio in Barcelona, Spain: "[The agency] FIG had designed a print campaign and we entered as the animation studio to this project with one purpose: give life to this exquisite world filled with wit, a charm, and humor. "We had to develop a huge set of characters and backgrounds to narrate these magical stories into animated films, for a combination of TVC's, Social and PR films "Simplicity was a key all over this project, everything should have a feeling of approachable ease and looseness. Many times we found ourselves taking out elements instead of adding details. "With such an imperfect and hand-made style, our main focus was on the acting and timing in the scenes as we wanted to communicate as much expression possible with very few and detailed movements. "The goal was to create a bespoke and functional animated universe that hopefully will become an iconic and long-running look for the brand. "This PR film called 'The Journey' was the most difficult as we had to complete a 45-second film in two weeks from scratch. And we wanted it to be more complex than the rest of the films, i.e. camera movements and rotating buildings. "It is not every day that we receive scripts like this one, where the fine and clever humor is the key, looking for the small pauses, timing, and subtle expressions. "Also working with such a loose style, as if the stories were created on hundreds of bar napkins. It was great and fun a challege for our creativity and gathered a lot of talented people to make it come true." Schedule: Two months.

records.description: Executive creative director, Chris Knight at The Mill in London: "We were tasked with creating a dystopian and ominous landscape, where aliens and their menacing spacecrafts threaten the world as we know it. "The brief also included the crafting of visuals that adhere to filmic values and are grounded in cinematic earnestness. "One challenge was to craft a unique spacecraft design that balanced both organic and otherworldly hard surface forms. "Another was making the exterior shots feel ominous, without them being too close and also keeping the beautiful light of the sunset. This positioned the viewer in a place where they sensed the immediate danger the protagonist is running from. "One of the technical challenges, was the scale of the spaceships had to be perfectly balanced. They had to be mobile enough to navigate and sift through the terrain in search of human life form, whilst creating a menacing presence at the same time."

records.description: Fabio Acorsi, director at LOBO in New York: "To let the public know more about where it has come from and where it's headed, Chobani released an environmental impact report and commissioned Lobo to create this companion film that offers a poetic counterpart to the data-centric document. "Up to this point, all of the films we've produced for Chobani have been mixed-technique tour de forces, combining live-action, miniature sets, stop motion, CGI, you name it. This time, however, it was decided to take a completely different route and go all-in on 2D animation. "Taking inspiration from Chobani's brand-identity artwork (delicate, colorful hand-painted illustrations), we brought to life an idyllic journey showing how the act of giving is the first step into making universal wellness happen sooner. "The film combines vector illustration and natural textures with a color palette that is both earthy and vibrant, enhancing the warm, caring and optimistic tone of the message. "The first step was drawing a very detailed storyboard at the same time that the artistic team was proposing style ideas for the illustrations. "After that, an animatic was built with a reference soundtrack to help our animation team understand the different moods during the story."

records.description: Robert Sethi, director at The Mill in Los Angeles: "The project started with an exciting idea from BBDO Guerrero, the client's agency: The hero of the commercial, a motocross biker, puts on a pair of AR goggles and reality then augments into an epic adventure as he rides into the waves. "Myself, Brent Bonacorso (creative consultant), and the team further explored the concept to develop components of the augmented world and create a visceral adventure inspired by a video game. "The key creative challenge was weaving the narrative together in such a short duration, condensing the action down to 30 seconds while still making sure the augmented reality twist clearly came out. "It was also important the sense of gamification came across. We needed to properly establish our hero drinking, riding, racing, reaching for the prize of a Mountain Dew bottle, and then coming back to reality to celebrate with his friends. "We wanted to inject the entire spot with adrenaline and that feel of increasing momentum, pushing towards the exciting end. "We worked with incredible riders and stuntmen to shoot all the stunts in Buenos Aires. Shooting authentic stunts ensured the piece was grounded in reality. "It was key to get the raw intensity, grit, and minute detail of the motocross rider traveling through the track, navigating the environment and making the movements seem as natural as possible. "Then, in compositing, the actor needed to be rotoscoped out of all the shots and integrated back into the massive CG water landscape – his augmented reality. "This was a detailed and intensive undertaking to replace the jumps with water simulation. Of course, we also can't forget about the "little fish" – a.k.a. the massive shark! "This was an exciting challenge that took a lot of research to get just right. There was plenty of tweaking in the animation to make the shark the right size, to nail down its movements, and to have it traveling at an appropriate speed. "The shark's visibility in the water was also a conversation, as we needed the actions to be balanced to create that suspense we were looking for. "The shark pushes the narrative to the next level, adding an extra element of danger. Its presence elevates the intensity and suspense, and it becomes the end of level boss in the augmented universe. "In terms of shooting, there was an Alexa camera, Solaris with stabilized camera rig, Phantom camera, camera mounted on a dirt bike, and then equipment required for the stunts such as ramps, water pools, green screen, and wire rigs. "In terms of software, we utilized Nuke, Flame, Maya, and Houdini."

"It was key to get the raw intensity, grit, and minute detail of the motocross rider traveling through the track, navigating the environment and making the movements seem as natural as possible. "Then, in compositing, the actor needed to be rotoscoped out of all the shots and integrated back into the massive CG water landscape – his augmented reality. "This was a detailed and intensive undertaking to replace the jumps with water simulation. Of course, we also can't forget about the "little fish" – a.k.a. the massive shark! "This was an exciting challenge that took a lot of research to get just right. There was plenty of tweaking in the animation to make the shark the right size, to nail down its movements, and to have it traveling at an appropriate speed. "The shark's visibility in the water was also a conversation, as we needed the actions to be balanced to create that suspense we were looking for. "The shark pushes the narrative to the next level, adding an extra element of danger. Its presence elevates the intensity and suspense, and it becomes the end of level boss in the augmented universe. "In terms of shooting, there was an Alexa camera, Solaris with stabilized camera rig, Phantom camera, camera mounted on a dirt bike, and then equipment required for the stunts such as ramps, water pools, green screen, and wire rigs. "In terms of software, we utilized Nuke, Flame, Maya, and Houdini."

records.description: "The CG creature crew at Framestore reteam with Rattling Stick director Daniel Kleinman and Arnold Worldwide to create the sophomore adventure for Santander's porcine hero. Chris Redding, VFX/2D supervisor at Framestore: "Arnold really wanted to create a new character design that was different from but reminiscent of the piggy bank from the first commercial. "The logic was that every person has their own version of Piggy, in the same way everyone would have a different dog. "We used a rigid stand-in model for the first Piggy commercial but because he needed to be so much more mobile this time and changed size from shot to shot, [we used puppets] to have a way of capturing great on-set reference. "The character needed to run the entire time, so we redesigned the pig from scratch to allow for its extended mobility. "The rigging and modeling teams built what was as close to an anatomically feasible skeleton as possible and then buried it under the caricatured look of the embellished piggy bank. "The variation in scale and environments meant we needed to be able to adapt the groom set up so, throughout the commercial, the hair on the main character also grew. "It also needed to be adapted in each shot to account for how wet he was or how sweaty he got in any particular scene" VFX supervisor Tim Jenkinson: "The most important thing was to make the character appealing and cute. "We spent a lot of time reworking and finessing the features of the pig as even the smallest change in the shape or size of the snout, eyes, brows or cheeks had a huge impact on its character."

records.description: The unexpected emotional ending to this Hyundai brand spot lifts the work clear of the usual clamor and testosterone of the automotive category. MPC VFX supervisor Jessie Amadio: "Most of the spot is played in reverse, showcasing special moments like slo-mo Phantom close-ups and sprawling time-lapse wide shots. "Following through on this mechanic meant we had to keep in mind the era-appropriate details for each shot and double-check the logic and continuity of our animation regularly. "A standout element of the spot is the CG recreation of the vintage 1975 Pony Mark I. With this being an older car, the team didn't have access to any CAD data, so they had to model based on limited photographs and a very handy blueprint they were able to find in a vintage mail-order catalog. "The elaborate city time-lapse scene proved to be one of the more challenging shots, and MPC were involved early on in developing how it would look. "A massive amount of modeling and continual creative refinement was needed to achieve the level of detail required in such a wide shot. While the rest of the job was done in Maya, the team migrated this shot to Houdini for faster scene management. "Our artists set up a pretty interactive system for scattering the layout, controlling the animation timing, and procedurally deconstructing each building. "Combing the CG buildings and flora with 2D elements from DMP and a time-lapse stills camera from the set, we were able to derive a fairly complex final image."

records.description: Paul Harrod, animation director at HouseSpecial in Portland, Oregon: "We were aiming for a nostalgic, stop-motion 'holiday special' look and feel. "AT&T and BBDO were in agreement that the visual approach needed to be retro, yet of a high enough production value to contrast with the gritty naturalism of the live-action. "So the idea of juxtaposing a Sergio Leone-inspired Western with family-friendly animated content really sells the idea that AT&T is a provider of a wide range of entertainment possibilities. "Creatively speaking, the biggest challenge was to create an animated sequence that served as comic contrast to the live-action segment, while still referencing it enough to feel like it's the same film transformed into a different tone of entertainment. "With that in mind, we made sure each of the train cars corresponded exactly to the train cars in the live-action and the human characters all were identifiable as representations of the actors. "Fortunately, we were able to bring in the wonderful character designer, Felicie Haymoz, whom I'd worked with previously on Isle Of Dogs. "The primary challenge was to create something at once charming and retro while at the same time being technically adept and pleasing to the eye of a contemporary audience. "To that end, we fabricated fairly sophisticated puppets for the locomotive and train car characters. The armatures were engineered to be very flexible, despite the fact that their shells were entirely rigid structures. "With the armatures' extended range of motion, we had the ability to make the train cars move on a number of different axes so one train car could go up the hill with a kind of a crab walk while another car pushed his buddy up the hill with his retractable nose. "For the final couple of shots, the train cars needed the range of motion to have their wheels on the track while at the same time doing a little dance from side to side. These are certainly mechanical challenges but they're also incredibly fun solves to execute! "The director, Dougal Wilson, and I were also very keen on doing as much as possible in-camera and not rely on digital set extensions. "The only significant composited elements were in the final shot, where we reduced the scale of our desperadoes while comping in the vulture that flies through the frame and the sky. "We just didn't have the stage space to convincingly pull off that shot with a painted sky backdrop, though we did use them for most of the other shots. We did, however, build a forced perspective desert set for that shot, which needed to be carefully planned out. "Normally, it isn't advisable to do a camera move on a forced perspective set, because the parallax will betray the cheat, but the end shot called for a boom with a pull back. To add to that, the train was traveling off into the distance, so the tracks and any foreground landscape had to be all to the scale of the train. "Only what you see beyond the train is in forced perspective, so the entire set was pretty big by stop motion standards – around 12'x40'. The camera move worked quite well in the end and any minimal betrayal of the cheat could be chalked up to the cartoon reality we were trying to express. "We were all very excited to get the opportunity to work with Dougal Wilson. Being familiar with his body of work, I really do consider him one of the best commercial directors working today. "Dougal wanted to be present throughout the entire animation process, which is very unusual when providing animation for what is primarily a live-action project. "But that's the kind of person he is, as he likes to get elbows-deep into the entire process. The first time we got together, I'd had a couple of foam-core mock-ups of the train cars made and we went on to a small stage and just did an off-the-cuff live-action shoot of a broad range of actions, manipulating the models like rod puppets. "Dougal took all of the footage and edited it in to what he refers to as a "crap-o-matic," which is essentially a workable animatic that had all the timing figured out and from which storyboards could be drawn. "It was really huge fun to hang with three or four grown adults, pushing little toy trains around. It was a great way to work and I think I'm going to use it a lot more in the future; this idea of just filming the action in the crudest, simplest way possible and then refining the whole thing from that point onward."

records.description: Buenos Aires animation studio Le Cube, prodco Final Frontier, and agency R/GA Shanghai reteam on a rampaging brand film for China's Boxing Cat Brewery starring Louis, a pugilistic super-hero of suds. R/GA Shanghai ECD Terence Leong: "We were in love with Wes Anderson's Fantastic Mr. Fox and we originally wanted Louie to be a charismatic and suave stop-motion puppet with a persona like Muhammad Ali. But we couldn't find the right voice for his trash talk. Then Shing played the Spiderman theme song and boom! Everything clicked - he's a superhero who fights boring beers." Le Cube director Ralph Karam: "In developing Louie's design, adapting him from the initial 3D plan into a 2D aesthetic, we decided to use a halftone effect to create a retro comic book feel. "It was a fine line to have him embody all the wit, coolness, and self-assured confidence of Muhammad Ali, and retain the essential humor, but without creating any sense of menace that could too easily have come across."

records.description: Charlotte Arnold, EP and Daniel Morris, VFX super / lead compositor at Blacksmith in New York: "Blacksmith created all the space shots in CG – from the planets to the spaceship's exterior and some interior details – as well as the zero gravity snow particles that form a key part of the narrative. "The exterior space shots were obviously a big one for us and we did a lot of planning with the director Martin on the look and feel of these. "We researched a lot of NASA footage, both videos and also some amazing imagery taken aboard the Apollo on a Hasselblad film camera which had a lot of amazing texture that both Martin and we responded well to. "We wanted to have the big epic feeling you get from space shots, but also introduce some of that texture and color palette from these older film images. We also discussed a lot the composition of these shots as Martin wanted to explore different angles and try to do something a little more unexpected with these. "For all the wide CG shots it was a challenge trying to come up with shots that you haven't seen before or had an abstract feel about them. "To bring Martin's vision to life, Blacksmith created an epic look with a filmic texture and color palette, using matte paintings to add another level of detail and realism. "The snow particles were also an important item for everyone. During the RnD phase of for this we studied the physics of space on NASA's website. "We went through many iterations of the snow globe effect as well as the interaction FX. In the end, we found a nice balance of physics and artistry. "On set, the challenges were making everything feel zero gravity without disrupting the flow of the shoot or performance of the talent. "We worked closely with the visual effects team to design rigs and come up with ideas for zero gravity objects. The suitcase scene is one example. "I asked for them to fill a light foil box with helium so we could suspend it in air using minimal fishing wire. We did many tests on how to make a suitcase pass from one person to another using wires. That rig was extremely successful as seen in the spot. "In post for the interior we added CG wires, added earth outside the window and nice window textures, plus CG zero gravity objects in many shots including suitcases, pen, sunny (the snowman), notepads on the walls. "We modeled the exterior of the spaceship, along with some interior details in Maya and textured in Substance Designer. Everything was rendered using Arnold. "We used Photogrammetry to make a fully CG roof for where the rigs were used to hang our talent. Using Houdini we built robust tools to allow us to mimic the physics on the ISS and still allow us to make creative changes to tell the story better. "This spot was always going to have two major studio builds. Exterior space station and Interior space station. "There was an interior set build of the space station which was built on a rotating gimble. There were movable sections and portable walls built so as to give the illusion of having multiple spaces in the ship. "A techno crane was able to move a camera through the set with a 360 (3 axis) camera head. The roof of the space station was then removed and the talent was lowered in on wires to give the illusion of zero gravity. This combined with a rotating set and 3-axis camera gave the full dynamic effect of living in space. "During the entire process we were constantly looking at references and brainstorming for how the wide fully CG shots would look. This was very important as I was able to gauge from Martin, Danilo and Marcos what kind of shots they were looking for. "From all the research it became quite clear all the types of shots that were available to try. Mainly separated by the real (documentary) and film (abstract) worlds. "A spaceship will orbit the earth every 90 mins so we decided to try and pull off one of each. We did extensive previz and quick slap comp ideas of every shot. Considering: what time of day is it? Is the shot timelapse? How close is earth? Do you see the spaceship much? "The previs and quick tests in 2D were so important for the process to decide what all these different shots would look like. We went for a wide, epic, beautiful earth with a small lonely spaceship which is very much in the film realm but went for odd/abstract framings. "The spaceship pod leaving for the earth is a big CG shot. We chose a good window that we shot on location and framed it as if someone was looking out at the pod leaving. "There is also a good POV shot of earth that shows how much she is missing home. All of these combined gives the sense of how long this lady has spent in space. Schedule: "Before we started working on the CG Earth, we had five weeks of R&D and prep time. From locked edit to delivery we had about six weeks and we did a total of 130 shots."

"We went through many iterations of the snow globe effect as well as the interaction FX. In the end, we found a nice balance of physics and artistry. "On set, the challenges were making everything feel zero gravity without disrupting the flow of the shoot or performance of the talent. "We worked closely with the visual effects team to design rigs and come up with ideas for zero gravity objects. The suitcase scene is one example. "I asked for them to fill a light foil box with helium so we could suspend it in air using minimal fishing wire. We did many tests on how to make a suitcase pass from one person to another using wires. That rig was extremely successful as seen in the spot. "In post for the interior we added CG wires, added earth outside the window and nice window textures, plus CG zero gravity objects in many shots including suitcases, pen, sunny (the snowman), notepads on the walls. "We modeled the exterior of the spaceship, along with some interior details in Maya and textured in Substance Designer. Everything was rendered using Arnold. "We used Photogrammetry to make a fully CG roof for where the rigs were used to hang our talent. Using Houdini we built robust tools to allow us to mimic the physics on the ISS and still allow us to make creative changes to tell the story better. "This spot was always going to have two major studio builds. Exterior space station and Interior space station. "There was an interior set build of the space station which was built on a rotating gimble. There were movable sections and portable walls built so as to give the illusion of having multiple spaces in the ship. "A techno crane was able to move a camera through the set with a 360 (3 axis) camera head. The roof of the space station was then removed and the talent was lowered in on wires to give the illusion of zero gravity. This combined with a rotating set and 3-axis camera gave the full dynamic effect of living in space. "During the entire process we were constantly looking at references and brainstorming for how the wide fully CG shots would look. This was very important as I was able to gauge from Martin, Danilo and Marcos what kind of shots they were looking for. "From all the research it became quite clear all the types of shots that were available to try. Mainly separated by the real (documentary) and film (abstract) worlds. "A spaceship will orbit the earth every 90 mins so we decided to try and pull off one of each. We did extensive previz and quick slap comp ideas of every shot. Considering: what time of day is it? Is the shot timelapse? How close is earth? Do you see the spaceship much? "The previs and quick tests in 2D were so important for the process to decide what all these different shots would look like. We went for a wide, epic, beautiful earth with a small lonely spaceship which is very much in the film realm but went for odd/abstract framings. "The spaceship pod leaving for the earth is a big CG shot. We chose a good window that we shot on location and framed it as if someone was looking out at the pod leaving. "There is also a good POV shot of earth that shows how much she is missing home. All of these combined gives the sense of how long this lady has spent in space. Schedule: "Before we started working on the CG Earth, we had five weeks of R&D and prep time. From locked edit to delivery we had about six weeks and we did a total of 130 shots."

records.description: Pete Candeland, director at Friends Electric in Los Angeles: "This was the second Great Western Railway production we worked on and the general idea was to appeal to a broad UK audience and excite them for train travel in the UK. "Just like the first, we knew we would be using the Famous Five books written by Enid Blyton from the 40's, 50's, and 60's, which are beloved in the UK. "Ultimately, the idea was to be as broadly appealing as possible, and the Famous Five would appeal to a lot of people, straight away. "I've been lucky enough to work with existing properties in the past and the most challenging thing is always to liven up to that property, take good care of the characters and do them justice so the audience can recognize their authenticity and we can reach the audience's expectations. "Whenever I have a project like this, I study the original materials, in this case, read the books, and I get to really know the characters so when I integrate them into a new project, it feels right to the viewers and I give them their proper due. "You have to take some ownership and make decisions on behalf of the author, which is why it's so important to be certain I know the characters and stay as true as possible. "The biggest technical challenge lay within the time constraints of the story. The toughest aspect was fitting in a lot of story in such a little bit of time. "It was a rich story, but only having one minute to tell it, well that takes a lot of storyboarding and making changes to the script as you go along throughout the process. "Another challenge is ensuring the look was not too computer generated. We wanted it to have an accurate feel that was true to the original, hand-drawn illustrations done by Eileen Soper. "For it to have a finished look that was hand drawn, we used a lot of compositing at the end and generally tried to disguise the CG, which was a nice challenge that was very rewarding once we got it looking right. "Although the animation is brought to life in CG, the final week of production involves us printing out every scene on paper and then scanning it back into the computer to give us the grain and texture of paper with the bleeding of the paint for a realistic finish that cannot be achieved digitally. "It's a handmade solution in a digital world, and I tend to gravitate to that kind of thing. Schedule: "We had a little under five months to work on the project, which was quite tight. The first month was storyboarding and creating animatics. The second was conception and background.

records.description: Directors Manddy Wyckens and Marc Craste at Studio AKA in London: "The concept for First Family rests on the assertion that new parents fundamentally understand what their child needs, and have done so since the dawn of time. "The brief was to create an identifiable, relatable couple with a newborn baby, and to follow their parenting challenges within the prehistoric setting. "There were a number of elements important to all involved with the production. We wanted to avoid portraying our characters performing traditional roles – and so shaped them to be a very ‘modern' family. "We decided early on to make judicious use of the prehistoric setting and not stray too far into territory already well-covered in animation. "We wanted the piece feel very modern in its design. It had to look beautiful, but also reflect the emphasis on the natural and organic that for the client was an essential part of the product. "To this end we made the decision early on to use hand-drawn animation, giving the film a hand-crafted quality and warmth. "This was such a rich concept to explore that the biggest challenge was to let go of the numerous ideas that occurred but which were too much for the story. "We probably had enough for a film twice the length, however, in the end, we pared it back so the focus was always on the family while the world around them, interesting and lovely to look at as it is, didn't steal the viewer's attention. "This was also reflected in the staging and camera movement in that everything is quite restrained, allowing the performance of the characters to shine. "And of course the design of the world, simple and sparse while managing to suggest a fully realized and expansive space, was crucial in achieving this. "Technically the job was a fairly straightforward combination of 2D and CGI elements although there are a lot of subtle textures and effects that help give the film the organic feel the client was looking for. "As much as we kept the focus on the main family throughout the film, there are lots of little details which we've added here and there. "If you watch a second or third time, you can always discover little activities taking place all around. We thought that would be a nice touch. Maybe you can spot them all!" Schedule: 14 weeks.

records.description: Sophie Lebreton (executive VFX producer), Marouen El-Bekri, (CG supervisor), Stephane Allender (VFX Supervisor) at Mikros MPC in Paris: "The real challenge was creating this creature from scratch in only four weeks, imagining how it would move, express emotions, its degree of wilderness vs. cuteness. Our brains were doing double-time. "Bringing life to the creature was quite tricky as we had to avoid all 3D cartoon animation, the director wanted real-life animal movement without any stretch and squash etc... "So, after at least 50 versions, we were really happy, when the director said 'GNUGNU is born!' "Texturing was also a big deal, it was hard to find the right combination and balance between all the different skin texture references (elephant, turtle, sea elephant...) "We also chose to let the camera move as much as the director wanted and also shoot through objects, people, etc. It doesn't make our job easier but it always feels more realistic when the scene looks alive already in-camera "We used Maya and Arnold for the CG, then Mudbox for digital sculpting to add wrinkles and skin pores, Substance Painter and Mari for the texture and finally Nuke for the 3D compositing."

records.description: Creative director and VFX supervisor Jordi Bares, at Framestore in London: "We were tasked with creating a host of CG characters to demonstrate Funding Circle's impact on inspiring businesses. "The figures of classic coin-operated rides are seen coming to life and powering through the city before taking off into orbit. "Framestore created ten fully-formed CG personalities, including headliner Captain Galactic, who was designed from scratch, under the direction of Antoine Bardou-Jacquet. "Other characters were based on scans of real-life ride models, adapted and later simulated as crowds for the spot's closing sequence. "Captain Galactic was both the greatest challenge and opportunity. Designed from a sketch, he was ultimately 3D-printed for use in the live action shots and photoscanned to ensure absolute accuracy in the CG model used by Framestore's artists. "The closing sequence called for crowds of characters in flight set against a custom Earth, fashioned in line with the brand and campaign's visual language. The backdrop was a high res digital matte painting, created to also be used for print. "We commenced building the CG assets mid/end of June. The shoot took place in mid-July. We worked on the 30" version first as that needed to deliver first for a TV air date. "We received offline edit approval at the end of July so we had approximately eight weeks from plates for shot execution, ready for delivery early October. "For this project we had a fairly standard PC setup running Linux. We used several pieces of software including Capture Reality for 3D scanning, Maya, ZBrush and Substance for asset builds, and Houdini and Arnold for rendering. "Some of the ride assets were manufactured as real objects to use on set. We chose to 3D scan these to help us achieve the most accurate reconstruction of the physical props. "Some of this 3D scanning data took place on set, however for the main Captain Galactic character, we transported the real prop to our Capture Lab where we used a custom camera rig to capture the best quality data. "We used Nuke for compositing, Baselight for grading and Flame for final mastering."

records.description: LOBO directors, Mateus de Paula Santos and Nando Cohen in São Paulo, Brazil: "5Star is a brand of caramel and cookie-filled chocolate bars. The main goal of the campaign is to speak to the youth market (from teens to college-age consumers), combining an irresistible appetite appeal with high entertainment value. "The agency's solution was to create a series of short spots full of moments of pure mayhem and dark humor. "They take place in a world made entirely of plain chocolate, where plain chocolate people lead their plain chocolate lives. "That is until the place is hit by a massive shower of gigantic, crunchy biscuit bits that crash through everything in their path and cause the ground to split open, releasing torrents of smooth caramel gushing through the streets. "It was particularly challenging to depict such tragic situations as comedy, with characters being killed in gruesome ways and yet still making people laugh. "The animations were created entirely in 3D CG, with the greatest care taken to reproduce the natural textures of chocolate and other ingredients. "There was a great amount of interaction between simulated elements, either happening at the same time or in a sequence of events as the comic tragedy unfolds. "Given the fact that we don't have full control of the result that comes out of 3D physics simulation, it was rather challenging to work with as many layers of simulation intertwined in most shots. "Another big challenge was in portraying the exact look and feel of the biscuit bits: we looked at 5Star print ads for reference and ended up photographing the actual product with macro lenses, in order to capture the true essence of their crunchiness. "At the end of each spot we reveal that the whole story takes place inside a 5Star chocolate bar, so everything in it had to be made of either chocolate, caramel or biscuit. "That left us with a very limited color palette, so the lighting and shading work had to be very well thought out in order to delineate the shapes and contours of all visual elements." Schedule: 1.5 months per spot.

records.description: John Sauven, executive director of Greenpeace: "A decade ago we persuaded brands including Nestlé, Unilever and Mondelez to sign global commitments to drop dirty palm oil from their products by 2020 – but with just 500 days to go, their progress is pitiful. "Orangutans have been pushed to the very brink of extinction, Indigenous peoples' lives are threatened and climate change is accelerating. "Around half of the products in our supermarkets contain palm oil, from shampoo to chocolate. This film aims to raise awareness of the issue among new audiences and grow a movement of people that can help force brands to keep their promise." Salon Alpin: "The scenes are designed and animated using various techniques including 3D and VR to bring to life the hand-drawn animation in a flow of action and immersive camera moves. "The film will run through Greenpeace and supporter social channels, online media and across UK cinema with thousands of screenings. In addition, Rang-tan's story has been made into a book, which will be distributed to supporting influencers and via the Greenpeace volunteer network."

For years it was also unofficially called "Hospital de amor" (Hospital of Love). "When the word cancer was finally removed from the hospital's name, we created this three-minute animated film telling the story of a girl who finds out she has cancer. But the love of her parents, her puppy, and the doctors changes the course of the disease." Schedule: 10 months.

records.description: Sean Cochrane, VFX director at The Vanity in Toronto: "Director Mark Zibert's treatment really had it all from a VFX perspective: surreal landscapes, character animation, matte paintings, physical simulations, a dozen different looks and loads of detailed compositing. "Unfortunately it also faced the challenge most projects seem to have lately, schedule. We were only going to have seven days to put all this together once the edit was locked – and the edit changed a few times before that week was up. "In preparation for the compressed schedule we started developing a lot of the VFX work early so when we finally received the footage we could hit the ground running. "The origami bill characters were going to take the most time so designing the look and creating those creatures was the first order of business. "Since everyone in the creative pipeline was very aware of the challenging schedule we received very little changes on our first designs. "The team sent us clear, intelligent, consolidated feedback usually within one hour of posting shots. Thankfully everyone was on board on how valuable every hour was used to meet our deadline. "In parallel to the design phase of our origami bill characters, we were also developing the wall cracking VFX. "This was all procedurally done in Maya and rigged so we could animate a simple line on a wall which would drive all the physics of the plaster veneer chipping, cracking away, and revealing the guts of the walls. "This simple line animation approach was the key to making any client and agency changes quickly. "The flickering lights of the shots forced us to get creative with the rendering. Within the timeframe we could not recreate the walls in CG. We had to project the original camera footage and bake it onto our cracking geometry which was camera-tracked perfectly. "This approach was highly efficient and saved us a massive amount of time. "As for the compositing, we had two Flames working almost 24 hours a day for seven days right through the Canada Day long weekend to meet the deadline. "For the optometry / orthodontist sequence, the baby was captured lying on and sitting with her mother. The mother wore a full green screen body suit and because babies squirm around quite a bit, we had to paint out the mothers hands and arms holding her. "Several plates of time-lapse orthodontists needed to be roto'd back over and getting the diopter transitions to look just right took a significant amount of time. "Of course the baby wasn't actually wearing braces or the headgear so stitching all of this into the baby's mouth to appear authentic was very tricky and completed all in Flame. "We really had a lot of fun creating the underwater landscape. We had a great shot of the mom falling into the water, but it wasn't nearly wide enough for the scope that Mark envisioned. "So we rescaled that shot down substantially and extended the water out to the edge of the frame. Mark captured a little library of underwater elements from the baby's room as full frame elements. We were able to rescale these elements and pepper them into this shot. "The western sequence was really fun and production did a fantastic job of finding a small western-esque town just north of Toronto. "Coincidentally, lead compositor Sean Cochrane had just been to Monument Valley in Utah and captured some great John Ford style backgrounds. "Using these background landscapes we were able to take this sequence even further by rotoing out the baby, mom and buildings and placed it all into an idealized wild west matte painting."

records.description: Matt Taylor, director at Titmouse in Los Angeles: "We were assigned to create a package of commercials to advertise what it feels like playing Clash Royale 2v2. "This project was like playing Clash Royale. We were constantly met with forces and challenges to defeat in order to keep the project from collapsing. "We wrapped on October 4th, two days ahead of schedule. I have my crew to thank for that, they were incredibly powerful and work insanely well under pressure. "On my way to the project's big production launch meeting I got into a car accident but still made it on time. A meeting that big you don't exactly want to concern everyone and I wasn't super injured so I didn't mention it. "Still, I was sitting there shaken and doing my best to focus on input about gladiators and hog riders – and someone didn't know what the movie ‘Gremlins' was and another person was asking in all seriousness who Ferris Bueller was and if he was a real person or not. Then that weekend my bank account got hacked. "John Watts (director, "Spiderman: Homecoming") did the live action sequences so we got to brainstorm together and saw eye-to-eye on these spots, it was cool. "At the time, I was looking after my sister's betta fish. I went over to feed it on the Friday after my car accident and decided I needed a beer. I wandered over to a bar nearby and seated right at the bar was John Watts. It was too crazy, I had the bartender send him a beer. "Working hard in Hollywood grants you the opportunity to wreck your car and buy a millionaire a beer in the same week."

records.description: Blinkink director Nicos Livesey and The London Embroidery Studio transform 227,000 meters of thread into 600+ frames of animated tapestry in this formidable launch spot for the BBC's coverage of the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia. From Blinkink: "Blending embroidery expertise and digitizing skills, the film showcases a wealth of color palettes and gradients, alternating thread textures and unique stitch patterns. "Drawing influence from traditional Russian tapestries, this work looks to the past and future, journeying through World Cup history, and previewing the most exciting talent coming up at this year's finals. "This visual style will then become the look and feel for the BBC's coverage, extending into programming graphics, website design, social media, BBC One's look, and more. "The idea will be fully realised in a real seven-meter long tapestry that will be put on public display. Moments from this year's competition will be added to the tapestry after the tournament's completion, creating a historical record of the 2018 World Cup."

records.description: Tour through 150 years of Wimbledon tennis, from a 19th century farmer's field to modern sport spectacle, with Nexus directors Alan Smith and Adam Foulkes swapping seamlessly between animation styles along the way. Smith and Foulkes: "The film features eight distinctly different visual styles and is constantly introducing new characters, so in order to maintain some narrative cohesion we structured it around the dynamic energy and flow of a single rally. "This also gave us that alternating left to right experience that is so intrinsic to the sport. "We chose different historical illustration styles which could immediately capture the spirit of each era, such as Victorian lithographs, the languid elegance of the 20s, overlaid colorization of the 70s, an 80s action film poster and a graphic novel style of the 90s."

records.description: Taylor Shortall, social media coordinator at Psyop in Los Angeles: "It's not often you get to create a project that can make a positive impact on the world. "This spot highlights Adidas' new UltraBOOST PARLEY shoes, the latest in their collaboration with Parley for the Oceans. Each pair of shoes prevents approximately 11 plastic bottles from entering our oceans. "The original brief was to create a fairly straightforward plastic-to-thread-to-shoe story, which was to play out on the surface of the shoe. "Although we liked the idea, we felt that the story deserved a more indepth treatment that also lined up with their wider social media-inspired campaign. "We wanted to get across the community spirit/effort that was making it possible for consumers to help stop plastic waste from entering our oceans and the mixed media approach felt right for that. "We went a little off brief with our treatment, but the guys at TBWA and Adidas supported our vision fully. "The fiber is not only the actual production process, from collected bottle to shoe, but it is also very metaphorical: the thread that connects everything. It shows how every action has a consequence and how the universe is connected – we can't isolate one thing from another. "Balancing the number of different styles was a challenge, but also a big reason why we were into the project as it gave us a chance to mix the best of Golden Wolf and Psyop into one piece." Jonah Friedman, technical director at Psyop: "We needed to make hundreds of these, CG embroidered patches to animate in stop motion, so we had to be very efficient. "Our solution was a new system, called the Patchtwiner, a system and toolbox for artists to turn 2D animation into properly 'entwined' patches. "Every frame of our animation looks as though an artist stitched a bespoke patch, creating contours and laying down stitches to represent the image in the best way possible. "Stop motion results in imperfections, and we recreated those for ourselves. The patches are differently deformed on every frame, as if they were sewn to a piece of fabric that wouldn't sit still. The light jitters on every frame, and the effect is complete." Psyop founder Marco Spier: "This project is very close to my heart. I got involved with Parley for the Oceans from the very beginning and having the opportunity to help spread the message together with Adidas and TBWACHIATDAY has been a great honor. "This is bigger than us. This is about survival. Psyop has helped a lot of brands to get their message out, so now it's time for us the make the ocean our biggest client." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: Taylor Shortall, social media director / PR liaison at Psyop in Venice, CA: "Travel Oregon wanted to do something a little different with their campaign this year. "Historically they would capture all the beautiful parts of Oregon on film but there was an openness to try something a little more magical, something that would spark the imagination. "W+K came to us with a lovely story and the thought of approaching this in a more traditional 2D animation style. "We wanted this story to flow from one moment to the next without it being jarring and taking you out of the magic. It was a fun puzzle trying to figure out how to gently move from one environment to the next. "We collaborated on refining the story making sure we covered enough landscape without anything feeling too rushed editorially. "We also wanted each landscape to feel like it had its own special quirk, whether it be a frog reading a newspaper, kids riding a giant bunny, or whales forming out of clouds. We wanted that whimsy to appear throughout without it feeling heavy-handed. "All of these landscapes were painted by hand but they needed to be recognizable as places that exist, so we had some creative license but it was a fine balance. "Because there were many artists working on it, we needed to make sure the illustration styles for each landscape felt similar. There was a constant process of refinement and adding details to bring everything together. Sun Creature did an amazing job with this."

records.description: Charlotte Arnold, executive producer at Blacksmith in New York: "The agency approached us in October 2017 to discuss a project they had in the works for a while about a drone delivering beer around the world for the World Cup. "With our passion for drone photography, we jumped at the chance to get involved. Our suggestion was to build a real hero drone and to fly and shoot him practically as much as possible. "We would then use a fully CG version of the drone for the more involved character animation to help with the personality, which was one of the key goals. We wanted the audience to feel for this drone. "Our production schedule was fast and furious. We kicked off the first shoot in Moscow in November 2017. We shot the Luzhniki Stadium (which is featured at the end of the spot) and Red Square. Then continued filming in January 2018, in Rio, South Africa and Shanghai. "Once in editorial, we coordinated with the editor Ross Birchall at Saints Editorial. As the VFX carried so much of this story, our team delivered elements, such as pre-vis, to help in the edit process. "Working closely with the Anomaly team and Saints, we were then tasked with bringing this campaign to every part of the globe, targeting cities in Russia, Argentina, China, England to name a few. "The design process was fairly traditional in the sense we started off drawing really rough sketches, lots of them, until we were happy with the drone silhouette. "We then moved into details, studying various types of engineering reference such as concept cars and motorcycles. We wanted the drone to feel futuristic and modern but somehow keeping a retro vibe, representing the legacy of the brand. "We started exploring creating facial features in a mechanical way, using objects such as cameras for eyes. It felt like the obvious thing to do at the time, but we were struggling to convey the range of emotions that we needed to, alongside creating a likable character. "That's where the digital face idea came into the mix. It was a way for us to communicate emotions in a very simple and playful way which the viewer could quickly read, whilst also keeping the design modern. "Everyone is familiar with emojis and smart phone screens so it felt like the right design language to communicate in. "As always our approach was to help achieve as much as we can practically in camera. "With the drone technology available today, we were able to design our hero around a current drone in order to fly it and shoot as much as we could in camera, especially the beer delivery shots in which people were interacting with the drones. "We very carefully designed our drone to work as a shell that could be retrofitted on top of the Inspire 2 drone manufactured by DJI, the current leading drone manufacturer in the world. "Our designers had to ensure the design was elegant but functional and would not interfere with the Inspire's rotors, weight and WiFi signal. "Once we had our design locked we approached Legacy Effects, the team that built the real Iron Man suit for the movie amongst other practical models for Hollywood. They took our digital model, 3D printed it and created a mold to be able to make multiple versions from light-weight material. "Legacy made three in total and also created the mechanism to hold the beer bottle so we could hand off the bottle to a person whilst flying the drone on set. "We knew that a large portion of the project would need to be achieved digitally but through this process, we managed to shoot some of the close-ups in camera, which made all the difference. "Finding a balance between real life dynamics and character was a big part of the exploration stage. records.description: Marcel Pelzer, creative and managing partner at dondon in Berlin: "The brief was to promote a breakdown service for cyclists offered to members of the German automobile club ACV. "The idea read like ‘... an animated crash-test dummy breaks out of its monotonous life and discovers cycling. Schedule: "Eight weeks from shoot to final delivery."

records.description: Director Ree Treweek: "We have long been admirers of the Hendrick's Gin aesthetic. Its Victoriana surrealism is so aligned with our style that you can imagine our delight when we were approached by agency Quaker City Mercantile to create an animated spot. "We loved the idea that the architecture itself reflects the theme of the spot, and is alive and changing . "Our commuters' office block works like an old-fashioned clock hand, while the homes of our lead characters resemble an alligator and a swordfish. "We played with scale within the environments and built on the idea that things are constantly changing, from the lighting to the sky tones." "Tulips and Chimneys created the layered illustrated artwork in Photoshop then animated and composited in After Effects adding grain, vignettes, dust, scratches, film burn, and light leaks associated with old film stock."

records.description: Director Keng-Ming Liu at Bito in Taipei, Taiwan: "Tatung is a well-known appliances brand in Taiwan founded in 1918. They wanted to discard their image as old, boring, and prudent and try to communicate with a wider range of their consumers, like late 20s, 30s people but still keep their die-hard fans. "The main creative challenge of this project was how to change the company's conservative image in Taiwanese minds. "For this purpose, we proposed combining mixed-media video with the hottest music genre (rap) to make this video. Fortunately, our client gave us lots of room to make the bold creativity. "Another challenge was writing the lyrics. It was the first time our copy director, who used to write advertising copy, tried to write Rap lyrics. "We started at the beginning of January, and the music was the first step we worked on, because we needed the lyrics to lock up the story structure. "After the lyrics were fixed, we started to design the style frames for each line, and delivered the first animatic on Jan 23. The final delivery was made Mar 14."

records.description: Director Zac Ella at Agile Films in London: "The client wanted to create a multimedia campaign for the release of the Glitch SS18 soccer cleat ‘Unexpect Me' series. "The films needed to be full of surprises, clashing different elements together to emphasize the unexpected quality of these two-part boots. "Main client instructions: We needed to included the two-part changeability ino the opening of brand and pack films. This was to show how the boots are made of two assets - the inner sole and the outer skin, making them totally unique. "Main creative challenge: Making sure that each film was unique to the individual pack style and included original assets that weren't repurposed. "Production stories: We shot the professional players Nelson, Solanke and Kimpembe in London, Manchester and Paris which was lots of fun! "With all post being done in-house at Agile, we are taken through a mixed media edit of animation and collage, mainly styled on 90's retro graphics and classic Microsoft computer interface. "The pop-up section features around 20 individual looping gif animations that were all bespoke creations influenced by the boots. The street fighter sequence required two weeks of hand drawn animation and character design. "As all deliveries were for the same week, we had almost a full studio of animators working on the project and two editors. Due to various formats and translations, we had over 100 deliverables."

records.description: Co-director Alan Smith: "There have been many memorable BBC Olympics title spots created over the years, so the pressure was on from the start to bring something special to the party. We tried to bring a new visual approach to portray the intense drama of winter sports. Nexus: "From the beginning, the ambition was to focus on the feeling that fear and anxiety induce in top level athletes rather than simply represent it as a physical monster. "The creative focus became how to dramatize the negative emotions that must be conquered in order to succeed. This drove the team towards a more shapeshifting, morphing animation style. "Smith & Foulkes researched live-action filming techniques for action sports in the quest to achieve an authentic sense of movement through a 3D space and a team of artists at Nexus Studios worked to create the entirely 2D spot which was drawn and animated in a virtual environment using emerging VR cinematography software. "Working in this way and with a perceivable depth provided the ideal testing ground and enabled the team to experiment at an early stage and consider different camera angles, just as if you were shooting in live action and with the sensibility of having a handheld camera."

records.description: Matt Tremaglio, 2D artist at MPC: "We didn't have the turnaround time to create a robot in CG, so we hashed out a plan with the production company and practical effects company to bring life to a puppet, removing the wires and rods that moved the puppet on set. "We used clean plates, rotoscoping and object tracking to achieve this end in post-production, utilizing the tools of Flame and Nuke. We had just about two weeks to accomplish the tasks at hand, including finishing the main :60 commercial and several teaser trailers. Tobey Lindback, 2D: Apart from removing the puppeteers and all the sticks controlling her, recreating the backgrounds and sort out any reflection issues on the table and elsewhere, we were also faced with the challenge of replacing the dialogue that Evelyn delivered. "This meant we had to rebuild a lot of her face entirely. First we had to plan out when each word was being said, then line the plates up in Flame and Nuke Studio to be able to determine that the parts we used from the footage worked with the audio. "We ended up stitching together several takes of her delivering certain lines, then warped the different takes seamlessly into each other using Nuke and Flame. "Since Evelyn's head was in such different positions for each take we needed to use for certain words, and due to the nature of how her face was moving while talking – jaw moving quite a lot as well as her cheekbones and general face profile being different for each take – we ended up completely removing the head and replacing it with one where we had stabilized the various takes, put it onto a neutral head that we then tracked and composited back onto her body." Schedule: "26 days from shoot to delivery."

records.description: A definite contender for top spot of Super Bowl LII, this rap battle stars Peter Dinklage and Morgan Freeman (plus cameos from Busta Rhymes and Missy Elliott) with The Mill handling 2D and 3D elemental VFX. Comly, 3D lead at The Mill in LA: "We're accustomed to going big when it comes to fire and explosions, so our initial tests were pretty extravagant. "The FX artists turned the room into this raging inferno with fire, explosions, smoke, and fiery elements flying everywhere. It was awesome. "But once we saw the raw footage taken and how amazing it was, we quickly realized our main challenge would be to find ways to enhance the already incredibly dynamic footage captured on set without detracting from the performance. "So we set out to find ways to subtly add layers of depth and richness to the room while still letting the viewer take in what was captured practically. "We used CG smoke, atmospherics, airborne ash, and heat haze to give organic life to the set. For Peter's fire breath at the end, we went back and forth with size and velocity. Initially we had him breathing fire like he had a flamethrower in his mouth. We ended on something we dubbed the "baby dragon". "For the ice room, the creative challenge was how could we visually communicate this room was instantly going from room temperature to below freezing as Morgan Freeman walks through it? "For the ice wall transition, the creative questions were: What does it look like? How thick is it? How wide is it? How fast does it move? Does it melt? Does it break? What shape or form does it take? It's so subjective. "In the end we settled on a more ‘wet ice' look that froze over and traversed the room in chunks like you would see at the edge of a frozen lake. "Once we found the right shading and the right shape, we had to figure out how we were going to make the ice appear out of thin air and then go away to reveal the iced plate behind it. "We ended up revealing the ice chunks in the predefined organic cellular fractal pattern, instantly freezing and generating geometry as Morgan passed by. "Then after a certain lifetime, the generated FX ice geometry would selectively either contract in shape and melt, or parts would sheet off the wall and fall to the ground leaving behind the frozen plates. "Aside from the CG ice transition we were going to put on the walls and furniture, we tried to find a way to introduce cold smoke volumes to not only give visual temperature cues but to also give movement and life to the plates. "We looked at a lot of references of dry ice and liquid nitrogen to try and get the speed and turbulence of the volumes right. "We didn't want to cover his mouth or his performance too much with cold breath, so we added it more coming down off the walls and in an ambient manner in the space behind him. "Probably the biggest technical challenge was the inability to use motion control for the ice room due to shooting schedule. "So we had to attempt to rebuild the frozen rooms in 2D using a mix of compositing and a lot of matte painting to make it appear as if the room temperature space and the frozen space were all shot in the same take. "Fortunately, we were able to get good LIDAR from the set that helped us create really good tracks."

records.description: Josh King, senior VFX producer at Framestore in London: "We were initially briefed with creating a fully ceramic, sentient piggy bank. "This developed into a furry, photoreal creature that displayed both recognizable pig-like and puppy-like features, but also leaned heavily on the form of a traditional ceramic piggy bank. Most important of all, our Piggy needed to be very cute. "The main creative challenges lay in finding that magic point between a photoreal animal and a ceramic piggy bank – real world, but not cartoon-like – and in creating a character that was cute enough to compete with a barrel of kittens. "There's a fine line between cute and creepy when you're working with a furry fleshy sphere with a face. Piggy also had to appear older than you may think, worn and ‘lived in', as it were. "We worked a lot on the overall shape of the pig, and the size, shape and sculpt detail of its features to create a soft and friendly appearance, that inferred both naivety and a confident curiosity. "The main technical challenge involved the intrinsic physical limitations of a traditional piggy bank: the size of the limbs, and the lack of knees or a neck. "It was a challenge to build a creature capable of zipping around the streets and twisting its head to the extremes, as denoted in the storyboards. "We did animation motion tests on an early rigged concept model to see how much movement we could get out of a creature with such a form. "These tests helped inform the shoot, where the director could reference how far and fast Piggy might be able to travel over a shot. We then worked on our model and built it up to a state in which it could carry out the actions desired. "The other main technical challenge was the sheer amount of interaction between the actors and Piggy, both in its full form and in specific smashed pieces which also had to be glued back together. "We supplied the on-set art department with the key dimensions of the character prior to the shoot. This allowed a model Piggy stand-in to be made, to allow the actors to interact with something of the correct scale and color that we could later replace. "Piggy was created using ZBrush and Maya for the creature modelling, Mari for the texture work, Maya for rigging and animation, Houdini for groom, FX and lighting, and Nuke for compositing." Schedule: six months.

records.description: Nicolas Cantarelli, CGI director and on set supervisor at Laposta in Buenos Aires: "Dallas Pets Alive is a non-profit organization that saves dogs and cats instead of euthanizing them. The agency Dieste partnered with Spotify to create Spoty Play: playlists that match listeners with adoptable dogs. "So far the campaign has been very successful and 90 percent of the dogs were adopted in just one month. "Here at LAPOSTA designing Jam (the mechanical dog) was our main challenge but the most fun because it gave us the opportunity to remember and do research of all the retro musical devices we used in the 80's and 90's, or even much earlier. "So the process had like a nostalgic feeling. And we chose very carefully what to use in each part of his body, so the animators could make him run, bend, jump and also express emotions that make you feel this robot dog can bark or drink water from the toilet as a real dog would do. "The main technical challenge was making believe that Jam was there. We had to fake the interactions with the sheets. We used a blue mockup of Jam to have reference of its scale and we got a real boombox to have reference of lighting and shadows. "Gabriela, the actress, did a very good job imagining Jam was there, where there was nothing. When we comp him on the scenes it matched perfectly and you can feel a real interaction between them. "The first part of the process was the research and design of Jam – that took two weeks until we were all happy with the character. "Then we had to model him, give him textures and little details to achieve his cute and cool look. Then comes the rigging, that is the process where you give him the ability to move. The best thing was that every artist put a lot of love in every shot. "Sebastian Lopez knocked on LAPOSTA's door for the first time with this project knowing that he would need a post house that not only shared his passion but also his work ethic. "As he was showing us the first storyboard we fell in love immediately and we got on board with the whole team. "We have a nice anecdote that illustrates the passion we put into the whole process. We wanted a shot where Jam barks at some birds, that typical scene of dogs chasing pigeons to have some fun. "So we went to a park and there it was, the perfect scenario, a whole bunch of pigeons standing on a grass landscape. We were about to shoot it when a tractor came and, in just one second, everything we had planned got ruined. "But we said to the director, don't worry just shoot the plate, we are going to add the pigeons in post. "There were other anecdotes that made this project very memorable, but most importantly it was a true labor of love that helped bring this project to life. And it will be the saved dogs that will make it stay in our hearts forever." Schedule: two months for post production.

records.description: Ole Peters, managing partner and ECD at Sehsucht in Hamburg: "At the heart of the campaign is a 44-ton, amber-like block installation, with an original 1979 model G-Class Mercedes SUV suspended inside. "This installation was produced in Hamburg then shipped to Detroit to be exhibited at the North American International Auto Show to celebrate that these first Mercedes-Benz G-Class cars are still on the road today and many of the iconic design elements from the original model can be found in the new generation G-Class models released this year. "Part CG, part live action, this film needed to take inspiration from both this epic installation concept and the new G-Class. Transitioning between macro perspectives of amber resin, to featuring the three new models of G-Class, each in their own unique environment. "The film starts in a wide cosmos of amber with the camera zooming to a macro perspective of the resin, showing insects and dirt detail trapped within the amber. "Since there is no way to travel through the solid material in real life, we had to reimagine this journey, building all the elements in CG, including the final installation and suspended car. "Apart from technical tasks such as building the insects in 3D, we also had the challenge of finding the right balance in the amount of cracks, dirt and air bubbles in the art direction of each shot. "The next step was to define the correct level of defocus and refraction necessary for the illusion that the camera is traveling through amber. "The amber world functions as a vehicle that transports the viewer from one world to the next. As such, we had to develop several transitions to move from CG into live action and back again. "The team invested in an upfront research period which was key in order to create a fluid journey throughout these transitions. The pack-shot in particular had to be as close to the real installation as possible, featuring all three models and the amber-cube with the original G Class staged in an industrial environment. "The trickiest part here was that the real world setup would only happen after work on the film had been completed. "Filming for the desert and green landscapes was shot on location in the Spanish Pyrenees. While the desert shots required standard clean-up work, the green landscape was transformed, using 3D matte paintings and compositing, to give the appearance of an Iceland-esque terrain. "For the city location, the challenge was much bigger. Due to the high security surrounding the new car models, filming on location in a real city was not possible. "Drawing on a mix of Gotham City and Bladerunner as inspiration, Sehsucht created a variety of buildings, road structures and signage for the scene. In order to create realism the team also created a special method to generate unique lighting and furnishings for each individual room in every single building."

records.description: Richard Payne, animator at Shotopop in London: "Spike wanted a cinematic animation to showcase a series 10 of Ink Masters. They had a loose concept, then my co-director Dipankar further developed it and created storyboards. "The biggest challenge, as with many projects these days, was time! With a relatively small team it was a constant juggling act to get all the artwork done in the seven-week schedule and avoid bottlenecks. "We used a combination of hand-drawn cel animation and After Effects puppet tool animation. Making those two animation styles work together was also a challenge. "The battle scene section required a lot of work, getting all the smoke effects and other tiny details in there took some time. "This was one of those rare jobs when the brief was great and the client was awesome. It was a pleasure to work on and the team was great." Schedule: "We began storyboarding mid September and completed the project November 27th. About 10 weeks in total, with about seven weeks actual production time."

records.description: Nirad "Bugs" Russell (senior producer), Gregory Gangemi (CG lead) and Nathan Kane (shoot/VFX supervisor) at The Mill in New York: GG: "The brief was to create an epic spot that really conveyed the feeling of being thrown into the VR world of Skyrim. We interpreted that as an opportunity to push the look and feel of the Skyrim world for the new generation of VR gamers." NK: "Getting the scale of the Dragon to feel right was definitely the biggest challenge of this job. We spent a lot of time in animation to make sure the dragon felt like it had enough weight. "We also created a lot of environmental effects that added to the weight of the dragon, like the snow interaction on impact and subtlety of wind created by the dragon's wings. "The fire created by the dragon was also an extremely challenging effect to pull off. After discussing it with the director Wayne McClammy, we all agreed that we needed to capture something in camera. "We did extensive tests with different flame throwers to give us the desired look of the fire. The in-camera fire would act as the main body of the effect, but we also combined CG fire for extra shape and intensity." BR: "We received assets about a month before the shoot to get ourselves ready for the scale of the dragon. The production included two 20-hour shoot days." GG: "Our 3D pipeline is Maya-Arnold based, with sculpting in ZBrush and effects done in Houdini. Comping was done in Nuke and matte painting in Photoshop. "One interesting note was that at the start of the job, Autodesk was in-house working on their new effects tools for Maya. Todd Akita helped them to work out some kinks by using some of the Skyrim shots as test cases."
