records.description: Jordi Barés (creative director) and Ben Cronin (VFX supervisor) at Framestore in London: "Framestore's brief was to deliver Paddington, complete with all of the nuances and character we see on the big screen, within a fairy tale-esque Christmas commercial. "Along with Paddington Bear himself, we knew there would also be set extensions, a digi-double, a certain number of additional assets that couldn't be used from the movie and a whole lot of expectation surrounding this highly anticipated Christmas campaign. "We had an extensive pre-vis period in which to iron out the narrative to director Daniel Kleinman's liking, followed by an involved shoot and a 12-week period from plates for post. "The advertising team's ability to work hand-in-hand with our film division (responsible for the VFX in both the Paddington and Paddington 2) would be of paramount importance in getting Paddington to perform just as he does in the movies. "Creative consistency was key for Paddington. Our team was uniquely positioned to embrace the film division's approach, tools and processes, whilst also absorbing the artists' collective years of knowledge of working on the bear. "Film and advertising tool sets, typically, are different. In this case, given the importance of our character and the need to create a believable, emotional performance, we embraced the film pipeline, which was a brilliant (and steep) learning curve for us all. "We were lucky to have the incredible wealth of knowledge of the film team to guide us through. Once we established scenes and assets the pipeline was a thing of beauty – we found incremental changes flew through it. "Our production team also had a more integral role on this project, with a greater administrative workload; they worked tirelessly to ensure we had answers to problems before they even happened." Schedule: 12 weeks of post production.

records.description: Marc Bodin-Joyeux and Emilie Walmsley, producers at Passion Paris: "This film is part of the Manor department store Christmas campaign made for the Swiss market. "From the start we had a clear understanding of the tone and the humor. We did however have a very open brief regarding the look and feel. "The directors AAO ran with this and we were lucky enough to get designers of the caliber of Peter de Seve, Francois Moran and Thien-Co Phan onboard with whom we developed the Manor world. "Though the whole film is 2:15 long, the story is very dense so every frame counted and the storyboarding phase was huge. "We also needed to tell the whole story without dialogue, so the animation had to be spot on for all audiences to be able to understand the story instantly. "We wanted to create a rich world, that did not look conventional and would draw the audience in. The main challenge was to perfectly meld together the 2D environments and CG characters. Rick Thielem creative director at RedKnuckles in London: "Making sure the craftiness of the initial concept artwork, moodboards and storyboards translate well into 3D is always a challenge. "With animation, creative and technical challenges go hand in hand and are one and the same. "Translating 2D to 3D, keeping animation styles consistent, making sure our characters deform properly without needing cloth simulation in every shot, facial rigging that works with a non simulated hair approach and being clever balancing time and budget and what is achievable. "All of these are both technical and creative challenges at the same time, because even though there are sweat and tears to solve technical aspects in a balanced way without compromising design, we also need to make sure it looks great every step of the way and consistent throughout shots when trying to translate to 3D the crafty, organic, analog essence of what makes 2D great. "It was a truly international collaboration with the director in Sweden, the agency and Passion Paris in France and the animation created in London for a Swiss client. "We mainly use HP computers, making full use of cloud rendering. We use Maya with Pixar's Renderman, Marvelous Designer and Nuke." Schedule: Six months.

records.description: Director, Adam Berg in Stockholm, Sweden: "Traffic jams are a widespread problem in every major city across the globe. The time spend in a car just waiting increases every year and the space needed for parking is also a problem. "Instead of using vehicles to illustrate the challenge of too much traffic, it was decided to use people carrying cardboard boxes around their waist. "We soon realized that to create the massive impact of people with boxes, we would have to look at crowd simulation. "Even though the production required a lot of extras, there would not be enough of them to fill up the streets of Bangkok or enough time to shoot the number of plates needed to get the effect for every scene. "The main technical hurdle in the project was the use of anamorphic lenses that always require more attention for the matchmovers and compositors. "Extracting camera data required both extra work on set with lens charts for the old Hawk lenses and also extra work with the undistortion of the plates before adding boxes and crowds. "Before we received the final edit we had a month of pre-production, creating assets and also testing simulations of boxes flooding and crowd simulations. "Stockholm post house Swiss completed 26 VFX shots during a three-week schedule. "The film can be seen on TV and cinemas in several Asian countries."

records.description: Director Hans-Christoph Schultheiss and lead 3D artist, Daniel Jahnel at Sehsucht in Hamburg: "In Germany, the transition to renewable energy sources is in full swing but not everybody is attracted to the way it is communicated by the suppliers. "With this idea in mind the agency tried to approach the subject of green energy without any moralizing undertone, but in a humorous and light-hearted way. "The agency approached us with a very early version of the script including the main characters and the payoff 'Guter Stoff. Grüner Strom.' ('Good stuff. Green energy.'). "At this point art direction was pretty much undefined and we were asked to make suggestions. But the main question was about storytelling. How do we turn a written idea into a film? "As we never seriously considered an abstract, super-stylized character design, but rather a realistic look for the birds, it meant we couldn't score points with the client by showing some neat character studies in the pitch phase. "Instead, we focused all our efforts on the script from the very beginning and carved out a detailed screenplay with the help of a comedy writer. "At the time, it felt quite strange not to present any style frames in the pitch and first production steps. But when you aim for a realistic look – a look which is complicated to create – it doesn't make any sense to prove your ambition with hastily knocked-up style frames. "Regarding animation, the biggest challenge was to find the right balance between lifelike behavior and characteristic personality. "We wanted to establish a somewhat realistic look and feel, as we felt a cartoony simplification like 'Angry Birds' etc. would have lowered the message to an abstract level. Yet we also wanted our characters to be engaging: Three little (or rather four) little stoners who get high on green electricity. "We invested a lot of research time on birds in general, before starting to design workflows or making decisions on how to approach the problems. "An ornithologist from the local natural history museum came to our office and helped us to understand the anatomy of birds better, resulting in more precise models and rigging mechanisms. "Feathers are a particular challenging in the computer graphics world due to the complex organic quality one is trying to recreate, both in terms of look and feel. "There are really only two ways of approaching realistic feathers or plumage: One is the simple way of textured and opacity mapped geometry and the second is remodeling feathers down to their basic components including barbules/barbs/quills all on a renderable curve basis. So every feathers consists of a few hundred curves in the end. "We went down this second route as we felt it was the only way to capture the necessary detail we would need for the very slow edit and extreme close-ups of the characters. "So for the modeling process we built a Houdini asset to be used within Maya, where we started modeling all the main flight feathers of the three birds in a semi-automatic way based on reference photos. "All plumage feathers were generated in a more procedural way straight within Houdini making every feather unique. The main flight feathers are all rigged and keyframe-animated by the animators. "After this we used collision geometry of the main feathers plus the body to simulate against the dynamic plumage using Numerions Carbon within Houdini. The result is a ton of renderable curves that we export to Arnolds ASS format for rendering. "The project took six months start to finish, with an extensive three month pre-production phase including R&D, refining the screenplay and creating a detailed animatic. "The film is the heart of a larger campaign and is accompanied by a range of print motifs, social media content and online material. All visual content is rendered in the same way as in the film. "We used Maya for rigging and animation, Houdini for grooming and simulation in conjunction with Carbon Plumage. Modeling was done in ZBrush and texturing in Mari, Substance Painter and Photoshop. Some Yeti was also used for fur. Everything was rendered in Arnold." Schedule: six months.

records.description: Kirk Hendry, director at HUSH in London: "It was clear from the first time I read the 'Dancing on Ice' proposal that this was going to be a wonderful directing opportunity. "The script was really strong and presented immediate visual ideas for both story and characters that made the boarding and animatic stage one of the most enjoyable I can remember. "It was an idea that was simple, clear, dramatic, touching and slightly ridiculous. We loved it. "The intense and exciting journey that the contestants of 'Dancing on Ice' undertake is at the heart of the show. One of our key aims was to mirror this effort in the animation. "We wanted to capture the progressive levels of ability as well as the feelings of joy and achievement felt throughout the process. It's a lot to convey in 60 seconds so our challenge was in finding the right balance in the narrative so the payoff didn't come too early or late. "To show the work that goes into these amazing moves, we were careful to include details such as the heaving chests at the end of the routine." "It was this excitement that inspired HUSH during pre-production, and the rest of the team in Stockholm during production, where we set up camp for several weeks. "The plan was to make the first half of the film feel like a wildlife documentary and try to play down any anthropomorphism so as not to tip off the audience as to what would to happen later. "I thought this would be the biggest performance challenge to get credible polar bears with all the subtle nuances, but the very talented team at Goodbye Kansas came out very strong from the beginning using a mixture of keyframe and motion-capture techniques. "It was one of those jobs that was fully formed from the beginning, with the great script, and the dominos fell from there – with every department plussing it along the way. I was just lucky to be part of it." Schedule: eight weeks.

records.description: Ben West, creative director at Framestore in Los Angeles: "I was giving a talk at ComicCon recently and discovered the huge interest fans have in seeing their heroes (like the Hulk) break out into sub-stories and plots outside those you see in films. "What's important is maintaining character integrity and the mythology of the worlds we create. Across each platform, continuity is critical. "Animating a character requires an intimate knowledge of performance. The benefits of exploring that performance in film brings a strong foundation to launch into other platforms. "With the Hulk we knew the fundamentals of his expression and physical performance. This allowed us to approach the sequence for Renault with confidence. From a creative standpoint, having that foundation allows us the freedom to push things further in terms of choreography, composition and performance detail. "We have a very tight transition pipeline from film to commercials, rides, etc. This simple exchange of characters allows us to maintain asset integrity with regards to shaders, rigging, grooming and so on. "With any CG character there are technical challenges beyond the animation that involve muscle slimming and sculpting, essentially a creature FX workflow. "This requires an iterative approach to take a character from being good to great. It's detail that to an untrained eye isn't noticeable but makes all the difference to believability when it comes to realistic characters. "This is spot will be seen on TV and in cinemas across Brazil. Expect more Hulk awesomeness from our film team and the feature film release of 'Thor: Ragnarok' later this year." Schedule: six weeks.

records.description: VFX supervisor Diarmid Harrison Murray at MPC in Los Angeles: "The brief was to create a full CG photo-real ostrich that would take us on an inspirational journey. The initial challenge was planning what could be shot practically and what needed to be CG. There were many discussions on approach and Matijias (director) wanted to get as much in camera (or reference) as possible. "Even though a lot of these shots ended up being replaced in CG it gave us a perfect reference to match to. "The animation had to be perfect. We had 90 seconds to show a lot of varying emotion. There is a fine line when you break the barrier of realism. For example, the moment the ostrich takes off had to be just right. Push it too far and you'll lose your audience. "Building a large creature that hasn't been done before is always a challenge. Ostriches are generally nine feet high with a six-foot wingspan and have a huge variation of feathers. "They're extremely detailed creatures that date back to the early Miocene era, some 20-23 million years ago. They're as old as dinosaurs. "Getting her run cycle right took a lot of R&D. They are able to run up to speeds of 70 mph. We had to find the right speed to work across every single shot. She had to have the energy but also look in control and grow in confidence as she progresses. "If you study nature footage, ostriches often look very clumsy. The way they use their wings to balance looks uncoordinated, like it's their first time. We resourced a lot of footage and found references for a lot of these shots. "For example there was a great clip of an ostrich race where one falls and rolls over. It was a great foundation for the animators to work with. "We also had to combine a lot of takes of the real ostrich, all shot with different camera moves. A lot of stitching took place. "On top of that, the plates we used had to have the real ostrich painted out. This is very time consuming given that we had a lot of parallax and perspective changes on the shots. "The show was run with artists and clients across four different time zones. We utilized MPC's global talent, which meant we effectively worked 24 hours a day on it. Schedule: "We started with modeling and pre-vis the end of September 2016. The edit locked around Nov 1, and wrapped at the end of March and shipped April 3rd."

records.description: The Mill joint head of 3D Michael Chapman: "The main challenge of this job was to bring a sense of drama to the iconic sporting locations through the butterfly motif. "The Mill's VFX team worked on a total of 73 shots, producing over five million butterflies for the larger stadium shots. They also carried out extensive matte painting work to enhance the stadium scenes, crafting some of the stadiums entirely in CG. "The team meticulously modeled six species of butterflies taken from real life references to create the swarms. "On set, we shot numerous butterflies to study how they behaved and reacted to the many different lighting conditions which we filmed in. "We based our shading and lighting on these references, tweaking the patterns of each species of butterfly to suit the environments so their presence felt tangible. "We knew the animation of these creatures was going to be integral to the whole piece so we focused on creating flap cycles from the reference we had captured on set and from other nature documentaries. "We then used these animations to drive simulations for the large-scale shots, making sure each individual butterfly had realistic movement. We also hand-animated the foreground butterflies in each shot to give us precise control over their position and movement. "We used Maya to build and animate the butterflies, we simulated the large flocks in Houdini and then we rendered through our in-house render procedural in Arnold within Maya."

records.description: Martin Woelke, managing director at Sehsucht in Hamburg, Germany: "The brief was to create a film that teased the launch of the new Mercedes X-Class, the world's first premium pickup truck that will enter the global market in 2018. "With this film the client wanted something that was as original and new as the pickup itself, that would leave the audience both impressed and curious to know more. "The core statement in the client's brief was 'Introducing a new kind of tough' and it was important to create a clear visual analogy between the power and beauty of nature and the pickup. "The agency approached us with visually-driven ideas featuring epic landscapes in which the car interacts in surreal scale, pushing us to design a drive through previously unseen and impressive perspectives. "As the car will not be released until next year, we weren't allowed to feature the car prominently. All the classic rules for car commercials – the ¾ frontal packshot, framing or animation – had to be thrown out the window and we had to get creative about how to capture the spirit of the car whilst showing enough, but not revealing too much. "We started the project researching given material and stock footage similar to the concept frames. We then edited various versions which included rough CG test sequences to create visualizations that would give us a better understanding of timing, flow and dramaturgy. "Whilst coordinating a large team of in house and remote artists and subcontract vendors throughout the project, we also had to remain flexible to find the best creative solutions for problems as they arose." Schedule: "We went into full production towards the end of October and finished work on the main film (60") towards the end of March, then worked on the cutdowns and other deliverables through until June."

records.description: Giacomo Vigliar, director rep at UNIT9 Films in London: "To launch Gatorade's new electrolyte water, G Active, to the global market in a way that would be impactful and differentiate it from the competition. "They developed this product because when we exercise and sweat, we lose more than just water. Therefore we need more than water to replace what's lost in sweat; we need an active water. "So the inspiration was the product. We brought water to life and made it literally and visually active. We let the product do the talking by creating a water character that can move, run, jump and kick right in front of our eyes. "The whole process for this campaign was unlike any other. We had to develop a completely new technology capable of generating a visual and literal representation of active water. An installation that combines art, photography and science to synchronize thousands of droplets of G Active. "Of course, pre-production was crucial, and by far the most important part of the process. It took several months of planning, problem solving and signing approvals to get everything ready for the shoot. "When it comes to fitness, Gatorade believes there are no shortcuts, so we decided we should take the same approach in the production of this campaign. From the very initial stages of the concept we always knew we wanted this to be done in-camera. No tricks. "In less than 10 weeks, using more than 5,000 man hours and more than 20,000 individual parts and custom-made components, we created a life-sized animated human made entirely from liquid, which moves and interacts with physical space like a real human. "Our custom-made 'rain rig' dripped water in complete sequence and harmony. It recreated the figure of a real athlete in a liquid animation. Each unit contained 64 litres of water, with eight units running at any one time. "This meant we used half a ton of water to bring the whole system together. To make the water character true-to-life, we motion-captured a human athlete running, jumping and kickboxing. "Then data from the motion capture told the water rig when to turn its nozzles on and off. The water droplets turned on and off using a series of 2,048 switches. The team used flash-lighting to illuminate and 'suspend' the water droplets in mid air. "This meant each frame had a millimeter and microsecond accuracy. As a result we transmitted an entire layer of data through the entire system in just a microsecond. "We had to take each frame and process it in two ways. First of all to squash it, to compensate for gravitational acceleration, and second to slice it. We stored the data for each frame in a controller unit and triggered it using the camera. "To have the camera positioned at the right angle for the shot, we programmed the water rig to sync with our motion control team. Every time our motion control specialists set a camera synch and a flash, the water was dropped at that precise moment." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.description: Executive producer Nina Pfeiffer at Tulips and Chimneys in Cape Town, South Africa: "We received a detailed script from FCB Durban about Mpho, a little girl dreaming of snow in a hot arid place. "Her dreams become a reality when her parents and grandma conspire to make her dreams come true by sprinkling salt from above the rooftop of her bedroom window. "Since we needed to fit the story into 30 seconds we had to take these beautiful ideas and rework them to develop the individual personalities of the characters and the narrative in such a way that the core idea came through in the best way possible. "We decided to set the story in the Karoo as it's one of the most arid but also most interesting regions of South Africa. We felt that the vast open spaces would support the futility of our lead character's dream. "We then decided she should be living with her grandma and grandpa rather than her parents which allowed us to eliminate one of the characters in the original script and still make the situation believable as a fair number of children in SA are bought up by their grandparents for various reasons. "This allowed us to spend a little more time on her grandparents and focusing on their personalities. We then looked at the different actions that Mpho could perform in each shot making it clear that she was dreaming of snow since we would have no narration over the story. "This resulted in the fun little skits she plays out in each shot: making snow angels, riding a makeshift sleigh and dreamily staring into a snow globe. "We also ensured that Gramps was constantly tinkering on something in the background so when the fantastic pulley system is revealed in the end it's clear he's been supportive of Mpho all along. "Creatively this project really was a dream; we had a great team onboard from the client to the agency to the creative team. We can honestly say it was one of the smoothest most pleasant productions we've ever worked on. Executive producers Marc Bloch and Marco Raposo de Barbosaat at Black Ginger: "For us the biggest challenge was to translate the 2D illustrations into 3D characters and bring them to life. There was a lot of back and forth getting Mpho just right. "We wanted the spot to feel like it's taking part throughout the course of a day so lighting was going to play a vital role from the beginning. The DOP Johan Horjus was fantastic at managing this. Here are a few technical challenges and solutions he faced: "The Flickering light from the TV was created by sliding 3 cm x 3 cm blue and diffuser gels between the light hidden behind the TV, about 40 times, without moving anything else. "A 30 kg light with a camera lens was rigged 2 m up looking down, then the spot of light was reduced to shine on an area of 4 cm, only to create more definition on the stove in the kitchen. "All the long traveling shots over the landscape were shot upside-down so that we get get closer to the ground. "The warm side light on the rope and gears that grandpa build was a slither of light about 2 cm and masked off the wall with black tinfoil of about 1 cm. Only to separate it from the wall and to add some texture. "The bedside light was created from a 360 LED light. A rod that was attached to the column of the light that continued all the way down to underneath the set. This is where I turned/rotated the bedside light every second frame by hand, the increments were as small as I could possible move, about 120 times. "The inspiration of the little round bushes decorating the Karoo landscape came from a hike we did near Kalk Bay. We came across an extraordinary patch of rust-colored moss that looked just like miniature Karoo bushes and kept that in mind when briefing the concept artists "Set decorating for the outside shots was a lot of fun, the textured ground was a mixture of sand, tiny pebbles and tea! "We then added hundreds of tiny sprigs of rosemary that lead up to the larger bushes that were created with moss died different colors. "We grouped various elements together and then gently made them bleed into the other elements to create arrangements that appeared true to nature even though our plant designs were stylised. "A lot of thought went into the shape of our characters ...Mpho is shaped like an upside down triangle, her cuteness factor largely comes from her having such a big head in relation to her body and her tiny feet. "Her grandma on the other hand is bell shaped, completely the opposite or rather the reverse of Mpho. Her shape is an ode to her larger than life personality. She is definitely the matriarch of the family. "Gramps on the other hand is a skinny bean of a man. He takes up very little space in the house and is quiet and unassuming. However he observes everything so closely, and in the end it's his patient tinkering and exquisite mind that brings so much joy to Mpho and Grandma. "Mpho's sidekicks are three chickens that ended up stealing the show! We absolutely love them and are hoping we have the opportunity to developed their stories further down the line. "We enjoyed coming up with touches for the set that were truly South African: pumpkins drying out on the red roof a Karoo farm house; old ginger beer bottles typically found in old farmsteads; a coat hanger being used as the TV aerial. "We took great care in the design and ageing of the 1950's couch in the lounge. It's quite obviously been sat on for years, and grandma carefully crocheted the doilies to prevent greasy hair staining the couch. It's these tiny touches that make the spot so special." Schedule: Eight weeks pre-production, 10 days shooting and 10 weeks post production.

"This allowed us to spend a little more time on her grandparents and focusing on their personalities. We then looked at the different actions that Mpho could perform in each shot making it clear that she was dreaming of snow since we would have no narration over the story. "This resulted in the fun little skits she plays out in each shot: making snow angels, riding a makeshift sleigh and dreamily staring into a snow globe. "We also ensured that Gramps was constantly tinkering on something in the background so when the fantastic pulley system is revealed in the end it's clear he's been supportive of Mpho all along. "Creatively this project really was a dream; we had a great team onboard from the client to the agency to the creative team. We can honestly say it was one of the smoothest most pleasant productions we've ever worked on. Executive producers Marc Bloch and Marco Raposo de Barbosaat at Black Ginger: "For us the biggest challenge was to translate the 2D illustrations into 3D characters and bring them to life. There was a lot of back and forth getting Mpho just right. "We wanted the spot to feel like it's taking part throughout the course of a day so lighting was going to play a vital role from the beginning. The DOP Johan Horjus was fantastic at managing this. Here are a few technical challenges and solutions he faced: "The Flickering light from the TV was created by sliding 3 cm x 3 cm blue and diffuser gels between the light hidden behind the TV, about 40 times, without moving anything else. "A 30 kg light with a camera lens was rigged 2 m up looking down, then the spot of light was reduced to shine on an area of 4 cm, only to create more definition on the stove in the kitchen. "All the long traveling shots over the landscape were shot upside-down so that we get get closer to the ground. "The warm side light on the rope and gears that grandpa build was a slither of light about 2 cm and masked off the wall with black tinfoil of about 1 cm. Only to separate it from the wall and to add some texture. "The bedside light was created from a 360 LED light. A rod that was attached to the column of the light that continued all the way down to underneath the set. This is where I turned/rotated the bedside light every second frame by hand, the increments were as small as I could possible move, about 120 times. "The inspiration of the little round bushes decorating the Karoo landscape came from a hike we did near Kalk Bay. We came across an extraordinary patch of rust-colored moss that looked just like miniature Karoo bushes and kept that in mind when briefing the concept artists "Set decorating for the outside shots was a lot of fun, the textured ground was a mixture of sand, tiny pebbles and tea! "We then added hundreds of tiny sprigs of rosemary that lead up to the larger bushes that were created with moss died different colors. "We grouped various elements together and then gently made them bleed into the other elements to create arrangements that appeared true to nature even though our plant designs were stylised. "A lot of thought went into the shape of our characters ...Mpho is shaped like an upside down triangle, her cuteness factor largely comes from her having such a big head in relation to her body and her tiny feet. "Her grandma on the other hand is bell shaped, completely the opposite or rather the reverse of Mpho. Her shape is an ode to her larger than life personality. She is definitely the matriarch of the family. "Gramps on the other hand is a skinny bean of a man. He takes up very little space in the house and is quiet and unassuming. However he observes everything so closely, and in the end it's his patient tinkering and exquisite mind that brings so much joy to Mpho and Grandma. "Mpho's sidekicks are three chickens that ended up stealing the show! We absolutely love them and are hoping we have the opportunity to developed their stories further down the line. "We enjoyed coming up with touches for the set that were truly South African: pumpkins drying out on the red roof a Karoo farm house; old ginger beer bottles typically found in old farmsteads; a coat hanger being used as the TV aerial. "We took great care in the design and ageing of the 1950's couch in the lounge. It's quite obviously been sat on for years, and grandma carefully crocheted the doilies to prevent greasy hair staining the couch. It's these tiny touches that make the spot so special." Schedule: Eight weeks pre-production, 10 days shooting and 10 weeks post production.

records.description: Gustavo Karam, executive producer at Le Cube in Buenos Aires: "The briefing received for the project was to create one of four spots for the children's day in China promoting an adaptation of the 'Play Hard' mantra. "The campaign reimagines bandaids as 'Badges of Honor', a device to allay the concerns of overprotective parents and encourage kids to have the courage to keep going if they stumble or face setbacks on the sporting field. "Our spot was a soccer match between Zombies and Firewolves. "Besides that day when a king cobra escaped in the office, I would say, without a doubt, fitting this story into 50 seconds was the biggest challenge. "We had to work the storyboard carefully and then cut several times to achieve the right balance between what we needed to show and what we wanted to show. "2D cel-animation and characters are already part of our DNA, but the crazy schedules of the advertising universe are always a huge challenge to be surpassing." Schedule: 4.5 weeks.

records.description: Marc and Denis Bouyer, directors at Feed Me Light in London: "We were approached by London start up TrueView (our neighbors at the time) about creating a series of animated shorts for their new dating service. "Online dating changed the game of romance and courtship. Does the person on the other side of the screen really enjoy long sunset walks on the beach, or do they prefer to spend their evenings perched outside your bedroom window? "Billy Bad Chat, Six Pack Stu, Two-Faced Tony – these characters are too familiar to anyone who has online dated. "The client approached us with a set of characters that had been created based on real research on the dangerous individuals you encounter in the pursuit of love. "Labeled the 'Undateable Suspects,' the series was developed alongside Matt Verity and the team at TrueView. "Matt had a very strong sense in the tone and humor that was to be at the forefront of these videos: smart banter and dry wit. We had the easy task of pushing this further in the storytelling, look and animation. Designing them was the best part. "The approach was taken for a heavily stylised character design that ensured the characters were ambiguous and could be seen as a representation of the online personas as opposed to their real life counterparts. "Remy Dupont brought the characters to life in 3D with meshes that allowed the creative team to play with distortions and dynamics that they wanted to execute on certain character transitions. "The CG team played with development in deformers and dynamic cloth simulations for character transformations such as Six Pack Stu's inflated abs and Two-Faced Tony's big reveal. "Ludovic Habas joined the team to rig the characters using his Auto-Rig system, which was incredibly useful in creating character rigs that offered a great deal of flexibility in the short period of time that the project allowed. "As an online service, the main channel of distribution for the TrueView team was through social media and other online platforms. The framing of the short allows for a punched-in view of the character segments that is almost reminiscent of the character profiles you see on actual dating apps. "Since releasing the project, Feed Me Light have had their own first-hand experience of online dating disaster, when one of our directors recently received an anonymous birthday gift hand delivered to the office by a Tinder match that had managed to track him down to our new studio, never mind find out his birthday!" Schedule: nine weeks.

records.description: Carsten Keller, VFX supervisor (CG) and MPC's head of 3D: "This is a huge, feature-film scale project – we're talking about six films in one, crafted by over 70 artists in over 90 days. "It's the type of project that every VFX artist wants to work on. Whilst immersing our audience into the extreme worlds, we had to keep reality at the front of people's minds. "Creating so many different worlds in one film saw our VFX teams working for more than three months to craft the visual feast – teams across London, Amsterdam and Bangalore worked collaboratively to pull it off. "Just some of the tasks involved included building two entirely CG ships, which required extensive pre-vis before the shoot itself, a spacecraft – which the director wanted to shoot up close – and a sequence where the guys scale Mount Everest with a Himalayas backdrop. And not forgetting creating a 10,000-strong Roman army from a cast of 100 actors!"

records.description: Director SOMEI in Shanghai: "OPPO asked me to make a new ID video for their newly released R11 mobile phone as we have worked together for four years. "The brief is very simple. They want to keep the color and fashion tone I have already built for them, and hope to see some new breakthroughs. "And they give me three or four selling points like the curve of back shell, dual camera, and the two-line design of the antenna. No other limits, I just play around with anything I want to try. "I think the most challenging part is to make design breakthroughs based on the existing style. I really hope the audience can get some freshness from the video and I was stuck for a really long time, until two days before the deadline for conception. "I saw a video called 'Unsatisfying' and I really liked it because it had a little story in every scene. It's more than just visual, there was some psychological chemical reaction happening. Then I decide to put the selling points into different scenes and design some little stories, like the unexpected moments. "And then I found there should be something that can trigger the unexpected moment, so I put a hand in the video. "The concept was completed in seven days and then I made the animatic (most of the animation) in another seven days, and then it took three-four days to approve it. "Then I did the lighting and pondering the design; it took 15 days to make the first version, and another 10 days to do some adjustments and changes according to the comments from client. "One interesting thing is that you will not see any blue color in OPPO's commercials, because blue is the main color of the competition's brand. OPPO's color is green, so as the result even the sky is green in this video."

records.description: Anik Rosenblum, animation director at Dancing Line Productions in Vancouver: "The video was produced as a creative collaboration between the ad agency Rethink and the animation studio Dancing Line Productions. "It started with an idea to celebrate Canada's 150th birthday with a fun animated video. "After discussing a few possible themes (Canada's history, nature, beauty), it was decided to focus on respect, tolerance and kindness to one another as one of the things that make Canada special. Canadian Centre of Diversity and Inclusion came on board as a natural partner to carry this message. "So there was no project brief in a traditional sense. When the creatives at Rethink developed the song concept, they expressed some thoughts about the general look and some of the possible character actions, but overall I had full creative freedom with the visual interpretation of the song. "The greatest challenge was the tight schedule. The initial idea was to produce a 30 second video, but that had to be extended for the song concept to work. "With multiple characters to bring to life, I had to come up with economic enough design and animation, while keeping it entertaining and flowing naturally with the song. "At Dancing Line we enjoy doing hand-drawn frame-by-frame animation which is good for achieving expressive character performance, but is a laborious process, so some carefully thought out self-imposed limitations were necessary to be able to release the video in time for Canada Day. "The effort was well worth it though and I am grateful to Rethink for approaching this project with so much enthusiasm and creativity, and coming up with such a fun and animation-friendly concept. Schedule: seven weeks.

records.description: Jonathan "Wes" Westley, The Mill creative director in London: "The script called for all manner of Virgin Media's entertainment package to be depicted hurrying down a fiber optic cable in a rush to get on to viewers' screens. "Working closely with director Sam Brown, we were tasked with bringing this vision to life, from concept drawings, pre-vis, and character builds to set extensions. "Initially, we were asked to draw up a concept still of the tunnel for the scene at the end of the spot at a very early stage, which the Sam Brown used in his treatment and which looked pretty close to the final shot in the ad. "The number of CG assets we had to design and build was probably the main creative challenge – spaceships, robots, cars, bikes, people, and a teenage mutant ninja turtle. We then had to seamlessly blend them into the hectic setting. "In addition to the number of CG assets we had to build, we also had to create a CG replica of the 180-foot tunnel the action was shot in. This enabled us to extend nearly all of the tunnel shots and partially destroy this in the robot and space racer scenes. "All vehicle interior scenes were shot against grey screen and were lit by LED screens playing a CG replica of the tunnel. The explosions were shot in a miniature tunnel at 1000 fps and comped together using six different explosions to get the impact we wanted. "We starting discussions with director Sam Brown in October 2016, helping him with concept stills for his treatment. 3D design and build started in December alongside the set build in Budapest. "Shooting commenced the first week of January for five days plus another day in Jamaica to film Usain Bolt. "The set build took over two months to complete and three days to tear down. It had to be secure enough to handle vehicles, a horse and carriage, and hoards of people rushing down it. "Overall, a really impressive piece of art direction, which we then had to match and extend in VFX. Another great and hugely enjoyable Sam Brown extravaganza which we were tasked with bringing to life."

records.description: Head of production/EP: Sarah Hiddlestone at Framestore: "Featuring Microsoft's Hololens and Surface tablet, this inspirational new campaign encourages girls to stay in STEM (science, technology, engineering and math). "Framestore New York and London teams worked around the clock to deliver the visual effects for this campaign's launch on International Women's Day, 8th March 2017. "For the 'Cancer' scene Framestore did extensive environment work in pre-production including practical and CG imagery for the scene's room. records.description: Joe Ball, director at Psyop in Los Angeles: "Publicis NY came to us to create a short animated film showing off Citibank's new wealth management solution Citigold. "They wanted to appeal to affluent urbanites by showcasing a customer's story through a bold, minimal style, using a striking play of positive and negative space in Citi's gold, white and black color palette creating something simple, yet cinematic, all taking place in New York City. "The main creative challenge of the project was the balancing act of having a very minimal, limited palette design throughout but still achieving a captivating, cinematic film that never felt busy. "We wanted to create something less motion graphics heavy, not only in how we treated the animation and transitioning, but also how compositionally we could treat this more as if a filmed piece, using many different compositions, but focusing on wider, light-driven shots with a nice balance of positive and negative space. "But keeping the simplicity and minimalism of the composition was key, especially when it came to transitioning. This is why we moved from scene to scene using a lot of positive/negative space lighting animation. "Not only did it give us a simple and elegant way to transition, but it gave us an element of time passing, all while not introducing any new colors or elements into the scene. "The other main challenge was the length of the film. When final VO was sent to us, we came out to alomost two minutes. Two minutes of animation is a heck of a lot no matter which way you look at it, and certainly was daunting at first. "The main technical challenge of this film was the workflow we set up through using mainly remote artists for much of the animation. "Most creative and design was done in-house in Venice, however, the animators were located in two different states, each with their own individual time zones. "Character cel animation was being done in Chicago with Matt Everton, while comping, character, and overall magic was coming from Chris Anderson in Arkansas. Scenes would be sent to me in LA for final comp and conform. "Overall it worked smoothly, but definitely added an extra layer of planning to an already complicated project with a small team. "The other challenging aspect was making all the backgrounds and elements in each scene seamless, regardless whether they were created in 2D, 3D or cel. "While doing some backgrounds in 3D gave us flexibility to do more with the camera, getting the look to match the 2D while having the same light transitions required some R&D. "Take the final NYC skyline scene for instance: We wanted to have the same light - timelapse effect on the buildings, but we wanted to have as many buildings as you would typically see in the NY skyline. "Creating the scene in Illustrator and then animating each shadow one by one sounded torturous, so this was one of the only scenes which was fully 3D. We modeled each building out as a simple solid, with basic details like ledges, rooftops etc. "Instead of assigning a color solid shader to each building, we instead opted to use multiple passes of sun objects colored to the different brand colors to create the fills for the building colors. "This way, we could animate each of the sun objects, and just like a sunrise on a building, the fill colors could then animate how they would in the physical world, replacing shadow. "We did a pass of this for each brand color, and then brought it into After Effects where we comped each of these passes together, making the final shot we have now. Windows were created in 2D, and were parented to a null created in C4D that was put into After Effects. "Once we figured out the lighting in the big NY scene, creating some backgrounds and elements in 3D to mix with the 2D became a lot easier. "Some of my favorite memories from this project had to do with how the animators were remote, and all the time change fun which came from that. "Chris Anderson, the lead animator on the project, was working on the East Coast and would send updated animation WIPs via GIF over Google Chat every morning around the same time as my morning commute. "As excited and happy as I was to get the animation updates, I want to publicly apologize to the city of Los Angeles for how bad a driver I was during December and February. "I was constantly checking my phone in the car, getting super excited by the new animations I was seeing, but ultimately almost coming close a couple times to doing something stupid. "To make matters worse, California made checking your phone illegal in a car during the production - so I could have gotten a hefty ticket if I had gotten caught. Be safe kids, don't gif and drive!" Schedule: "Design started in early December. Animation begun in mid-late December, wrapping everything up in early February."

records.description: Ben Smith, executive creative director, The Mill in New York: "The project brief from JWT Atlanta was to create a film that celebrated the history of the US Marine Corps, in order to inspire future generations. "An underlining visual theme for the campaign was the work of sculptor Kris Kuksi [American fantastic realism]. We wanted to create a film that was inspired by his work visually, but encapsulated the key heroic moments, selflessness and the fighting spirit of the US Marine Corps. "The brief was pretty open in that sense - we were able to look through the history books and find the best moments. "The agency provided us with an eloquent and beautifully written script about the core values of the Marine Corps. Our job was to find battles and then deconstruct moments within those battles that represented the cause of the Marines into a beautiful and cinematic film. "Our first job was to literally scout history. There was a team of us that did an immense amount of research into each of the main battle arenas. "From there we proceeded to find a particular moment from a battle, distilled that into acts and then from those written acts. We would begin storyboarding based on those written descriptions. After storyboarding we blocked animation before finally finessing the sculpture. "One of the biggest creative challenges was fitting everything into our story. There is a lot of Marine Corps history out there, so finding the best moments and trying to distill those stories into 60 seconds was hard. "The whole tone, pace and feel of the film is slow, but purposely so. As soon as we tried to put too much in, or move the camera too quickly, it was at odds with the overall feel of the film. "Therefore, a big challenge was reducing the amount of story points and creating a nice visual arc within editorial. "The biggest technical challenge of the project was making each model look and feel like a real, handmade bronze sculpture. One of the things we really wanted to do was to make the whole thing feel like it was made by people. "We didn't want it to feel computer generated or synthetic. We purposely left in the human traits of fabrication such as rake marks of sculptures, tools and bumps in the camera. By adding a sense of imperfection in our shots this gives the film a handmade feel. "The team used Maya, Arnold, ZBrush for sculpting, Nuke for compositing, Photoshop for textures, along with Substance Painter for texturing, Marvelous Designer for modeling the clothing. "Getting to work with Kris Kuksi was incredibly exciting. Kris came into The Mill and we talked about his style and the rules he employs when designing and building his sculptures. This was extremely helpful to in designing our scenes, particularly the final shot of the large marine statue." Schedule: four months.

records.description: James Allen, shoot supervisor and 2D lead artist at The Mill LA: "Our job was to aid in Wieden+Kennedy's retelling of a classic story by creating a photo-real character with a real person's face and an oversized model of an egg. "Our main creative challenge was to create Humpty in three distinct stages of repair. The first stage takes place immediately after Humpty falls off the wall: shell, egg yolk, eyes and mouth scattered in a mess on the ground. "The second stage sees the aftermath of the Kingsmen's unsuccessful attempt to put him back together. In the final stage, Humpty's in the hospital. "Legacy built a fantastic practical oversized egg which we augmented and manipulated to illustrate Humpty's painful road to recovery. "One of our primary technical challenges was marrying a solid egg with a real, moving face as it spoke. It took considerable stabilizing and morphing to achieve a seamless composite. "We shot at multiple locations in LA over a period of four days last November and finished the spots in January. Schedule: six months.

records.description: Mateus de Paula Santos and Fábio Acorsi, directors at Lobo in São Paulo, Brazil: "This campaign was created for the launch of the Leica M Monochrom, the next generation of the world's first digital black and white camera. "The idea was to pay homage to the monochromatic universe, encouraging the customer to break free from the constraints of color in order to see the world with more poetic, imaginative eyes. "From the script provided by the agency F/Nazca Saatchi & Saatchi,we created over a minute of animation, largely abstract and all in black and white (naturally), inspired by two main aspects of visual representation: the symbolic and the physical. "The symbolic aspect is mostly present during the first half of the film, with minimalistic digital animations representing elements like grass, water, camera diaphragms etc. in a very iconic way. "The physical aspect manifests itself on the second part of the film, which explores analog means of image creation, such as light projections, transparencies and stop-motion animation, filmed and photographed using the M Monochrom itself. "The biggest challenge was to create a different animated sequence for each of the script's sentences, with two distinct 'flavors': a more geometric, minimalistic one for the first half of the spot, representing the rigidity of the color world; and a loose, anarchic style for the second part, where we speak of the creative freedom that black and white photography offers. "Working exclusively in black and white posed a significant challenge, for we had to create a wide pictorial variety to make the film interesting while staying within the confines of the monochrome language. "We also took quite some time experimenting and developing an ideal 'aged' look for the animation. "The digital animations for the first half of the spot were done in Adobe After Effects. For the second part, based on analog techniques, we created a lot of footage using a light projector and geometric patterns printed on transparent sheets, all shot with the Leica M Monochrom. "Leica is a brand that played a major role in establishing the language of photojournalism. We referenced this fact by employing as a recurring visual motif throughout the spot a dotted pattern, reminiscing of the traditional halftone printing process used in newspapers – while also offering a counterpoint in the form of square shapes and patterns that reference the digital pixel. "Work started in mid-February, 2017. The first week was spent researching references and developing style frames based on the text blocks into which the script was divided and split among the creative team. "On February 20 we had a meeting with the agency where we presented a basic boardomatic with voiceover and a first soundtrack experimentation. "After receiving creative input from the agency, where it was established the importance of the two distinct halves of the film, we began planning for the final version of the piece and doing digital animation tests based on the approved layouts for the first half. "This phase lasted for 13 days, until we had a complete work-in- progress preview of the spot on March 6. "With the M Monochrom in hand, we moved into production of the second half of the film, based on analog techniques like stop-motion animation and light projections. In another week of work the film was done, and delivered to the client on March 15. "The campaign will run in Brazil, France and Germany, with the spot being shown in movie theaters and online."

records.description: Smith and Foulkes, directors at Nexus Studios in London: "The main brief from the client was to make an entertaining piece of film that used an inanimate object to show how we overcome the everyday dangers that surround us. "It has a very positive message, asking us to imagine the best outcome of each potentially lethal scenario, rather than fear the worst. "Using a balloon gives you a license to show a much more ludicrous degree of jeopardy than you could with us humans, as it is clearly damageable. "This allowed the exaggerated perils of modern life that we brought into the story to be comic instead of frightening. "The song is basically the voice inside our hero's head. We treated this film as if it were a scene from 'BalloonHead The Musical', so it was critical to establish the rhythmic flow of the track before we could start to choreograph the balloon's journey. "We saw our balloon as a choreographer sees a dancer, crafting every gesture and movement to precisely synchronise with the music, so it was vitally important to lock this down at the earliest possible stage. "But the track was continually changing through production. Every time a new version of the track arrived it would have a subtly different pace and structure, so we would have to quickly adapt our balloon's movements. "I think we managed to just about exhaust the amount of dangerous situations that a balloon could possibly encounter in an urban neighborhood. And there were a few fairly unlikely ones in there too. "We tried to mix up the different ways that a balloon could meet its maker; obviously ridiculously sharp objects, but also intense heat and things that could crush it. The fun part was to stitch them all together into a choreographed flow. "We wanted to create an illustrative look that was graphically ordered but not cold and inhuman, bathed in golden light. "The difficulty was how to blend the animated 3D objects with the 2D matte paintings. This meant a lot of R&D in shading and comp to get all those soft gradients, light and shadows right." "We opted for a small crew over a longer period as if you have the luxury of a longer schedule it really means everyone can invest more time and love and really flesh out the tiny details". "There were all manner of discussions about whether our balloon changed its facial expression. "We tried various different faces to illustrate the different emotional beats of the story, but we always kept coming back to the purest idea of all: keeping it as an inanimate object with an insanely fixed grin, helplessly at the whim of natural forces. "There's just something in its optimistic little face that makes you root for it and understand what it is experiencing, allowing the audience to see those emotions without having to show them on the balloon's face." Schedule: "It was a three month schedule, starting early August 2016 and delivering at the end of October 2016."

The fun part was to stitch them all together into a choreographed flow. "We wanted to create an illustrative look that was graphically ordered but not cold and inhuman, bathed in golden light. "The difficulty was how to blend the animated 3D objects with the 2D matte paintings. This meant a lot of R&D in shading and comp to get all those soft gradients, light and shadows right." "We opted for a small crew over a longer period as if you have the luxury of a longer schedule it really means everyone can invest more time and love and really flesh out the tiny details". "There were all manner of discussions about whether our balloon changed its facial expression. "We tried various different faces to illustrate the different emotional beats of the story, but we always kept coming back to the purest idea of all: keeping it as an inanimate object with an insanely fixed grin, helplessly at the whim of natural forces. "There's just something in its optimistic little face that makes you root for it and understand what it is experiencing, allowing the audience to see those emotions without having to show them on the balloon's face." Schedule: "It was a three month schedule, starting early August 2016 and delivering at the end of October 2016."

records.description: Tom Graham, shoot supervisor & 3D lead artist at The Mill, and Michael Comly, lighting lead at The Mill in London: "The instructions were fairly simple. Everyone was in agreement that we had to make all of the CG seamless. "With full CG ocean shots with a whale and a digital double, a tree falling off a cliff, icebergs crumbling, and a rhino, we knew this would be a challenge in the amount of time we had. "The clients were mainly concerned with keeping the story clear to the viewers with so much happening." "For the CG team, the main creative challenge was art directing how all of the simulations work in the story. For example, for the iceberg cracking, we had to take very broad strokes for each shot to see how the simulation worked from shot to shot. "This meant creating quick, low-resolution simulations for each shot to see how the continuity of the iceberg breaking worked through the edit. We did the same with the ocean shots. "We put quick procedural oceans into each shot to test the speed of the zodiacs and the look of the ocean throughout the sequence." "We rendered all aspects of the ocean and arctic environments in Houdini [save for the ship, which was rendered in Maya]. It made sense to proceed with rendering whole sequences in Houdini due to the large amount of FX work that was being generated, and Melissa incorporated into. "The main technical challenges of the project were dealing with a massive job like this in the midst of Super Bowl season! "We had some heavy rendering to do with large Houdini sims. Therefore, we had to manage our render time and set priorities for each sequence in the commercial. "For example, we set high priorities on certain shots for water simulation and ice breaking to get the heavy rendering in a good place that kept us on schedule." Software breakdown: • All assets were modeled in Maya/ZBrush • All assets were textured in Substance Painter, except for the whale which was textured in Mari/ZBrush • The rhino, tree, and ship rendered in Maya using Arnold • The whale, water, zodiacs and ice were rendered in Houdini using Mantra Schedule: "The schedule was relatively tight considering the amount of VFX involved. We started working on assets such as the rhino in the beginning of December, followed by the shoot around mid-December. Before we received a locked edit in early January, we started R&D for the water and ice and got a head start on the full CG ocean shots."

records.description: The Mill 2D lead artist and shoot supervisor James MacLachlan: "This commercial creates the vision of a super-computer and aims to answer the question, 'What if artificial intelligence could dream?' "I've always loved doing projects with [director] GMUNK; his approach to an ever-evolving aesthetic is one I really respond to. He came to us with a number of really great references and ideals of which we could build on. "It's always a very collaborative process with GMUNK and this project was no exception. "The biggest challenge when approaching a project of this scale is sustaining the pace and enthusiasm GMUNK brings to an ever-evolving design. He's relentless. "One minute you will be talking about the level of luminance in a fiber optic wolf fur, and the next you will be discussing why a digital seed explosion requires deep compositing, and what that can offer the final piece. "GMUNK often brings a very organic approach to the digital visuals he wants as a final product. Onset we shot camera filters, prisms, LEDs, screens and torches, to add to the layering of the compositing. Then, once back in the studio, we also constructed and shot giant kaleidoscopes and prisms. "These elements were then digitized and reconstituted as camera effects and UV displacement maps in Nuke, adding to the final visual effect. "There were a number of firsts in this project that really added to the final piece. At a technology level the list would be very long, but we spent many hours hard at work to ensure we were hitting everything required." The Mill 2D artist Stefan Susemihl: "Throughout the process, we kept on trying to push the look through different techniques, even sometimes techniques that were completely new or never tried before. "Most challenges related to the fact of it being an edit with almost no cuts and heavy on design. There was a lot of work done not just on generating the FX, but also to make it as seamless as possible in between transitions from languages/looks in FX." The Mill VFX supervisor and 3D lead artist Alex Hammond: "Early meetings with GMUNK and BBH were crucial to understanding the complex idea. We needed to create a world where a computer was dreaming of forms augmented by data. "The biggest challenge was to understand what this world would look like. This job also required heavy amounts of simulation which can be time-consuming to generate so we wanted to make sure we locked down all the components of the commercial. To do this we spent a good amount of time developing concepts and a detailed Pre-vis which helped us understand the visual language of the film and allowed us to decide where to focus our attention. "The Audi job required us to use all the tools we had - and ones we didn't yet! Multiple techniques and software were used to meet the demands of the job as we had to generate a 'physical' version of our world and then augment it with data to mimic the effect of lidar scanning. "In this commercial, the data was in the form of millions of points of light scattered over various architectures and landscapes. In effect everything was unique in this ad - right down to the 'data' of the wolf's hair. "We created some tools to add high-detail to low-res geometry based on textures - this came in particularly handy for the sections inside the computer and architecture scenes where we needed to pick out lots of nice 'specular bokehs'."

records.description: Simon Reeves Head of 3D at Analog Studio: "The brief was to visualize the concept of the Steep game designers building a full open-world environment as if they were physically creating it inside a huge warehouse. "We had to create a landscape that could be viewed at a distance externally, and then dive into and be fully immersed in that landscape as its details are created. "We had to create detailed landscapes that were flexible enough in scale to hold up when seen at large variations of distance, from whole mountains to individual trees. "Large volumetric time-lapse weather systems were needed for transitioning the landscape from fresh earth to snow-covered wintery environments. "We also had to create smaller-scale simulated snow, which was being thrown up by objects as big as chalets and ski lifts bursting up from underneath the snow." Schedule: two months.

records.description: David Casey, head of commercial production and VFX supervisor at The Embassy in Vancouver: "The brief was to have the Nissan Rogue face off against an evil horde of snowmen in a frantic battle sequence! "Telling the story of the battle in 60 seconds was the challenge. With so much frantic action going on it was important to focus on the key moments and give those clarity for the viewer. "Once the concept of the battle is set up in the story then we addressed each individual vignette. The spot becomes a wonderful montage of moments. Director Cedric Nicolas-Troyan helped us focus on the key beats throughout animation development. "There is almost an unwritten shorthand on how to shoot those scenes. The initial tension builder, the faceoff, the initial chaotic montage, the second wave of attacks and the final showdown. "The shooting location was a car park on the outskirts of Toronto. This gave the crew flexibility to shoot lots of running car footage. The car park was surrounded by a treeline that we knew we would have to augment with snow etc. "To get the epic feel required for the spot we pushed that treeline further back in some shots and added distant mountains and hills. The compositing team also added lots of atmosphere, snow flurries and dramatic skies to the shots. In the end it all came together really well. The next challenge was the weather. The spot was shot in the middle of summer over two days in Toronto. Temperatures soared up to 35C during the shoot. "We knew early on that we would require large set extensions but the extreme heat meant that we would have more than initially planned for. "Once the spot was cut we roughed in some 2D treeline elements in what could be considered a 'post-vis'. Once Cedric and team were happy with these we fleshed out the scenes with fully digital CG tree environments. "The assets and lighting team at The Embassy did a great job creating our digital forest replete with snow clumps and interactivity as the giant snowman passed through it. "With an army of snowmen bearing down on the Rogue cavalry we knew early on that we'd be creating a lot of interactive snow effects. The FX team led by Adam Harder worked on developing the simulations for those impacts. "There was a fine balance between chunky wet snow and fine powder. Too chunky and it looked like slush, too powdery and it looked like dust. As an avid skier I know what snow looks like!" Schedule: "From edit lock to delivery was about 10 weeks. We had three weeks preceding the shoot where we worked on creature design with concept artist Tyler Gibb."

records.description: Thomas Bay, executive producer and partner at Frame in Copenhagen, Denmark: "The client Louis Poulsen showed us some images from an exhibition Danish designer Verner Panton did in 1998, just prior to his death. "They thought it would be great to use that exhibition as a main inspiration for the spot and as we are huge fans of Panton, we were totally on board with that. "There were two key challenges. One thing was to make a design that was light and contemporary while still having a clear reference to the aesthetics of Verner Panton. "In the first set of style frames, we did have color combinations that were closer to some of his original ones for instance, but the client wanted to give it a more modern look. And I think it became more fresh and more its own thing actually, which I like. "The second challenge was to create the edit. It had to have the right pace, present all the lamps in all their colors, have the right balance between abstract and product shots and have a meaningful transition from shot to shot. That took a lot of feedback sessions and fiddling around to get that right. "The biggest technical issue was the light emission in Octane, because it gave a lot of noise, so we had to render out with a lot more samples than if the lamps had been turned off." Schedule: "We had one month from our first meeting with the client. So it was pretty tight. With one guy on it from start to finish, and another couple of guys on for three weeks."

records.description: Flink creative lead Daniel Balzer in Hamburg, Germany: "This 50-second ad brings together 39 of the BBC's learning titles [across TV, radio, digital and social media] into one carefully crafted movie, combining a large variety of subjects and content into one visually connected piece. "'Every Element of Wonder', is a celebration of learning built on a slick reimagining of Tom Lehrer's 1959 periodic table song, 'The Elements', in which BBC titles replace the scientific elements. "The titles and content whirl together and transform into a cubical shape, and thus retaining its visual connection to the BBC periodic table from the start to the end of the film. "In the ad's whirling culmination, the titles come together in their own table to form 'Every element of wonder available across the BBC'. "The song was brought to life by the impressive lyrical talents of Golden Globe award-winning actress Olivia Coleman, who mastered her recital of all 39 BBC titles! "We used a combination of fully CG generated content, footage and motion design elements to illustrate the learning content available across BBC's factual TV and radio output, its digital resources and learning initiatives, highlighting shows from Brian Cox's 'Forces of Nature' to 'The Infinite Monkey Cage.'"

records.description: Raminta Poskute, VFX line producer at Mathematic in Paris: "This film is part of a MTV safe sex campaign to show that condoms are not a barrier to freedom. records.description: Michael Boamah, international PR manager at BETC in Paris: "We had to make a film as if we were launching a new brand. We had to show to consumers all of Canal, in a spectacular, generous way. And get people to pay attention to what Canal is offering. "For this film, we went through a longer preparation phase than usual. We spent three weeks before shooting on it and had a 3D animatic made. The animatic included everything that was going to be shot, with the right camera angles, the right camera movements, the right characters movements – all in 3D. "This way, we knew exactly what to do during the shoot and where to place the camera. They started to render some elements in 3D before the shooting even started. "Picking the music was complicated. The music is always complicated. When we selected the director Antoine, we made him a mood-tape made of several kitchen scenes. The music there was a bit jazzy. "And then when he made us the 3D animatic, he put another cut of music on it. A salsa, that we actually kept for most of the editing phase. We asked Schmooze, our music production company, to make us a playlist. We also searched on our side. "So, in the end we had like ten songs to pick from. We went through a lot of debates and discussions with [agency ECD] Stephane Xiberras, with the director, and with others to end up selecting the soundtrack of 'Aile ou la cuisse' which was a proposal from the sound guys at Schmooze." Schedule: "We had almost two full months of post-production, if you count what we did before the shoot."

raw_source.description: Michael Boamah, international PR manager at BETC in Paris: "We had to make a film as if we were launching a new brand. We had to show to consumers all of Canal, in a spectacular, generous way. And get people to pay attention to what Canal is offering. "For this film, we went through a longer preparation phase than usual. We spent three weeks before shooting on it and had a 3D animatic made. The animatic included everything that was going to be shot, with the right camera angles, the right camera movements, the right characters movements – all in 3D. "This way, we knew exactly what to do during the shoot and where to place the camera. They started to render some elements in 3D before the shooting even started. "Picking the music was complicated. The music is always complicated. When we selected the director Antoine, we made him a mood-tape made of several kitchen scenes. The music there was a bit jazzy. "And then when he made us the 3D animatic, he put another cut of music on it. A salsa, that we actually kept for most of the editing phase. We asked Schmooze, our music production company, to make us a playlist. We also searched on our side. "So, in the end we had like ten songs to pick from. We went through a lot of debates and discussions with [agency ECD] Stephane Xiberras, with the director, and with others to end up selecting the soundtrack of 'Aile ou la cuisse' which was a proposal from the sound guys at Schmooze." Schedule: "We had almost two full months of post-production, if you count what we did before the shoot."

records.description: Mill creative director Jorge Montiel: "Working with specialists in robin behavior helped us with our detailed observation of the classic behaviors of the hero birds. We then worked to match these behaviors to the various settings and experiences the protagonist in the story faced. "The way robins move, their size and their lack of facial expressions meant that the bird's personality had to be evoked almost entirely through its body language. This had to then be linked directly to changes in environment and the bird's interaction with the things around him. "Every little breath, heartbeat, twitch had to be present, and in time, allowing this tiny creature to take center stage amongst the dramatic landscapes behind him." Lead 3D artist Adam Droy explains: "Building on our previous knowledge of feather work, we knew that creating a photo-real robin was going to be our most demanding bird job to date. "With that in mind, we went about crafting a bespoke feather tool that would allow us to create such accurate feather simulations, down to the micro details such as how many barbs a feather has, how soft they feel and how each feather reacts to the light."

records.description: Director MARTIN STIRLING Production PARTIZAN VFX MPC moving-picture.com Matteo La Motta, VFX supervisor 3D: "Although it sounds ridiculous, we started by using a life-sized toy tiger on the shoot to bring it to life. "When it came to animating the CG creature, we used references of real tigers for its different expressions and movements, for example when he is in pain, sleeping, or walking down the stairs. records.description: Producer, Steven Riley at Passion Pictures in London: "The brief asked us to create a warmhearted, stop-frame animation with a typically British feel, the joyful filmic experience of a Pixar film with the added bonus of a catchy musical song. "The main objective was encouraging the message that despite the demands of modern life, the best gift we can give our loved ones isn't material, it's our time. "The character puppets were created with metal armatures, silicone/foam bodies with silicone limbs and carefully constructed costumes. The heads and faces were printed using 3D printing technology on a Stratysys J750 machine. "Sets and props were made out of conventional materials including wood, metal, plaster, resin and plastic and painted to look right within their world. "CG modeling, texturing, and animation of the character heads and faces was done using Maya, ZBrush, Mari and Photoshop. Postproduction was done using Maya, Nuke and Flare. "Technical challenges included the incorporation of real-sized food with the smaller models and sets, scaling lenses and motion control moves to match these two scales, and incorporating new 3D printing technology into our designs and characters. "The spot is part of the Sainsbury's Christmas campaign which includes additional TV and print commercials based around Sainsbury's food products. All produced in a similar style." Schedule: "Thirty weeks including a six-week studio shoot."

records.description: ManvsMachine creative director, Adam Rowe in Los Angeles: "Our brief was to conceive and produce the campaign creative for the Nike Air Max '17 with the core callouts being comfort and breathability. "The main creative challenge was trying to get buy-in to the edit style and audio approach. We had something in our minds that was tricky to storyboard and turn into an animatic without going ahead and creating the final piece. "Thankfully, Nike trusted us and allowed us the freedom to flesh out the concept enough to push it through. "The trickiest aspect of the project was one of quantity. Our aim was to visually overload the viewer with as many metaphors as possible. The catch-22 was that we had to produce a plethora of shots, many of which were completely different from one another. "In order to make this more manageable, we had planned to work on each scene for slightly less time than we usually would - purely due to the fact that each would be on screen for such a short amount of time – but, true to form, we ended up crafting every tiny detail to the nth degree on twice as many shots as normal. "With the edit being comprised of so many different scenes, each designer used various combinations of software packages. Our main tools of choice were Cinema 4D, Houdini, Maya, V-Ray, Redshift, Adobe Creative Cloud and ZBrush. "Perhaps noteworthy is that the shot of the shoe sucking into a fabric sphere was created as a small motion test in the first week of the project. It made the final cut without any simulation tweaks at all." Schedule: "It's tricky with this project to put a time stamp on the production as there wasn't a definitive split between creative development and production. All in all it was somewhere in the region of two months."
