records.description: Kasper Verweij, director and founder at ONESIZE in Amsterdam: "FX was very clear in what they wanted for this promo and why they wanted us to use the key art of previous seasons: They wanted to leave the viewer guessing what the final season was going to be about, creating buzz amongst American Horror Story fans. "The main focus for this promo was to reacquaint the viewer with the memorable marketing in AHS. For the pitch we set out to create a seamless ride through all the previous seasons, without adding any new design element to tie them together, so all elements used are derived from the key art posters. "Since this is in the horror genre, we felt we needed to have a retracting motion in the camera, symbolizing running away. "The gimp trying to grab the camera sets off this backward pull. To keep the stylistic feel of the prints, we decided to create everything in CG, even the black figure in the first scene. This way we had full control over both camera and animation. "Second creative choice we had to make was the way we would go from one to the other scene, while keeping it completely seamless. All of the scenes had one thing in common: they all feature characters. Going through the mouths of these characters felt like the way to go. "Other elements that could tie the scenes together were specific materials. Combining this led us to go through either the mouth or by tying textures together from one scene to the other. "To test if this approach was going to work, and to convince FX of this treatment, we created an animatic showing most of the elements and the transition we wanted to go for. Subtle details like the crying of the nun's eyes and life-like animation of characters like the gimp and the snake, would make this spot more than just a simple pull through five pieces of key art. Animating the fabric and the sky would only add to this feeling. "To really craft this sequence, the team at ONESIZE employed a series of different techniques, including 3D, camera mapping, modeling and animation." Schedule: one month.

records.description: Pablo Alfieri, founder and director at Playful in Buenos Aires: "The brief has been totally open since the beginning of our relationship with Hatsu, a Colombian tea brand only five years old but with a big potential in a new and increasing market of healthy drinks around the world. "They wanted consumers and future clients to feel the soul of the product. So we played on the idea of 'Hatsu meets Memphis Milano' an excuse to travel between different sets and the nine bottles of tea showing the exotic and fresh spirit of Hatsu. "For Hatsu 'Better Together' the creative challenge was to produce it in only one month with two days of shooting. Everything was made and approved for the client in only 12 days. "For Becho & Mab, the great animators of the spot, the technical challenge was how to animate the bottles at the pack shot, so they created an awesome mechanism to make them go up and down fluidly. "With the 'Hello Hatsu!' spot, we couldn't afford a real handcrafted spot, so we ventured into realistic 3D animation with fancy, exotic and colorful sets. "For 'Hello Hatsu!' we used C4D and Nuke. For 'Hatsu Better Together' we used C4D for the set design, shot with an Alexa for live action, and the stop-motion was made with a pair of Canon 5Ds." Schedule: "'Hello Hatsu!': six weeks total: two for design, three for animation, one for rendering and post production. Hatsu 'Better Together': One month total: two weeks for design, two weeks for post-production."

records.description: The team behind the emotional 2015 John Lewis holiday spot "Monty's Christmas" (Blink director Dougal Wilson, MPC and agency adam&eveDDB) are back and while the tear-jerking factor is lower in "Buster the Boxer," the story telling and VFX work remain exceptional. MPC creative director Diarmid Harrison-Murray: "These are the sort of jobs we wait for. When Dougal and adam&eveDDB approached us, I felt a healthy dose of trepidation as it really is an enormous job. "The creatures are hand-animated and totally photo-real, so there are phenomenal complexities involved in engaging the audience with the cast's performance, and achieving the huge level of animal interaction on the CG trampoline. "We were careful not to communicate human characteristics, as the audience will project their own emotions. Mother Nature was our best reference, helping us to understand how real animals behave and express themselves." Tim Van Hussen, MPC animation supervisor: "We see dogs all the time, so people are able to spot when the characterization doesn't look right. To develop Buster, we shot lots of reference footage of the real dog from every angle before crafting the texture, from the wrinkles to the hair direction, of the real animal. "With six creatures to animate and plenty of extreme closeups, and slow-mos, the creative and technical scale of this film is unparalleled; animation tests started before the shoot even begun. "MPC built its most advanced rigs yet – five in total – and developed bespoke software to perfect the animals' skin sliding so that every jump, twist and bounce is rendered completely authentic."

records.description: Daniel Jahnel, 3D lead and set supervisor and joint head of 3D at Sehsucht in Hamburg, Germany: "The project brief was to create a photorealistic T-Rex that had a human nature, in the sense that the audience should relate to his emotional progress throughout the film. "The idea was to think of him as a human being, telling his life story in the form of an interview. So he was human size, expressed human emotions and could also talk. "Because of his human nature, the underlying idea of exploiting the shortness of his arms in a comical way was of great concern for all sides from the beginning. "We never wanted him to be disabled in any way, it should just come across as a fact that the T-Rex simply had developed short arms through its evolution. The animators did a great job here in making sure to never go too far. "Both the prep and the actual shoot itself were certainly a challenge in terms of technical and organizational aspects. We only had two days of shooting all over and around Berlin with a very small crew. "We usually did a pass with the actor (who is also the narrator), followed by a pass of a dummy T-Rex head that sort of represented the volume and height of the CG T-Rex's head so that we would later have a reference in VFX as to how large this guy should be and also to sometimes frame the shot a bit different to compensate for the difference in scale between the actor and dinosaur. Last but not least an empty plate to be used for VFX. "Later on in post the creation of the T-Rex took some time. We gathered all the references that we could find and decided to go for a very classic look (if one can say that of an animal no one has ever seen) in order not to distract from his human character. "On the 3D side of things we had a great ZBrush, Mari, Softimage, Arnold pipeline with some additional simulation support in Houdini. All shots were composited in Nuke." Schedule: eight weeks.

"On the 3D side of things we had a great ZBrush, Mari, Softimage, Arnold pipeline with some additional simulation support in Houdini. All shots were composited in Nuke." Schedule: eight weeks.

records.description: John Shirley, VFX supervisor and Ed Boldero, 3D lead artist at The Mill, Los Angeles: " Our job at The Mill was to facilitate not only the obvious effects, such as the shattered glass ceiling, but to use VFX to assist in the reverse storytelling." "Obviously, a big part of this piece is that you're watching a narrative in reverse. When we were animating certain elements like the lobster claw, the big question for us at beginning was: should we simply animate forward and then reverse the shot? "Would those elements end up needing further adjustments after reversal? We ended up making small adjustments to the shots after watching them in reverse to accentuate and help the shot along. "In reverse, your brain doesn't easily register the sequence of events – so making small adjustments to help facilitate that was something that we were really cautious about. We didn't want to make it visually apparent that we'd adjusted the animation on top of reversing it, but we wanted to make sure it worked." Schedule: "Total time was about two weeks. The time from locked edits to finish was about a week."

records.description: Creative director Mike Moloney at Art&Graft in London: "We were tasked with creating an integrated campaign comprising a set of charming animated commercials and promos, point of sale and out of home collateral for The National Lottery and ITV's support of Team GB at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games. "Working in collaboration with ITN Productions, ITV Creative and ITV AdVentures we directed, designed and produced a range of items which aim to inspire and represent the 'togetherness' that each Olympic Games brings to the nation; that we're all joined together as we get behind our athletes. "We wanted to create the epic, cinematic scenes synonymous with an Olympics launch, yet also introduce a warmth and charm that is sometimes missing when representing our heroic athletic superstars. "The 'Road to Rio' focuses on the story of Camelot being a key funder of Team GB: supporting over 1,300 athletes on their Roads to Rio; allowing them to train full time and have the best coaching, facilities and medical support in the world. "Every National lottery ticket and Scratchcard sold across the nation helps contribute to the over £80 million per year that goes to Team GB. As such, the film focuses on a transformative flock of tickets as they journey throughout the day to each corner of the UK – from the shores of Loch Lomond to the Angel of the North and Giant's Causeway, magically transforming the equipment and kit of the heroic training athletes it encounters. "We wanted to create cinematic, sweeping landscapes and 3D character animation combined with a rich illustrative approach to create a memorable series of animated films and print which capture the true celebratory spirit and humanity of the Olympic Games. "Influenced by the paintings of Norman Wilkinson - his beautiful representations of British landscapes and sense of four seasons in one day - we sought to incorporate stunning lighting and a warm color palette into the design of the environments. "We wanted the tickets to feel magical and mischievous as they spring to life in the morning sunlight then, once they join together in a flock, to feel graceful and elegant as they sweep through the air and transform our Team GB athletes."

records.description: Golden Wolf producer, Ant Baenain in London: "With the launch of a new look and brand positioning for The Mirinda brand, the Barbarian Group approached us to bring some madness to the campaign 'Mess With Your Senses!' "We were brought on board to help develop and define the 'non­-stop sensory overload' that was to be the online and TV campaign. They asked us to create wild animated content that would introduce a new audience to the brand. "The biggest challenge was to hold back on the complexity of some of the ludicrous transitions and animations we had come up with - we were our own worst enemy on that one! "The brief required a lot deliverables, with each asset used to complement another part of the campaign and hammer home the 'Mess With Your Senses' theme. At any one time in the process we were working on multiple assets, which meant we often had to shift focus between the various deliverables. "In addition to the two :30 hero spots, we created an interactive poster, six flavor clips (each of which featured five individual animated loops) and 15 social media stickers. "Here's a quick story to finish up: Just before Christmas, we'd received four prototype cans as reference to build our 3D models. These cans were a limited production of the new design - there were only a few in the world - and we needed to return them to the client once we'd finished. "To keep them out of thirsty hands, we'd been storing the cans out of sight in our conference room. But then we had our annual holiday party and things got a little out of hand. "We woke up the next day to find all four cans had been opened and consumed. As it turns out, sample cans aren't filled with the real drink so when the culprits opened the first one and it didn't taste like Mirinda, they just kept trying each can! "With a heavy heart (and a hangover) we confessed our sins to our forgiving client and got back to work with our empty cans."

records.description: Luisa Murray, executive producer at Psyop in Venice, CA: "We've been working with Cricket since 2014 when the brand was relaunched. We have been slowly evolving the look of the brand into something more premium while always making sure to keep it fun and engaging. "For this year's anthem spot Cricket and Argonaut tasked us with coming up with visuals to reinforce their new tag line "Great Big Network." The song written by the creative team at Argonaut opened us up to play with some fun vignettes." Producer Lucy Clark: "We developed new environments, new props and wardrobes: Comb-overs and mohawks, guitars and aeroplanes - all of these little details created a rich world for our story to play out in. "The challenge in the pre-vis and edit phases was to seamlessly move the action from one scene to another along with the tempo of the music." 3D animator Chris Sage: "The shot where we look through a spy glass from the biplane is a series of snap zooms, bringing us all the way down to a super close-up where we can see the tiny grains of sand being shuffled around by a dancing crab. "In order to create that close-up, we used Houdini to create a dynamic sand performance with varying sizes of grains and pieces of shell and rock. We were able to control the color of each grain by using customized data assigned to each sand particle based on a range of sand-like shades on a ramp. "For the crowd in the concert shots we used Houdini to generate a point cloud on the surface of the ground. Each point was given a unique character ID as well as a skin color ID. "A range of animated cycles were then used to attach a dancing character to each point and, similar to the close-up sand shot, we used a color ramp to adjust the color of each character and make them unique. If we needed more blue guys for example, we could just make blue more dominant in the color ramp."

records.description: Executive producer Alberto Lopes at Vetor Zero in São Paulo: "The request was to create an animated policy trailer for theaters associated with Caixa Cultural, a nationwide cultural initiative launched by Caixa Econômica, Brazil's largest government-owned bank. "The piece should take place in a fantastic, Willy Wonka-like factory, presenting a whimsical version of the theater's backstage and all the pre-show preparations. "The biggest creative challenge posed by this project was the design of the whole environment where the action takes place, the 'Emotions Factory.' It's a single setting, yet a huge one, with a lot of nooks and crannies and a great amount of detail – not to mention the large number of supporting characters and extras roaming about. "The film was produced with a combination of 3D animation and model settings filmed in studio. We built the 'stage' scenario as a scale model and did all the camera moves inside it using our motion control system. "The characters, machines and more complex props were created in CG, with a rendering style that realistically simulates natural materials and textures. The result was composed with the live-action footage in a seamless, organic way, thus giving the piece an overall artisanal, tactile feel. "The film was adapted into :60 and :30 TV commercials, and the campaign also includes several print and online ads. "The film includes several visual references to folk arts and cultural traditions from Brazil's different regions. The soundtrack also mixes classical orchestration with Brazilian folk instruments like the zabumba drum, fifes and the triangle."

records.description: Saschka Unseld, director at Passion Pictures in London: "The brief was to create a narrative about the history of advertising - how advertising changed the food industry in a way that initially it started out being about good food and it ended up being about selling. "The main creative challenges of 'A Love Story' are telling a story through Evie and Ivan's brand identities. "During the timelapse you can see how those elements evolve, representing the passage of time and how their competitive spirits get out of hand. We go from the 1960s to present day, from something child-like and playful to something corporate, shiny and aggressive. "At the end of the story Evie and Ivan's corporate identities return to their 'roots' and merge into a mature, sustainable, and conscientious brand that is about what they love to do: make delicious food together. "Aside from the obvious hurdles that come with creating a four-minute film in CG, and having to refine and re-refine each frame, it was tricky to get the character transition right, as we had to find the right volume language to make sure we kept to the simplicity of the designs. "Our art director Katy guided us with what textures the characters should have. We wanted everything in the world, especially the characters, to have a friendly physicality, taking it further than 2D but not going too photo-real. records.description: Marcio Leitão (AKA Squarehead), director at Stink in São Paulo: "Pedigree, as a brand, is tightly associated with dogs. That's why it made so much sense to create a campaign showing why dogs are the way they are and encouraging people to make the most of their lives in the same way. "The project's concept was very simple with few elements. The challenge was to grab attention in a long commercial (1:30). So we decided to make a frame-by-frame animation to have texture, an interesting look and, in the end, have something different from many digital animations. It was something that I had never done before. "The most time-consuming was the approval of the animation, which took about three weeks. Then we had three days to print the frames, draw, photograph, edit and finalize. "When we approved all animations, which we created through After Effects, the frames were printed on recycled paper with a very smooth ink. "I then drew with a pen brush each frame (more than 700 of them) and, finally, photographed everything. The final steps were color correction, editing and adding the sound track via Premiere. "I drew all 700 frames in one night. Stayed awake until 3 am. I took the photos and finalized the whole project in one day." Schedule: "Three weeks and three days."

records.description: Michael Aimette, executive creative director at BBDO NY and Benjamin Walsh, senior visual FX supervisor at Method Studios in LA: "Our brief was to talk about the amazing things GE does and its unique relationship with the world at large via their role as a digital-industrial company. "The ask from the client was for our work to (hopefully) be as innovative and unexpected in our storytelling as the company itself. "Specifically, we wanted to present a hypothetical problem that the world is experiencing, something really captivating and visually stunning, as well as a little strange. For us, that was a world where it's raining octopuses. "And then we matched the corresponding GE solutions that fix that problem. The challenge is always to tell our story in a clear, simple way, because a lot of what GE does is highly technical and not exactly easy to articulate. "So we focused instead on the outcomes of their technology. Everyone can understand that it's good when trains run on time, flights aren't delayed and power is re-routed almost instantaneously. So we wanted to show how everything is copacetic, even in such extreme circumstances. "The main technical challenge was integrating practical silicon octopuses with CG octopuses – both in the background and through a hero CG octopus. Though the art department created 200 practical octopuses, CG ones were needed to achieve depth and specific choreography that could not be captured in-camera. Method modeled the CG octopuses off the practical ones so there was seamless consistency across look, behavior, and color. "An additional challenge was creating CG rain. Most of the shots were captured on sunny days, so we had to flatten out the lighting and replace the skies before adding rain. Colorist Stefan Sonnenfeld at Deluxe's Company 3 was very helpful in that task, working under a lookup table to keep all the information in the plate so we could manipulate it even further to get the desired look. "Finally, for the plane shots we also created a CG plane; CG clouds, rain, and atmospheric effects; and CG octopuses. "The shoot was four days in New Zealand. We then had approximately three weeks for post production from edit lock and a couple of weeks prep time whilst we were shooting to build the CG octopuses and start R&D on their movement. "The commercial was shot on Alexa XT with a combo of anamorphic and spherical lenses. We modeled the octopuses in Maya and ZBrush, and look development was done in Mantra. "For animation, we used Houdini and Maya: Houdini more for the background octopuses and Maya for hand-animating the foreground ones, then we simulated the squishiness for each in Houdini's FEM solver. That squishiness really gave the octopuses an organic feel. "We also created a custom sticky octopus rig in Houdini that determined how long each octopus stuck to a given surface, and we had a bouncing setup to match how much the practical octopuses bounced on set. We rendered in Mantra."

records.description: Lead 3D artist Elizabeth Mitchell at The Mill in London: "The campaign brief was to bring the new Guinness Africa artwork alive. As the ad is so vibrant and fast paced (capturing people from Ghana, Nigeria and Kenya) it was important to present the bold colors and striking pattern design in an exciting way. "The CG tiles had to look natural and organic, like a tiler had placed them all individually, so we animated them in Houdini which helped them to appear as though shot in stop-motion and as if each tile was positioned separately. "We tried a few color variations to display the pattern in the best way, while at the same time still connecting to the real artwork. The biggest challenge was having the rectangular wall tiles break up to construct the curved bottle shape and create an attractive mosaic design."

records.description: David Casey VFX supervisor at The Embassy in Vancouver, BC: "The BMW M4 is delivered tuned and race ready from Germany. To expedite this the car would have to be tested and 'broken in' on its journey from Europe. The only way to do this was to create a floating racetrack that plied the waters between Germany and North America. "Telling a continuous race story: One of the earliest outlines for the project had the driving occur in vignettes of action around the track. As the project progressed, director Ozan Biron and creative director Andrew Simon wanted to create a blow-by-blow race film, where we logically follow the car around the track. This involved immense planning from the team and an intensive pre-vis development before the shoot. "Making the racetrack believable: We really had to hit home with the believability of the track for the spot. We went through many design discussions as to what kind of ship would carry a racetrack like this. "An aircraft carrier may now seem like a logical choice now but we explored many other options early on. The aircraft carrier was chosen as it is already 70 percent of the way towards being a racetrack. It is a wide open space, visually familiar to many and would only need minor modifications to make it race-able. "Any other ship we discussed needed major modification to hold a racetrack, lurching the visuals more towards science fiction, something we wanted to avoid. "Shoot: We shot for one day here in Vancouver. Our location was to the same scale as an aircraft carrier deck and we could have marked out a full-size replica of the aircraft carrier track. "However doing so would have restricted the camera car's actions and driving. We figured earlier on that if we broke the track down into modular sections it would give the camera car more flexibility. More flexibility on the shoot day meant more coverage for editorial which is always important for car spots. "Match-moving: In total we had three cameras running at all times, which meant a lot of footage. It also meant we had to come up with some solution for tracking markers that would be visible to all three cameras. "There was some initial discussions about traffic cones but we felt these would restrict the driving and would reflect in the body panels of the car, entailing additional paint-out work. "The solution we came to was hockey pucks. There is a particular kind of hollow orange training puck made from soft plastic. We would lay out track corners and straights with the pucks. It didn't matter if the car or camera car drove over them, they wouldn't burst and they wouldn't damage the cars. In the end we used over 400 pucks on the day. "I like to think of it as a uniquely Canadian solution to a match-moving problem! The pucks are now a mainstay of our VFX kit on every shoot." Schedule: "Nine weeks. This included two weeks for prep and pre-vis, one-day shoot and one-week edit. This left six weeks for VFX work."

records.description: Steffen Röthinger, VFX supervisor at TED+FLO in Berlin: "The idea was to push a bearded naked guy down a hill full of grass rolls, wood and pebbles to bring his experience of working with those materials to life. It had to look dangerous and painful, but at the same time he should really enjoy it. "German home improvement retailer Hornbach's DIY ­philosophy contrasts with today's abstract digital lifestyle. This campaign promotes the intense and sensual freedom one gets having a tactile experience – reminding people they are still alive. "The intention was to display those emotions as vividly and intensely as possible whilst keeping the look and feel absolutely natural and convincing. "Therefore we worked closely together with Tom Noakes (director), Antonio Paladino (DOP), Swenja Babucke (producer) and Fiona Crombie (production designer) to find the best possible approach for every shot and not hurt the protagonist (too much). "So we had to come up with techniques that allowed us to achieve those dangerous looking images and his moments of enjoyment. We came up with lots of different ideas and approaches, some were too complicated or expensive, some funny, one even involved a giant hamster wheel to have more control while shooting the close- ups. In the end I think we've chosen the right ones. But how it's been done remains a secret. Sorry." Schedule: "The first brief came on January the 5th. We shot three days end of January. After they edited for one week, we had 2.5 weeks for 3D and compositing. So all in all around two months."

records.description: Adam Foulkes and Alan Smith, directors at Nexus Productions in London: "The client was very keen to show Slack as a collaborative messaging tool, so that's where the idea of an unlikely team being able to communicate smoothly came about. And what is more unlikely than a random collection of animals? "Slack is a new product so there was an obvious need to explain what it is and what makes it different from other messaging apps. But it was very important that this did not turn into the dreaded product demonstration video. "There were all kinds of features they wanted to highlight such as uploading and downloading files, searching in a specific Slack channel and staying in touch with the team while being out of the office, so we tried to seamlessly weave all these into the story. "Whenever you create a new universe of characters you have to invent all the rules to go with it. Which animals and in what roles, do they wear clothes, can they speak, do they want to eat each other, how can a goat type? "All of these questions had to be answered and it seemed that everyone had a different opinion. But mostly you go on your gut instincts on what makes you laugh. "If there's ever been a lion and prawn on screen together before we can't think of it, and it just seems funny that they have to queue up to use the photocopier. "The other main challenge was to give them a task to complete, and after much debate about the size and nature of this task the client came up with the idea of the drone umbrella. We could then tell this story by showing the way the team use Slack to communicate their ideas to each other. "We considered many techniques but finally decided on portraying recognizably realistic settings. This gave us an enjoyable oddness, seeing our animals living alongside humans and inhabiting the same world as our own. "It also established a very matter of fact documentary performance style, almost as if we filmed real office workers and then turned them into animals. It was more 'The Office' than 'Madagascar'. "The main challenge with any photo-realistic project is believability, so getting the fur renders to react with the practical lighting and making sure the animated characters interact correctly with real props was paramount. "We first filmed real people acting out each scene to give us a sense of how the animals would behave and what sort of difficulties they would encounter as they moved around the office. We could also work out what the camera had to do. For instance, filming focus pulls in camera really helped merge the characters into the scenes during the composite."

records.description: Andres Rivera, art director at Brand New School in New York: "We were asked by Nike to create a short animation featuring lacrosse stars the Thompson Brothers and the new Huarache V Creator cleats. Since the sport originated with Native Americans, Nike wanted to draw inspiration from the spirit animals prominent in their culture. "Each specific spirit animal had a clear spotlight and we had to present them without the link feeling too convoluted. We also needed to highlight the shoe in a non-conventional way with 2D animation – most athletic gear is presented in slick live action or 3D contexts, so this was a chance to do something that stood out. "It was the challenge trying to make a worthwhile animation in the short timeframe. We did about four days of design/exploration and asset creation, then four days of animation. We wound up designing through animation and up until the very end, continually tweaking to get everything to that sweet spot. "We tried to fit in as much cel animation as we could get away with and the time limit would allow – it's a time-consuming process, but if done correctly, it can produce something fascinating. "While stressful, this became one of the most rewarding jobs I've worked on and made me hungry for more cel animated projects. The team became a well oiled machine, sharing breakfast, lunch, and dinner together every day. While in some cases like this people might lose their minds, everyone was level-headed and worked really well together. Good times."

records.description: Tokyo-based director Alessandro Pacciani travels to Shanghai to capture BMW's M4 then conjures 90 seconds of vehicular adrenaline called "Factory Trailer" with the help of editor Marco Battiloro and the VFX skills of Warsaw post house Juice. Director, Alessandro Pacciani: "In order to highlight all of its beauty the team decided to place the car in a very industrial environment. "After filming the machine on a race track – specially prepared and set up for the shoot – the entire location was recreated to make it look like a very large refinery. Extremely detailed surroundings with the number of lights reaching tens of thousands. "The goal was to seamlessly blend the footage with a carefully generated CG night scenario, sparingly lit through fog – to create the mysterious, slightly dark mood of Nowhere City without losing the realism and distracting the viewer from the main attraction and emphasizing the predatory and aggressive nature of the car."

records.description: Twelve months and 52 VFX artists later, fluid simulation and refracted light take on the starring role in the launch campaign for Sky Q's wireless TV products courtesy of The Mill's CG work in collaboration with Biscuit director Johnny Green thru agency Brothers & Sisters. The Mill in London: "Each liquid pixel was fully crafted in CG to create something truly beautiful and memorable, using a range of techniques created specifically for this project; bringing to life over 4,000 individual simulations all full of individual personality and pace. "In order to create water droplets with real depth and consistency, the team created their own fluid system allowing them to dial in dynamism and life to the liquids. Each droplet was made from an inner and outer shell. "The inner membrane contained the imagery from the original TV screen, whilst the outer acted as a magnifying lens to distort and exaggerate the vivid colors within each frame and provide a reflective surface for the filmed environment." Francois Roisin, lead 3D artist and joint creative director: "Working on Sky was a real opportunity to push The Mill's fluid simulation to the next level. We had to carefully direct, tame and animate each drop of liquid in order to bring the textured fluid to life, as well as develop a number of techniques in-house to apply the screen-like texture onto these fluids and craft a beautiful color palette for the spot. "The CG liquid is the hero of this commercial, and crafting a journey with such a volatile element as fluids, whilst also retaining a natural motion, was a real tour de force." Dan Williams, creative director and lead 2D Artist: "None of us had seen liquid behave or look like this before and it required a giant leap of faith for Johnny, Brothers & Sisters and The Mill. "What we've achieved with these droplets is that we've taken something incredibly complex to control and choreograph, and imbued it with a seamless simplicity, elegance and meaning."

records.description: Directors Guto Terni, Sam Mason, and Vinicius Costa at Roof Studio in NYC: "The original brief was an exciting challenge from day one. The client provided a script with references of our own work, so of course this was right up our alley. "They had specific things they wanted us to touch on, but the brief really challenged us to create a surreal artful spot by taking our aesthetic, and applying it to a large-scale car campaign. "The client wanted to showcase the Civic's new beautiful design and its performance while having as much fun as possible. The spot really illustrates both the way Honda thinks and the byproduct of their thinking. We were so fortunate that all the teams involved trusted us to take the brief and push it to the limit. "The main creative challenge was to create a whimsical world with the responsibility of illustrating Honda`s imagination. This visual journey through the engineer's mind showcases the Civic`s 2016 redesign and also its power and performance. "Surrealism was an obvious choice for us to bring the ideas of the engineer to life, and the whole design was dictated to materialize those thoughts. We had lots of fun creating the quirkiness you see in the spot. "Another fundamental importance of surrealism is that it gave us the right amount of freedom to explore and create something different, it was very important that the viewer could visualize Honda's unique creative way of thinking. We did a huge round of exploratory concept art to find the right one for the spot and tried to explore as much as possible with colors, textures, and shapes. "Colors were crucial to set the right mood for the film as we wanted people to desire to be on this colorful and imaginative landscape. Utilizing a vast array of colors helped us to enhance how playful and enjoyable the journey would be. "Another key point for the visuals was texture. We knew that in exploring realistic textures we could make the ride believable, creating a strong connection with the viewers. We tried to push the design of the environment and the elements in the film as much as possible giving it strong personality and at the same time, conveying all." "We had many technical challenges on the project such as creating nature in 3D, simulations, and most importantly scale. A high priority was that the car shouldn't feel miniature (as the car is 3 cm in comparison to the engineer and the office). "We knew that using point of view shots of the engineer or even shallow depth of field would reveal how tiny the car was in comparison to the real scale. To really solve the issue we decided to have the camera on the car the entire time. It was better to have the engineer as a giant than having a car as a miniature." Schedule: five months.

records.description: Christopher Vulpi, co-founder and executive producer at Trizz in Düsseldorf, Germany: "The client referenced two of our existing projects (Nika and Armani) and asked us to make a concept where the product is formed in a dream-like way. "This project involved everything in 3D, so we had to not only replicate the product's mechanics, but also every element that would appear. We researched and casted for everything from surfaces, LEDs lights, clothes, interior decor, architecture to plants on the floor. "Creating everything in 3D means that the client has to clearly understand our vision in steps - from mood boards to style frames to render tests and pre-vis - we make sure they see everything we see, and have a chance to ask questions before going on to the next step. "It's our policy not to scare clients with technology, so we don't talk tech, but rather we play show and tell and take their comments into the work right away. "We use pencils. A photocopier. And a creative robot, named Oriol-One-Thousand. Only kidding. We shoot live-action on Alexa, edited in FCP, animated in Maya, rendered in V-Ray, some elements in Reflow, and we comp on our 2D and Smoke and color grade on our DaVinci."

records.description: Director Marc Craste at Studio AKA in London: "The brief was to create a heartwarming story with the feel of a classic cartoon short. The story needed to convey the dogs' friendship and the desperation they feel at being forced apart. That Morton Salt should be the catalyst for reuniting them was the key beat that had to be absolutely clear. "As always, the main challenge comes down to telling the story in the most effective way possible within the time frame. There were a lot of lovely ideas built around the dogs' friendship in the original script that we had to jettison in the interest of getting the important beats of the story across. "That's always hard. We were also keen to create something reminiscent of golden age cartoons, but without slavishly adhering to the style or becoming too nostalgic about it. So we took elements of the look and the storytelling of that era but kept the visuals crisp and contemporary. "The rigging of the dogs was a challenge. A tight schedule meant moving the production into animation early on, leaving little time to test the rigs – which included finding one solution to work for both bulldog and fox terrier. In addition, all CG elements had to be designed to incorporate the final 2D look, including hand-drawn linework." Schedule: three months.

records.description: Buck creative director Joe Mullen in Los Angeles: "We were originally approached by Casper and director Mark Romanek to put together an animation test based on the burgeoning print campaign that Casper had developed with branding agency Red Antler and illustrator Tomi Um. "After a successful round of tests, Casper decided to approach their first ever broadcast work from two directions. The first was developed and executed from start to finish with Red Antler and was intended to be a whimsical romp through the Casper world of characters, conveying that this really is the 'perfect mattress for everyone'. "The second spot, on the other hand, took a more direct approach with regard to the brand's key selling points, guided by Mr. Romanek and narrated by none other than a mystical Sannyasa Squirrel. "We initially explored a number of different ways to tell these stories, from a very linear narrative approach that takes place in a completely fleshed out world, to something much closer to the existing campaign - simple cuts between different characters on the mattress. "The main challenge was: How do we preserve what we loved about the existing campaign, which work great as static images, and translate that into a format that is much more fluid and energetic, and create a quasi narrative that is easy to follow?" Schedule: "Production on 'Perfect For' spanned from late July to early October, lasting about ten weeks from initial concepting and script development to final delivery. Production on 'Sleep Better' began with initial script development in late July and saw storyboarding wrap mid-August. Design followed for another two weeks, but seeing that this was part of a two-spot campaign, we wanted to preserve as much continuity between the spots as we could. We therefore delayed principal animation until mid-October once the first spot wrapped. Overall though we spent roughly eight weeks on this one."

records.description: Director Noma Bar in London: "This is the first in a series of films meant to increase understanding of new therapies at the frontiers of medicine. 'Unmasking a Killer' explains the science behind immunotherapy. Instead of 'talking lab coats' or difficult technical jargon, the film uses metaphor and story-telling. "The client had a need to create a piece of content to better explain some advances currently being talked about in mainstream media healthcare. This needed to be something that an educated layperson could understand and the concept should provoke encouragement and engagement. "The overall creative solution was quite open for interpretation. My only boundaries were to use the red square as a graphic start and close, and also not to use weapons or negative battle symbols. "When someone comes to a gallery to see my work, he can stay as long as he wants – when my work is translated into motion and on TV, you just get one go, therefore the images should be as clear as possible. This is what led me to using known iconography "I start to draw, read the story and start to imagine how one thing links to the next word, taking me to different visuals. It sounds very simple, but it's a lot of sketching and editing – figuring out the clearest way to express the text. I'm trying to tell a story with effortless transitions from one scene/message to the next." Schedule: two months.

records.description: Director Guilherme Marcondes at Lobo in New York: "The goal of the campaign is communicating the signs of autism in children to help parents recognize them early. "That's Autism Speaks' mission, and BBDO NY decided that the best course of action for the campaign would be to hear the signs from those who actually experience them and recreate it an universal way through animation. "The first step in our creative process was to spend some time with Jacob (an 11 year-old boy first diagnosed with autism at three) and his family. "The situations portrayed in the script originated from Jacob's recollections, but we showed them through a fable-like lens, emphasizing their emotional core turning his personal incidents into a story anyone can relate to. "For example, one scene that speaks of the boy being scared and upset by changes was inspired by the one day when Jacob's mom had to take a detour from their daily path to the supermarket, causing Jacob a great deal of distress. Our version of this moment doesn't show cars or city streets, but the boy sailing on a river in a little boat until he is diverted from the main stream into a scary forest. "Another scene, where the boy is surrounded by bug-eyed creatures, is inspired by the fact that Jacob doesn't like looking people in the eye – making eye contact with others can be very challenging for some people with autism – and also influenced the design of the characters in the scene. "The idea of creating a fantasy world grounded in reality was reinforced by the decision to build all settings as actual scale models in the studio. Everything you see in the film apart from the animated characters are real miniature objects, a combination of fabricated props and natural materials that give the spot a tactile, hand-crafted feel. "The intricacy of detail, the richness of texture also contribute to an immersive experience which draws the viewers in, helping them empathize with the boy's condition. The integration between real settings and CG characters was achieved using three different motion control rigs, capable of performing small and precise moves. "A compact Black Magic camera was chosen for its ability to slip into the narrowest spaces on our model sceneries. The camera movements were then transposed into the 3D software where the characters were being animated, so it would seem they were all part of the same shot. "Meticulous texture, shading and lighting work was employed to mimic the materials used in the sets, in order to create a seamless blend between natural and digital elements. "Throughout the whole process we never lost sight of the real motivating force behind our work: Jacob's story. By sticking to this principle, we expect to have crafted a film that is worthy of his life experience – and one that helps parents and families of many other children with autism as well."

records.description: Stephen Simmonds, creative director of weareseventeen, in London: "When we met Andy from Regenerate UK and found out about The Feel Good Bakery and the great work they do, we immediately wanted to use our skills to help get more awareness for the charity. There wasn't a brief as such; we just wanted to work with Andy and help in any way we could to raise awareness of his great organization. "Originally Andy was looking for more of a traditional 'explainer' to inform viewers of what the Feel Good Bakery does. We thought it might be a good idea to start our relationship by just simply spreading a little of the 'Feel Good'. "So the challenge was coming up with an idea that touched on what happens at the Feel Good Bakery, make people feel good about it and not come across as too worthy. "Originally we set out to do this in 2D which fit nicely with the feel we were going for. However, it soon became obvious that if we approached the animation in a 3D sense we would have a lot more flexibility with what we could do. So we needed to recreate the illustrative look and feel we had created in 2D in 3D. Ultimately this was that difficult but we had to change the way we were working and approach things from a slightly different angle. "If you ever get the chance to work with a charity you believe in, do it! It makes you feel great to think that the job you love doing will actually do some good for real people that need it. It makes a real change to the commercial world we are all too familiar with." Schedule: three months.

records.description: Ryan Goodwin-Smith, executive producer at Passion Pictures London: "'Lotería de Navidad' is Spain's national lottery, drawn once a year at Christmas. More than just a prize draw, the Lotería 'El Gordo' is considered the world's biggest lottery; a highly anticipated yearly event in the Spanish cultural calendar with more than 46 million entrants. "For the second year running, the lottery's campaign came in the form of a short narrative film, and this year, Passion was approached to create an animated spot. The idea was to create a strong narrative that would reinforce the spirit of excitement, sharing and kindness associated with Loteria and the festive season. "It was going to be a challenge to maintain the magnitude of the campaign, particularly after the huge success of the 2014 ad and the significance and cultural context of this lottery. Taking a film-like approach to this project (because of its longer running time), we needed to create a character that would warm the nation's hearts. "The main technical challenge was translating the 2D design into 3D, as the chosen character design for Justino (the protagonist) was very much 2D and that left a lot to interpret once it came down to giving him volume and definition. "It was also a challenge to find the right balance between realism and stylisation throughout the film, knowing at which point that line should be drawn. "Everyone who worked on this project was excited to create a short film with a real story and characters, rather than something that is totally product-driven. We couldn't be happier with the response the film – and in particular our character Justino – has received across the world." Schedule: four months.

records.description: Hornet directors Dan & Jason with Hyesung Park: "We wanted to tell a story with real emotional weight. It's a timeless story with three main beats – a character falls in love, falls out of love and then falls in love again. "To get the story to come to life we needed to create two memorable characters: Lily an imaginative little girl and her creation, a sweet and tender snowman. If we could make the audience see how much these two characters cared for each other, and enjoyed being together, we knew the story could have that great emotional resonance we were looking for. "To help bring all of this to life we brought on co-director Hyseung Park who developed the aesthetic look and feel of the film, designing elaborate, original style frames to reinforce the film's central thread. He also created customized color scripts and unique lighting sequences for each scene to underscore the story's mood and to invoke an unspoken connection between audience and animation. "We also wanted to make certain that the characters were unique to this film, and so we tapped acclaimed illustrator and veteran Hollywood character designer Peter de Sève to achieve the right attitude and atmosphere for each character's expression and idiosyncrasies. Additionally, there were two elements of memory that were important to the story – the first was how to show Lily growing older and gradually forgetting the snowman (in a condensed amount of time), and second, what triggers her memory of the snowman and their adventures together. "Technically, making sure that we maintained both theatrical and human aspects of the story during the 'puppet show' scenes took a bit of planning. We needed the audience to easily interpret the transition between the snowman's 3D hands and the 2D shadow on the fence, and make sure that the contrast between the two was apparent. "Luckily, we had very talented artists on our team who used the power of CG and cinematography to interpret the narrative, using subtle camera movements and understated actions to keep the focus on the hero characters while elegantly telling their story. "In retrospect, creating 56 shots using seven characters, three main environments and two shadow puppet movies in under three months was ultimately our largest technical challenge. But it was all a true labor of love. "Character animation was very important to us in this project, especially Lily's behavior and facial expressions and how they changed over the years. Conversely, the simplified behavior of the snowman was just as crucial for his quiet and gentle character. "Lighting played an imperative role for the mood by amplifying the sound design and accentuating the emotional tone of the narrative. "But the most exciting part was that our only allegiance was to the story, which is not something we get to do often in the commercial realm. The positive energy of the entire 'Lily & the Snowman' team was infectious, and something that everyone gravitated toward and really leaned into. It was really humbling and inspiring to work with so many talented people on such a rewarding project." Schedule: "Pre-production began on September 21st and production started the week after, ultimately wrapping up on December 10th. "The quick turnaround forced us to be efficient with our plans, so from concept art to compositing we combined production stages, so that multiple phases were all moving at the same time. "For instance, we developed the environment design and models while animation was underway. Our design, lighting and compositing teams collaborated interactively to progress the color scripting, matte painting, lighting and comp all at the same time. "Although we were pressed for time, we tried not to neglect or skip any steps of a proper 3D animated film process, which let us build up a strong structure from story to animation."

records.description: Psyop executive producer Lydia Holness: "The brief that Heimat gave us was to develop an online film for the Christmas season which would connect with [European online retailer] Otto customers emotionally, embody and integrate the brand, and most importantly, make grown men cry. "The main creative challenge was the edit. The budget dictated a shorter schedule and much shorter story from what we first envisioned. As we fell in love with these characters and their story, we had a hard time editing the film down to what our production team could handle within the time and resources. "We were already pushing very hard on crafting the most beautiful moments, so we needed to make the shorter edit work for us. "In editing down the story we realized the most important thing was that viewers got a chance to connect with Mr. Banks throughout his journey, to empathize with him when he realizes the error he's made by losing the letter, and to be inspired by his efforts to deliver on a forgotten wish. "So that was the challenge. As always, there are a few scenes we wish could have played out a little longer, but the core story and emotional journey is there. "We wanted the look of the film to be highly cinematic and traditional at the same time. The challenge was to create a stop-motion animation look in CG. "We modeled in CG as you would practically in a miniature set, hand crafting every small detail of the characters, their wardrobes, and all the set pieces. "We drew inspiration from classic stop-motion films like 'Rudolph the Red­ Nosed Reindeer' with their charming characters and animation style. Finding the right balance of cinematic versus whimsical stop-motion style was challenging, but that's what makes our job interesting." Schedule: "The job awarded in mid August. We had character design, CG character models and pre­vis approved by the end of August. Animation was approved by the end of September. And we were lighting and compositing all through October."

records.description: Heather Kinal, senior producer at Framestore in London: "The initial brief was to create an animated Mog, using the original children's picture books as a reference point, in a new Christmas story written by author Judith Kerr for Sainsbury's Christmas campaign. "Framestore were tasked with recreating the recognisable, established and well-loved cat character in a 3D world. Not only did she have to appear realistic in the spot, she needed to be able to portray Mog's personality, and the emotions that feature so prominently in the original books. "One of the key creative challenges of the project was getting across the humour and emotion of the character. She needed to appear a real cat, yet convey emotions in an almost human way. "James Rouse, the director, felt it was important that the performance wasn't over-acted or cartoonish; instead he wanted to pare back the performance to create a subtle, more nuanced characterisation, to convey Mog's emotional state and make the spot 'readable' to TV audiences. "Creating fully CG Mog was the overarching challenge. As Mog has only ever existed in 2D, with each drawing being slightly different from the next, making her anatomically correct yet also indicative of the books was a big obstacle the team had to overcome. "Many rounds of animation testing led to the final Mog model. As Mog is a little on the rotund side, the animators had to account for the layer of fat that sits between her muscles and skin, which drove to the development of a whole new system for simulating organic material. "Once the volume of fat was created, it was given varying density and stiffness properties. The end result is a weighty, squishy cat which animates and deforms in a highly realistic way. "With the commercial running over three minutes long, the sheer number of shots involved was also a big challenge for the team. The production was more akin to a short film than a standard commercial, with rendering a key technical issue." Schedule: "Initial pre-vis work was done in May of 2015. The shoot took place in June, with post-production ramping up from July up until launch date."

records.description: Solid VFX Lab producer Hazel Jung in Seoul, South Korea: "The concept was to highlight the performance of the new Hyundai Santa Fe as it makes its way down the obstacles of this high-rise concrete construction site to the ground floor. "Because it was impossible to shoot these scenes, it was produced by utilizing CGI elements for the majority of the backgrounds and elements of the sequence. "The top priority for the clients was to create adventurous, dangerous scenes like those one would see in a circus show. It was also requested that each scene looked real and completely realistic. "Creating a complete section of the construction site through CGI was one of the biggest creative challenges. We used extensive photo references and data to find out how the functional layout of a construction site was built then carefully arranged the right layout. "The most important task was to make the live footage mix naturally with the CG elements. A pre-visual animation was created and used as a reference during the actual shoot. "Details of the buildings were made up of over 400 4K texture maps. In addition, the biggest challenge was to render the scenes in time to meet the short post-production schedule. "Much of the advertsing work done in South Korea does not allow for much post-production time. So to create the most realistic visuals, the director agreed with us to shoot much of the cuts with as little camera movement as possible. "After completing the rendering process in 3D, we added more dust and dirt using Photoshop tools and retouched the maps where needed."

records.description: Strange Beast producer Kitty Turley in London: "The three characters – Robot, Bat, and Eagle – and the World had to be incredibly detailed, but we did not have time to create photo-realistic concept renderings of every element before production started. "To an extent, we were feeling around in the dark to discover the look and the approach. It was a process of discovering at the same time as we built. This was a leap of faith for everyone – artists, agency and client. "Building real stuff always seems like the hardest part of this sort of production. We erected a model shop in an empty warehouse in Brooklyn and brought together a talented team of artists and model makers to build all costumes and sets. MPC VFX supervisors Stephen Ross and Tom Robinson: "All the shapes and forms of most of the major elements, from the main cloud, to the rocks and the trees were designed and originally drawn by Daren Rabinovitch of Encyclopedia Pictura. "We had to learn his style and incorporate this into our workflow. We worked very hard to facilitate his desires and bring to life his vision. Because of this, there is a stylistic consistency on all levels that holds true to Daren's art direction as we tried to keep it as pure as possible." Director Daren Rabinovitch: "The process of making great-looking CG animation is becoming more honed every day. But, as a filmmaker, nothing equals the magic of being on set with life-sized creatures – it is still the most magical experience." Schedule: "We had under three months to deliver. Everyone we worked with on various aspects of production said the timeline was pretty nuts - even impossible. It worked out to about three weeks of writing/concept art/storyboards, three weeks of building, one for shooting, and four weeks of post-production work, some of which started prior to the shoot."

records.description: Director PES in Santa Monica: "[The brief was] to tell the evolutionary history of Honda, from the very first generator engine that Soichiro Honda placed on a bicycle, up through the latest Honda/Acura NSX, one of the coolest cars in the world. "The vehicles, robots, and engines were all to be hand-drawn on pieces of paper and those physical illustrations were to be manipulated by hands (metaphorically the hands of Honda engineers) in front of the camera using stop-motion animation. How exactly that happened was largely up to me. "How to keep it exciting the whole time [was challenging]. It's a two-minute film, so that's a long time and you've gotta keep it fresh and unexpected. "As far as animation goes, coming up with a different paper manipulation technique for nearly every sequence was a big challenge, but I thought it was absolutely critical to creating a compelling piece. Around every corner I wanted the viewer to find some new surprise, so the film is constantly changing, shifting, evolving just like the Honda engine. "There are dozens of different animation techniques featured in the film - from paper folding to paper flipping to paper sliding, timed exposures and blurred frames, optical illusion drawings that can only be seen properly from one camera angle, traditional flip book style animation, hands holding drawings in mid air, replacement animation…the list could go on. "[The main challenge technically was] how to pull the entire thing off in camera, all in one continuous shot. How to create nearly 3,000 separate images in less than a month, and to figure out exactly how they should come to life in animation. It was without a doubt the most intense production of my life." Schedule: "One month of detailed CGI pre-vis; one month of animation testing, illustration creation, board construction and set dressing, and motion control testing/programming; shoot seven days; edit, one month for post, and sound design."

records.description: The Line directors Sam Taylor and Bjørn-Erik Aschim in London: "We received a script from the creative team at Leo Burnett that contained many of the elements you see in the final ad like the dystopian future, the evil regime, and the good TV. "We were lucky enough to be involved at a fairly early stage though, and were able to bring something of our own to the story as well as defining the visual direction of the piece. "Over the past few years we've mainly directed 2D animated projects, so moving into the realm of 3D was a really interesting challenge. Though we've both been involved in designing for 3D in the past, this was the first time we were put in the driver's seat – alongside Rogue director Sam Brown – and tasked with developing a new and distinctive style using 3D tools. "We always felt that in stylised CG productions, the charm and life of concept artwork often falls by the wayside in favor of a kind of realistic vinyl cartooniness that has become the norm. Angles get rounded off, designs get watered down. With this project we were extremely focused on retaining the intention of the artist all the way through to final product. "The scope of the project was really big. Alongside the two-minute launch film, there are four shorter stand-alone ads that feature a total of 24 unique characters, and bespoke environments. All this had to be designed and built at the same time as the launch film. "The town itself was also a massive undertaking. Each building, car, street lamp, post box, and bus stop had to be designed, modeled, laid out, textured, and rendered. ETC's ultra-committed team, and custom pipeline tools, were the only thing that enabled us to manage it all in the time we had. "We had to design A LOT of buildings for this ad. In order to populate the town with buildings that look authentic, the design team took inspiration from the buildings outside of their window. This means a lot of the buildings in the ad are real buildings on the other side of the street from work. We also stole our best mate's face for the main character." Schedule: eight months.

records.description: MPC head of 3D Anthony Bloor in London: "To get the right feeling for the story Johnny wanted to tell, we needed to have full control of the way the brick wall was built, what elements were made of and how they behave. "The treatment gave us a good initial idea of how things should look, but it was important to be able to iterate fast and make quick reviews to fit into the agency's and director's vision. "To complete the project quickly and efficiently a procedural modeling and animation system was written to build and animate the walls. With this system the artists had the ability to dial the parameters and have all the elements automatically placed and modeled with physical accuracy. This allowed for great creative control and artistic fine tuning to achieve the director's vision for each shot. "Some of the elements – bricks, breeze blocks, plasterboard, studs, tiles and even 1980s style wallpaper – frenetically build behind the leading edge of the walls automatically responding to the character of the wall. "Thousands of high-detail models populate the house as it builds through the environment, but also much of the environment was enhanced too with everything from the sky to the grass replaced in several shots. "The walls had various moods throughout. At first it was able to build quickly and straight, but as the kids tried to trick it, the walls start to twist and turn getting less perfect and building with more and more random items. "Towards the end it's already wobbling ready to fall over before the final destruction. We also simulate some light dust which helped to add realism without excessively covering the action."

records.description: Parachute director Sam O'Hare in New York: "We wanted to do a piece to show our ability to create a fully CG film. "Tesla is a company with a philosophy that I admire. They want to change the world by changing our transportation system, and were willing to spend all the time and money to develop an EV people love, only to turn around and open-­source all their patents to encourage others to follow suit. Their goal is a fully sustainable, zero emission transport system. "[I was] walking through Central Park a couple of summers ago, the fireflies had just come out, there is something magical to me about those flashes of light. "In the UK you don't see them, and encountering them for the first time as an adult still generates child­like wonder. Their bio­luminescence seemed like a good metaphor for the use of natural energy to power an electric car, and the story flowed from there. "As described above, coming up with and telling a coherent story using the fireflies to bring the car to life [was the main creative challenge]. A lot of time was spent on the camera work to ensure both the environment and the tiny heroes were understandable. "The fully CG environment had a lot of large maps, displacement, and animated plants. This required a lot of RAM to render, and we spent some time optimising and breaking up the scenes to get them to render. "For the gathering scenes, every firefly is a light and because the lights were so small, we had to drop the cut-off for each to 0 to have them show up correctly in reflections, which made for some heavy renders. "I wrote a script based on one of Borislav Petrov's to have the fireflies correctly follow the particle system we used to animate them, and the lightning effect was built using a distance pair matching data operator based on work by Khye Kading and took a while to get right. "The majority of the work was done in 3ds Max, using RPManager to organise and V-Ray to render. Plants were made using GrowFX and distributed with Forest Pack Pro. Mari and Photoshop were used for texture work, and FumeFX, Krakatoa and Frost were used in the cottonwood and large volume firefly animation. "Terragen was used to generate the distant mountains and skies, which in turn were used for lighting. Everything was composited in Blackmagic's Fusion Studio, and edited in Adobe Premiere." Schedule: "This was a job that we worked on in our downtime, so the schedule was weeks here and there spread over the best part of two years. The majority of the work was done by myself and Andy Gilbert. We spent a couple of months at the end to push it through to completion."

records.description: The Salon Alpin team in Vienna, Austria: "We were asked to produce and illustrate the new cinema spot for the Austrian newspaper 'Falter'. "Together with the agency Jung von Matt/Donau we developed a script: This interpretation of Dante's Inferno takes you on a journey through eight layers of hell. "The team's vision was to illustrate the modern, 21st century take on hell, where people are stuck in smartphone jails, big brother is watching you, civil courage is missing and questionable factory farms produce our food. "The closing line and claim of Falter, 'Hol mich hier raus', translates loosely to 'Get me out of here.' A clear message to end this metaphorical spot and contemporary take on the dark side of today's life: the only escape from everyday madness is reading Falter, gaining information and forming your own opinion. "It was our main goal to deliver a very clear and readable style, suitable for a fast paced sequence and able to carry simple statements. The briefing said black and white so this artistic limitation for sure pushed us to get the most out of our value structure and shot composition. "Technically we tried to make various ways of animation and different types of effects footage work into one single illustrative look. "Given the very narrow timeframe, we tried to use minimal animation without making the shots feel static and flat. As a matter of fact, we used for all figure animation acted references by our diligent coworker João 'Tausend' Faria. "It is always a pleasure to work on projects with serious topics and to create a clip that is not showcasing a product to buy or a corporate image, but a statement." Schedule: two months.

records.description: Nexus wunderkind director Johnny Kelly pulls together 100+ artists, designers, craftspeople, architects, engineers, scientists and musicians; assigning them each a scene, then merging it all into a hypnotic brand film for Dropbox. Stash: Working with over 100 collaborators seems overwhelming. How did you select them? Johnny Kelly: Finding contributors was a fun task. My first step was to trawl through my bookmarks folder, but this was mostly illustrators and animators. Dropbox and 72andSunny wanted to show the sheer diversity of their users so we spread the net wider to include architects, engineers, musicians and more. This meant looking into the different kinds of people using Dropbox, and approaching friends, friends of friends, and other connections with a view to gathering all of this in a very short period of time. When I tendered on the project I put together a little pitch video. This proved really useful to send out to contributors so they immediately understood the broad idea behind the film, and also to make SUPER CLEAR that their work would only be on screen for a nanosecond. Everyone seemed okay with this, thankfully. Stash: Did you create any of the vignettes yourself? JK: I had my grubby mitts on quite a few of them, but resisted the urge to do more. I wanted to make sure it felt like a mix of different creators' work, and making most of the vignettes myself would have broken that rule. That said, I did thumbnail out a storyboard at the start of the production (I'm incapable of directing without doing some kind of board) in order to plan out the flow and balance of different techniques. Stash: How did you handle the logistical problems of so many assets? JK: Part of my initial idea was to make a film that could only have been made using Dropbox. So genuinely, the product was a key part of the production (I can say the same for a Bacardi ad I did a few years ago) and it allowed us to sync a bazillion shot folders on our local server with dozens of contributors around the globe. Stash: What was the greatest creative hurdle to making such a collaborative piece? JK: The traditional production of a 60-second spot involves tight storyboarding, design and shot approval. records.description: Executive producer Jeremy Smith at Nexus in London: "Umpqua Bank has always done things differently to other banks. The brief was for an advert that was unlike any other bank commercial. The financial advertising sector felt very tired and not very engaging so Umpqua and CAA decided to approach the problem with a short film aesthetic. "They wanted to change the mindset of how people felt about banks. To create a modern fable set in a magical and imaginative world that would captivate the audience." Director Kibwe Tavares: "I wanted to create a beautifully simple, magical narrative that would hit the key themes of Hope, Empowerment and Triumph, showing how something relatively ordinary, that we take for granted, can transform into something spectacular. "The devil really was in the details; both plants and cities have a lot of character. Getting that level of detail accurate not just for the 'hero' seed but across all the vegetation, and the whole city both above and below ground, re-creating a magical environment that resonates with the viewer and delivers an emotional impact, was quite a challenge." Jeremy Smith: "From the script and storyboard stage, it was obvious that this job was going to be particularly complex. "We knew ahead of time that a shoot would not be possible so our principal concern was re-creating the environments in a style that retained a sense of magic. We were fortunate to have a month long R&D period at the beginning of the job when we tested several new techniques in order to meet the ambition of the director. "For example, we have worked with lidar data before but building several photo real environments and large props from scratch (with scales ranging from individual stones in tarmac to entire city wide shots) from several lidar scans and then texturing it using HDR spherical projection in Mari was a complex process. "The character of the plant provided its own unique challenges too. We had to cover every stage of plant growth, from tiny seed to giant tree, often covering several stages in one continuous shot. The city needed plants and vegetation growing all over it too and we were happy to have the support of the development team at ExLevel and their GrowFX plugin for Max. "The ad was produced entirely in house from modeling to final comp, with a final grade and master being done at Time Based Arts." Schedule: ten months.

records.description: Creative director Benoît Leroux at TBWAParis: "The purpose of the campaign is first, to make people understand and remember that every tire designed by Michelin brings every single type of tire performance together and second, that this development philosophy has a name: 'MICHELIN Total Performance'. "The main creative challenge was to create a complete world populated by fantastic creatures in an 80-second CGI video. Another creative challenge was to create from scratch a character which represents each performance of the Michelin tires. This work imagines each facet of tire performance as a living creature with a unique personality. "Another important point was the realism that Moonbot and the agency wanted to give to all the characters and the epic landscapes' shapes and textures. This was an essential point to create empathy for the characters. "The realism they gave to all the weather conditions was also essential. The work on the lights, the rain, the snow was really important to underline Michelin's words on the tires' performances in extreme conditions. "Regarding the animation: each character was original so no references on how they move really exists. Of course some parts of the characters are based on existing animals but the character design guideline needed to include some vehicle parts on each character. So Moonbot Studios generated from scratch all the original character movements trying to be physically realistic given each body design." Schedule: "Moonbot started the character design and CGI work in January 2014. The final film was delivered in October 2014."

records.description: Senior producer Nirad Bugs Russell at The Mill in New York: "The director Wally Pfister and the creative team at Droga5 wanted to create an epic film that was cinematic and not an exercise in CGI. They wanted it to feel powerful, visceral and dramatic. "The main creative challenges were to create armies of athletes for Misty Copeland, Stephen Curry and Jordan Spieth. It was important that it translated as if they were real performances versus CG as much as possible. "Time on set with celebrity talent is always a challenge - you need to be super efficient with the shooting day. Preparation was key, as well as finding technical solves. We worked with the director, agency and production to develop the right blend of techniques. "Together we developed a camera array system to capture simultaneous actions and performances from the same take, which was then tiled in post. To make the CG crowds as convincing as possible, we took CG scans on set of the athletes and also motion captured performance to drive the animation of our characters. "It was a really collaborative experience - incredible crew, great director and agency. We are very proud of the spots." Schedule: "VFX for the campaign was roughly eight weeks end to end."
