records.description: Blinkink director Elliot Dear in London: "The agency wanted to appeal to a wide audience. They wanted to include all the family - the idea being that die-hard rugby fans would recognize the players even in animated form, and that the overall aesthetic would appeal to people who weren't familiar with the players, or even the sport. "The film is about including everyone and getting everyone behind the team, and the animated style we chose to with was very accessible and in many cases nostalgic. It's quite a warm aesthetic with just the right amount of slickness. "I think the biggest challenge was consistency. Finding an aesthetic that works for the job is one thing, but communicating that idea to dozens of people (some artists were working abroad too) can be a real task. "Every animator, background artist, and designer has a 'native' style - a particular process and habits. I had to recognize each person's specific way of working and understand how to guide them through the project so that we'd end up with a seamless film with a unified visual language. "I wanted to give the animation a freshness by using CG to plan the backgrounds and camera moves. The film is peppered with 3D camera moves through hand-drawn backgrounds, which gives it a dynamism that you don't always see in traditional 2D animation. "It meant that I wasn't limited in terms of the camera and could move the camera in a way more similar to live action. The challenge was getting these shots to work without sticking out, to keep the technique feeling traditional." Schedule: "We started pitching in late February. Animation started in May and we delivered in early September."

records.description: Nicolas Cantarelli, CGI director at Laposta in Buenos Aires: "The client wanted to show a new smartphone with a smart idea and wanted to make it in a fantastic and surreal way. "Directed by Jonathan Gurvit, the spot focuses on the speed of the red 'play' bar trying to catch up to the grey 'download' bar and extends as a metaphor showing us how dramatic slow downloads could be. "At the beginning we had to choose which actions we wanted to show, so we had to draw lot of ideas from the agency and from ourselves. The selection process was tough. Lot of good ideas were thrown in the trash. We especially loved one with a Chinese dragon chasing a Samurai. Maybe we have to wait for a second part of this campaign to see it. "Our main challenge was to design and create all of the CGI environments because the only thing they could shoot was the actors and extras running in the studio. "It was really difficult to understand how the bees fly to make them look real but technical at the same time. The smoke of the train was another issue we had to take care of, because we had to simulate lots of frames to have it in slow motion. "After finding the correct hardware to cache all that, we managed to process all that data to generate the long and realistic smoke effects. "During pre-production we decided the best way to shoot this spot would be in a dark place to emphasize this dramatic staging. At compositing we had to rotoscope all the characters on all the shots. "We knew this would be artist-intensive, and we would have to use lot of time to make all the masks to composite the backgrounds but with this method we achieved a much better comp." Schedule: two months.

records.description: Limón Estudios co-owner and post-producer Albert Montero Vera in Barcelona: "We wanted a piece people would talk about, which would be active on all social networks. In reference to all those who talk just for talking's sake (the 'haters') and turn them into the main character of the campaign. "The main technical challenge was the shooting. The players could only stay on the set for two hours and we had a lot of scenes to shoot with each player. Thanks to the professional team everything turned out smoothly. "At post-production level, the main challenge was the huge number of scenes. Almost all shots have post-production and the great majority using very different techniques. "From breaking the ground with dynamics, to scanning James Rodriguez in a set in order to have a 3D model and turn it to gold, and to remove chroma and wires, ah! And of course design and create Gareth Bale's house. "It was a tough task which took a lot of hours to combine all those techniques, but we enjoyed it a lot and the result is awesome." Schedule: "The production calendar had to match the players' availability given that they have a lot of arrangements and you have to adapt to their schedule. Shooting with Madrid CF and FC Barcelona involved traveling to Madrid to shoot with Benzema, Bale and James, and four weeks later shoot with Luis Suarez in Barcelona. "Post-production started right after the shooting ended in Madrid. It was edited and all scenes were post-produced with the players we already had, waiting for Luis Suarez's scenes. Once we had filmed Luis we had four weeks to finish the piece."

records.description: Nexus directors Smith & Foulkes in London: "The brief was to tell the story of an unlikely hero, an underdog born with a disadvantage who refuses to accept his lot in life, a classic rise to the top against all the odds tale – something which could emotionally mirror the real life stories the Grand National always seems to reveal. "The original script could almost have been a feature film. But we had 60 seconds. So the challenge was to tell as much story as we could, while establishing an entire Fantasy Universe and giving enough time for the audience to care about our hero. "It was also hard to show the passing of time in such a short format, so we used the different seasons as an immediate read. "Any film which gives animals human emotions is immediately labeled as Disney. But we had to go about things slightly differently, as much a creative choice as a logistical one. "Our 'World of Mythology' was entirely created with textured matte paintings, which were then composited with 3D characters and real effects to create atmospheric environments. "We have worked with [composer] Alex Baranowski on several projects but this is the first opportunity we had to record with a full orchestra in a studio. Watching them re-work and improvise live to picture was an education on how to score a film. "We had a pretty strict deadline, as I don't think they could delay the race. We did ask though!" Schedule: 12 weeks.

records.description: Producer Pierrot Jacquet at ChezEddy in Paris: "The directors wanted to captivate the public with a Disneyesque universe with 'Tangled' and 'Frozen' as the main references. The founding idea was for model Hannah Ferguson to be immersed in a fairy tale universe as she entered the Triumph store. "We faced two big artistic challenges at ChezEddy: synthesizing Disney's CG feature style to be able to get a final result with the right feel but that was achievable in the three-week animation schedule; and finding a color harmony between all the furniture and lingerie items to recreate this radiant fantasy store. records.description: Mill+ director Russell Tickner in London: "Collaborating closely with the agency creative team, all of the various VFX specialists worked together from the outset, involved in every element from the pre-production, storyboarding and character design, to the 'bricking' animation tools developed specifically for this job. Joint head of 3D at The Mill, Dave Fleet: "Firstly, our characters were modeled as polygonal meshes. These were then rigged and animated, then passed from Maya to Houdini using Mill+'s custom caching format. "At this point the animators would also export what we refer to as a 'call sheet'. This is basically a live list of ingredients that go into each scene. Russell and the animators were regularly changing characters, so it was vital to make this as easy as possible so the FX and lighting teams were always up to date. "We then started the process of turning the animated characters into bricks, by creating our own plugin aptly named Bricker. Bricker was seamlessly integrated into our existing pipeline and automatically picked up animation updates and knew when new characters got added or removed from a shot. "As LEGO bricks come in all different shapes and sizes we built sliders within the tool so the artist could decide which bricks were used and ultimately how the character was built. "The Pirate ship had the most, at around three million individual LEGO bricks, not including the huge wave it was riding. Bricker included many other optimization features like camera culling and hollowing out the characters to save on bricks and to speed up the whole workflow. "The bricked characters were then passed onto our lighting team as a huge point cloud, each point representing the location and color of a brick. This allowed our lighting scenes to be very lightweight as the LEGO bricks themselves are only created at render time using Arnold's powerful instancing system." Schedule: "Eight months from initial concept images to the final spot."

records.description: Alter Ego executive producer Cheyenne Bloomfield in Toronto: "We were brought in for the initial brief to help design and solve a host of creative and technical challenges to create the bikes with no riders. "Our main creative challenge was to maintain reality. In regards to bike performance, environment contact and interaction, we really wanted to make the CG also hold up to scrutiny next to the live shots of bikes where we had to paint out riders. "One thing we learned along the way was that bikers are very passionate and extremely detail focused. Pedals, chains and other mechanics had to work properly and also believably. The weight of the bikes needed to be maintained without the riders' actions to help sell performance. "Golaem crowd simulation software provided us with flawless wheel traction and wheel ground contact. We explored several methods to obtain the most reliable motion library possible, and ended up using mostly keyframed motions because the 'real' motions had nuances that looked unrealistic without the rider. "The entire VFX team was tasked with executing a paint, CG or hybrid approach to removing riders, animating bikes or creating pelotons of bikes on beautifully captured locations across Canada. "An EXR Linear workflow was designed and implemented within Nuke Studio to allow us the ability to grade, edit, animate and render without having any duplication of data. We used the Baselight plugin for Nuke to enable us to view dynamic grades with all the shapes and layers as quickly as the colorists made changes. "We joined the small but dedicated production team for every shoot, capturing 360-degree HDR's of locations and reference stills of bikes, riders and anything else that came up along the way. These were invaluable for matching lighting and also as elements needed for painting riders off the bikes. "The film had 50 shots in total, including 25 CG shots, four of which used Golaem, and 18 paint/roto shots. Throughout the process, the Alter Ego team also drew from their personal knowledge about cycling, a shared passion in-house, to help make the film more real." Schedule: "We began shooting in September 2014 and our delivery date was March 2015. We shot additional BMX footage in November and the final Velodrome shoot was February, once the Velodrome cleared all safety checks (brand new, built for the Pan Am Games)."

records.description: Producer Marta Staniszewska at Platige Image in Warsaw: "The client came to us and said: 'We need a fresh outstanding idea that will introduce the ebook to the readers. "We want something that has never been done in the Polish market. We want to extend the world of the novel in every possible way, creating an enriched reading experience.' "The spot was supposed to be something that makes the post-apocalyptic world alive for just a brief moment. It's a teaser for the plot – just to make people curious enough to buy the ebook. "A crucial challenge was to translate the world of literature into the visuals (both movie and illustrations) and to keep the novel's nostalgic and melancholic tone. "The most tricky part of the project was the shots with close-ups of the 'sculpting' process of the figure. We wanted to avoid heavy simulations and use as little CG as we could. "So finally we shot some slow motion footage of sparks, smoke and electric arcs and then composited it with the robot and some additional rendered particles. "The idea for the campaign and all the additional materials for the ebook was design in Platige's creative hub Fish Ladder (fishladder.is). All the materials were produced by the Platige Image team. "A few printed mech figures were painted by the writer of the ebook Jacek Dukaj, Tomek Baginski, Marcin Panasiuk, Maciej Jackiewicz and Alex Jaeger (who designed the models of the mechs) and will be sold through a charity auction in Poland. "We also did something extra. For the first time, a literary project can enjoy the advantages of 3D print. Readers will have the opportunity to order a mech, printed by a 3D printer. This service is available via the campaign website at http://jacekdukaj.allegro.pl/en." Schedule: "First we shot the girl on the beach. Then we were looking for the right industrial interior for the final shots of the spot. It took some time to find it and to arrange everything. We finally did this at ABB Transformer Factory in Lodz. Finalizing the CG visuals took three months."

records.description: MPC VFX supervisor Diarmid Harrison Murray and lead animator Tim Van Hussen in London: "The brief from the client was to make photo real t-shirts that look like they could plausibly fly with the characteristics of migratory birds. "There was a strong emphasis on the characterization of the t-shirts in order to engage the audience and have them relate to their journey. "Our main creative challenge was to get an emotional performance out of realistic t-shirts, which was a difficult task because they are inanimate objects without any consistency in shape or form. "Working with director Dougal Wilson, we set out to create a level of performance that would be clear enough to read despite their physical lack of expressiveness. "At the same time we aimed to maintain their realistic qualities, such as the way they fold in on themselves, flutter in the wind and behave/look depending on their direct environment. "T-shirts do not really have any body-parts, so we had to find a versatile way to digitally puppeteer them. "We ended up using almost their entire shape for wing surfaces with a fold along the center, as that gave a powerful feel to their flight and added to the visual credibility of the film. When on the ground, this would change - their neck opening would serve as an expressive head, and the sleeves simply hang loose. "On top of the basic animation, we simulated the cloth to get detailed interaction between the t-shirts and their environments – wind, hard and soft surfaces. In many shots they also interact with water – landing on it, floating and drifting, taking off and being rained on – which required a range of CG water and simulation shots. "We also wrote bespoke tools for a faster animation workflow, so we were able to efficiently animate and lay out hundreds of t-shirts in a shot. "In the shot where they murmur like starlings, we simulated thousands in numerous flocks, with each t-shirt making its own decisions, like sticking close to the group, or leading a change in direction. Some stray off and join a different flock or start their own." Schedule: Oct 20 - Dec 1: modeling, RnD and lookdev Nov 18 - Nov 27: shoot Dec 1 - Dec 23: animation and lighting, comp Dec 24: delivery

records.description: Seamless and surprisingly extensive VFX from The Mill for the Snickers Super Bowl spot starring Danny Trejo as Marcia Brady and Steve Buscemi as Jan. Visual effects supervisor Nick Tanner at The Mill, New York: "2D lead artist Nathan Kane worked with the team to build a pre-vis to try and figure out the spatial representation of that old Brady Bunch set. "Then, on the shoot day the whole set was replicated as closely as possible to the original to give Danny Trejo and Steve Buscemi an environment grounded in reality, with furniture they could interact with. This allowed for the axe throwing improvisation and Steve's tantrum at the top of the steps to occur. "The approach to filming was an intensive part of the final visual effects. We needed to capture 180 degrees of the stand-ins' faces and place Danny and Steve in the Brady living room. "We made sure the stand-in actors were fixed in place to minimize their movements, and set up five witness cameras on all sides to capture their performance from every angle. "Their faces were then tracked onto CG geometry of the original characters' faces. The team was cautious about tracking with the decades old footage that included a high level of artifacts and grain. "The body doubles (cast for their mouth, chin and lip features and filmed against greenscreen) would say the lines and this footage was tracked and transplanted onto the original footage of Florence Henderson as Mrs. Brady and Robert Reed as Mr. Brady. But the actual voice of Henderson heard in the spot was a character voiceover artist. "Finally, grain and texture was added to each shot, giving it the vintage treatment to fit in with the rest of the footage. "Even though the team hasn't seen either actor in many commercials, they knew Steve Buscemi would be the perfect person to convey the internal angst of Jan. He was interested as soon we reached out. "Danny Trejo took his turn as Marcia Brady extremely seriously during filming. Watching Danny angrily yell at Mr. and Mrs. Brady was a treat."

records.description: Co-director Boris Croise of Zeppelin Pictures in Paris: "Every year Dior wants to tell a little Christmas story by putting its Christmas collection in a magical and enchanted world. "The main creative challenge with this type of client is to bring the products in a different world full of fantasy without breaking its codes. It has to be balanced. "Making a factory to be magical wasn't easy at all. We liked the idea of bringing something cold and mechanical into a more poetical and warm mood, something more stirring, like all these little sounds becoming a melody. "The main technical challenge was the fact that we were only two working on it. "Dior wanted us to start with the last two shots to make a teaser. They wanted to present it at a worldwide meeting to introduce the next Christmas video. So we had to start making the last two shots before having a real layout of the clip. "We've directed other the Christmas clips for Dior over the past years. They are as similar as they are different. We started working on the next one, and we are trying to push the level a little higher!" Schedule: "Production started at the beginning of April and finished the beginning of July."

records.description: MPC in London: "The brief was to create a completely photorealistic CG penguin called Monty that would behave in a naturalistic way but also deliver an engaging emotional performance. After initial discussions, an Adelie penguin was chosen. "The main challenge was developing a convincing performance from Monty, but never veering away from what a penguin could do in real life. "We studied archive wildlife footage and photography of the Adelie. Dougal Wilson is meticulous in his research and gathered a great library of material that he shared with us at MPC and we created a shortlist of clips and images that exemplified the characteristics we were after. "An individual Adelie can dramatically change how he looks moment to moment. This is what makes them such expressive creatures. Sometimes they are squat and chubby and fluffy with their neck totally hidden inside hunched shoulders, the next minute they are slick, fast and athletic. records.description: Electric Theatre Collective in London: "After two highly successful brand ads ('Tadpoles', 'Cat & Budgie') in recent years, Leo Burnett were tasked by Freeview to come up with the next great ad in the 'Entertainment is even better when it's free' series. "What a brief! The task was essentially to create a piece of branded content to celebrate the fact that 95 percent of the nation's top TV is available on Freeview at no monthly cost. "Collaboratively, we needed to make a decision on how to best execute the 40 characters. They obviously needed to look real and move realistically. Turns out it's quite tricky to figure out how stiff a taxidermied marmot should be. "We spent a lot of time with Sam discussing each character, their movement, their personalities and emotion, how they were manufactured. It was imperative that their look, movement and behavior were spot on. In order to achieve this we ended up using actual, puppeteered toys and full CG doubles and in some cases a mixture of both. "The sheer volume of characters was quite the challenge. Especially as different methods were needed for certain characters. Each object was scanned, remodeled, textured and then rigged to create a fully animate-able digital puppet. Our animators worked their magic to make these puppets come alive, and then we worked to perfectly match the lighting and environment of the original plate. Finally, in the compositing process, we replaced the real shot objects with our all singing, all dancing CG toys." Schedule: "We had just over three months to complete this spot. Character R&D started at the end of August, we shot for two days at the end of September and carried out post-production for seven weeks."

records.description: Hue&Cry creative director Magnus Hierta in Richmond, Virginia: "The client brief was simple and direct. It consisted of a song and lyrics paired with a set of simple visual guidelines. The song is based around a simple question asking: 'Wonder if I gave an Oreo to someone, would it give them an optimistic outlook?' "The visual guidelines spoke of bold vibrant colors, simple graphic uncluttered space, and a focus on impactful typography. In fact, they wanted the typography to be see-and-say in the fashion of a karaoke video. Very fun indeed! "The creative challenge was fairly straightforward: Design a spot that fit into the bold, clean look of the new Wonderfilled campaign. We were tasked with creating a spot based around typography with supporting elements and design vignettes that worked in support of the type. "And it had to bridge the high school theme of the lyrics with the hip-hop music track aesthetics into an aesthetic appealing to everyone, from kids to moms (OREO's core buyer). Oh, and of course it needed to be watchable again and again. "The project had an extremely tight three-week timeline and an approved look that included a lot of cel animation. Needless to say, this combination is not the most forgiving! "So we approached it systematically. We created scenes that utilized a lot of repeated elements which created a graphic, grid-like quality. This allowed us to minimize the amount of cel animation needed so we could focus our animators on some of the bigger key elements. "For the typography we built a Cinema 4D rig that allowed us to iterate type changes quickly. We rendered them with the Sketch and Toon shading plug-in for the cel animated look. That output was paired with standard render passes using clamped ambient occlusion maps to create natural shading to the Toon rendered lines. It did the trick just right." Schedule: "We had a three week production schedule to deliver :15, :30 and :45 second spots!"

records.description: Director Kris Hofmann in Welham Green, UK: "[The brief was] to draw attention to the plight of the urban hedgehog. Hedgehog numbers in Britain have fallen from 30 million down to only one million, due to loss of habitat and a variety of man-made dangers. "Once we decided upon the simple story line (a set of magical paw prints guide Harry the hedgehog out of the city and back into the safety of the forest) the main challenge was how to visualize the journey from city to forest in the best possible way. "This was a collaborative process between illustrator Sandra Dieckmann, model maker Joe James and myself. I gave Sandra a storyboard and asked her to draw the environment Harry would be traveling through. I sketched a fairly rough design for Harry, noting I wanted the paper cut pencil-style spikes and passed this on to Joe. "We then built the different elements of Sandra's world (walls, trees, bins, etc.) from grey card. This allowed us to give the illustrations 'body' and merge the worlds of the flat drawings and the model puppet. For example, when Harry is walking through the forest the trees cast shadows on him, etc. "In the final stage we mapped Sandra's illustrations onto the 3D paper world in order to merge our 3D puppet hedgehog and the hand-drawn environments he is traveling through. "We shot on a Canon C300 with a set of Zeiss lenses. Comp work was done in After Effects." Schedule: five months.

records.description: Le Cube executive producer Gustavo Karam in Sao Paulo, Brazil: "The animation briefing was to create a dark animation, portraying the wind as the avenger of nature created by the anti-ecologic men. "At Le Cube we support at least one cause per year and after reading the beautiful script sent by the agency Porta we decided to accept doing the animation as a pro bono. "The wind needed to be an ascending power, growing during all the animation until the twist moment when everything collapses. The search for an aesthetic that could represent the power and at the same time be sympathetic was a challenge. The timing of the animation to fit in one minute was also another issue. But with care and love, all the problems were beautifully bypassed. "In contrast to the deep and dark mood of the animation, the production process was very relaxed and funny. As an example of this, JuanMa, an executive producer at Le Cube, in the second email of the project called the agency CD Gonzalo 'Marta' by an insane mistake, of course. "Gonzalo, as the funny and irreverent creative director that he is, transformed the mistake into a joke, calling JuanMa 'Mirta' in the subsequent email. 'Marta' and 'Mirta' stayed with us during the whole process of Greenpeace and are still in contact for other projects." Schedule: eight weeks.

"Technically the biggest challenge was to translate the flat, photocopied feel of our style frames into a more dynamic and dimensional space, which needed to include both greenscreen footage and live action from other sources such as their awesome Robbie Maddison film where he does the Olympic Ski Jump in Park City. records.description: Neil Davies, executive creative director at The Mill in London: "The brief was to create a fully CGI, 100 percent photo-real orangutan and place her seamlessly into both jungle and city environments. "No one wanted to use a real orangutan, but we didn't want to end up with an obviously CG looking character in each shot. Creatively we wanted to make sure you believed Maya as a creature and connected with her on an emotional level as well as being able to tell a story through her. It was very important to us that we never crossed the line of making her too human. "It's always tempting to take the easy route and get her emotions across by using more human characteristics such as smiling, but this was something we were constantly aware of avoiding. "Instead we took the trickier but ultimately more rewarding route of trying to portray emotions through subtleties of eye movement, head movement or even very small facial muscle movements. The animation team led by Jorge Montiel had to study hours and hours of orangutan footage to be able to handle Maya's movement in a sensitive, believable way. We purposefully avoided the motion capture route, knowing we could end up with something more believable spending more time animating by hand rather than using data. "It also meant we could be much more flexible as we weren't tied into pre-determined actions. In collaboration with director Frederic Planchon we could adapt the creature's performance and emotions to suit the flow of the edit. "Finally the CG had to be composited in seamless way, so the viewer could follow the story rather than try and analyse the work. "It was hugely challenging technically, maybe one of the biggest we've been faced with to date (and we've had some pretty challenging ones). Alex Hammond our CG lead, did an amazing job running the CG team of riggers, sculptors, hair groomers, muscle builders, animators, lighters and renderers etc. "Obviously the eyes are all important when it comes to believability and a huge amount of work went into ensuring that the eyes were photo real. Details like moisture collecting at the bottom of the eyes, making sure light reflections were technically correct, and even down to tiny details like the pupils dilating with bright light. "Skin texture was hugely important with every wrinkle being sculpted by hand based on high resolution photographs. "Hair was probably the biggest challenge as the long hair needed to be groomed correctly but also needed to react to gravity, wind, body movement and even muscle movement. The team of simulators had their work cut out to make sure the hair behaved in a believable way in every different circumstance. No detail was overlooked - even down to the very fine facial hair and bits of dirt in the hair. "Every technical consideration was chosen to make the end product look as least technical as possible. We didn't want the huge amount of technical work to show - we just wanted to aim for reality. "The conform was done using Flame. The compositing was shared between Flame 2015 and Nuke, each completing roughly the same number of shots. Interestingly it was the first time any of the Mill offices had used Flame 2015, which is radically different to its predecessor, but it proved to be perfect for the heavy composting of linear 16-bit CG layers required. "All of the 3D was created using 48-64 gb/multi-core machines with Nvidia Quadro FX graphics. The 3D software used to create our orangutan was XSI using Arnold renderer, Maya, ZBrush and Mari. "What really helped the way the spot turned out wasn't just the hours and hours of dedication the team put in on both a technical and creative level - it was also the way the job was run. From the very first meeting it was a true collaboration between client, agency, director and The Mill. "We weren't just a post house doing what we were asked, we were creative partners pushing the project along with everyone else to deliver something fairly groundbreaking. "Finally, and very importantly, thanks to Adam&Eve's understanding of the complex nature of the work involved, we had the right amount of time to complete a project of this enormity, which is increasingly rare these days." Schedule: "Our first meetings started in the latter part of 2013, with the shoot being three nights at the end of February 2014 after which the CG team swung into action creating Maya before the compositing started in mid June. We finally completed the work in mid September 2014 for an early October release."

records.description: WIZZdesign directors Andy's and Paris CG house Unit Image push their latest photo-real CG collaboration to a new level for this remake of a classic Bond-inspired spot from 1987. Except for the vehicle interior and the actors, everything after the :18 second mark is CG, including the transition shot from 4/3 to 16/9. Matthieu Poirier, producer at WIZZdesign in Paris: "The main idea of the campaign was to create a spot as an homage to the original film directed by Gerard Pires for the 205 GTi Peugeot in the '80s. "We had to imagine a new version that kept the mood and the feeling of the previous film, which was very epic to the audience at that time. We focused on the direction (storytelling, acting, styling) to make the new film current and fresh. We kept the same overall outline of the old 205 spot, but we updated the approach for a 2014 campaign. "The main challenge was to produce a film entirely in photo realistic 3D. No scenery, no helicopter, no bomber and no car exterior was filmed in the creation of this campaign. records.description: Jayson Whitmore, executive creative director/partner at We Are Royale in Los Angeles: "Nike came out with a new type of eco-friendly dying process called dry dying, a technique that actually saves the world by reducing the water used in dying clothing to zero. "Pretty good reduction if you ask us and it's a rather remarkable process. Dry pigment is literally baked into the fibers of fabric through heat and pressure creating the most brilliant, evenly spread color across the entire roll of fabric. Nike coined this process 'Colordry' and AKQA came to us to help them tell that story. "The idea is to start with a single 'mote' of color. Abstract, like a little world all to itself. As the pressure inside this chamber increases, the mote collapses in on itself, releasing color. At the same time, it begins to fall into the fabric like meteorites hitting the Salton Sea. "Each mote impact spreads more color across the landscape. It's a turbulent scene that culminates in a grand reveal of a single, perfectly constructed Colordry jersey suspended in a roaring stadium hallway. It speaks to sport, and abstracts the process into something bigger than itself. "There were a few creative challenges, one of which was making photo-real fabric and the other creating a particle system that made the collision of the particles feel natural. Our goal was to make it feel impactful and realistic. "Rendering is always a challenge on a project like this. Also writing a realistic particle system that showed impact and while making it feel otherworldly." Schedule: "We had a little over a month from start to finish."

records.description: PostPanic director Mischa Rozema in Amsterdam: "There was just no way to turn a script like this down, even though it had 'IMPOSSIBLE' written all over it. The complexity, the size, the craziness. Maybe that's what really pulled me in to this. I just loved stepping into the unknown and finding out how we could make this work. "The biggest challenge was how to avoid the VFX becoming the focus of the TVC. PostPanic is set up differently than most production companies because we have our own in-house post production team which works instinctively with the directors. "The temptation would have been to apply all that specialised knowledge and make this into a VFX fest but actually we threw out a lot of VFX when we started the project. "We decided to really push what could be achieved in camera by actually creating a full size human truck on the set. It worked by having a huge, truck-sized, metal rig that could be pulled by an actual truck. "We then filled it with an incredible Czech stunt team (famous for big Hollywood blockbusters) that had been rehearsing for weeks and gave the whole project a realistic approach. "To be honest in the end, we used more VFX in the backgrounds (creating a non-existing airport, alpine road-tunnels and cities) than on the actual vehicles where you'd expect them." Ivor Goldberg, head of post and creative partner at PostPanic: "Of all the challenges on this project (which were numerous) two were clear winners. First was creating CG humans to go alongside real humans in the same shot. Everyone is an expert and a critic on what a human should look like – there is nowhere to hide. "Secondly, it was always the intention to shoot as much as possible in camera (mostly because of the problems of the first challenge). Logistically this became undoable. "In the end we had to shoot not only multiple takes but also multiple takes in multiple locations and stitch these all together to create one good image that we could then embellish with CG. Typically in one shot there could be up to 10 elements shot at three or four different locations." Annejes van Liempd, PostPanic executive producer: "Our choice of using real people for this rather than CG humans dictated the nature of the shoot making it an extremely technical one both in pre-production and during actual filming. "We had so many variables which had to work together and fit perfectly for multiple passes on most of the shots. This resulted in agonisingly time-consuming days, almost two weeks away filming but the stunt team kept us all laughing. We really enjoyed working with the whole Czech crew (via Savage) - they were amazing." Ivor Goldberg: "I take enormous pride in this team here at PostPanic. They are true all-round artists. In an industry where pipelines and workflows can be so rigid and constricting I love that they, as individuals, can not only undertake such a wide variety of disciplines from matte painting to animating and compositing but still get genuine pleasure from the creative and technical process. "It is this which I feel is quite rare in the industry and really allows us to produce such quality in such short turnarounds without people running out the door in terror never to be seen again." Schedule: three months.

records.description: Jon Park, VFX supervisor at MPC in London: "The brief was to stick to the anatomical constraints of a frill-necked lizard but creatively make him behave like a human being trapped in a lizard's body. The spot was shot on 35mm Kodak film, which is quite rare in these digital times. "The main creative challenge was to raise the bar on the previous first direct 'Platypus' commercials. Secondly, our Little Frill character spends all his time standing upright, which a real lizard wouldn't do. "The team manipulated his body to stand in a human position; referencing footage of comedian Seann Walsh holding a giant phone recorded during his voiceover. It then became a balancing act between human and lizard performances for the animators. "The main technical challenge was that the lizard has very small arms and animating them to make human gestures made him look pretty awkward but without changing his body shape there was no escaping this. "So we decided to embrace the fact he has tiny little arms (like Rex in 'Toy Story') and made the most of it by making him gesticulate a lot, which makes him look pretty funny. "Also, the opening shot was difficult as it is an extreme close-up of the DJ-ing tarsier's eyes. Creating 3D realistic eyes is just about the hardest thing to do, so a lot of time was spent getting them to look just right." Schedule: 2 1/2 months.

records.description: Directors Smith & Foulkes at Nexus in London: "4Creative came up with the concept to turn the tables on cancer, depicting the disease as an aggressively spreading civilisation unable to prevent its own Armageddon. "The 'disaster movie' trailer format provided the ideal condensed storytelling to show how a bloated, complacent society, overcrowded through its own relentless need to spread, is unable to deal with a mysterious invasion. "The main challenge was just how to visually portray the cancer cells. We wanted to steer away from the obvious route of showing cells as a bunch of grotesque alien germs, but we were also acutely aware of not making them too human or cute. "Nobody wants to sympathise with cancer. So we created a society of self obsessed cells whose collective purpose is to aggressively, relentlessly spread. Ultimately it is this perceived success, the endless construction and polluted, overcrowded streets, which precipitates their own downfall. We just had to think of as many spectacular and comic demises as we could. "We also had to find a way to illustrate the new therapies, drugs and scientific breakthroughs which are turning the tide in the battle against cancer. We represented this as the arrival of a magical blue orb, an unexplained light descending upon a shadowy world. "Then we see how this mysterious alien substance begins to spread through their society, with a few spectacular and comic demises along the way. It is only at the end of the film that we reveal our human scientist introducing the blue drug into the cancer colony. "Disaster movies rely heavily on vast visual spectacle and a cast of thousands. The budget didn't quite stretch to that so we used 2D matte paintings to create a sense of the city without having to model every building. "3D characters gave us the flexibility of performance we wanted. Then it was a case of how to composite them with live-action fire and smoke and simulated 3D splat effects into a cohesive, visually rich world." Schedule: "We initially started discussing this way back in October 2013 and had the luxury of a few months to really hone look, tone, and storytelling approach. Once production proper began it took 3 1/2 months."

records.description: Psyop and CD Gerald Ding spent six days in Kingston, Jamaica, scouting for talent and locations to serve as the base for their free-wheeling 2D cel animation in one of four videos commissioned by The House of Marley to launch the company's latest portable audio system, an eco-friendly Bluetooth unit called The Get Together. Gerald Ding: "We wanted to show how a song can bring together friends and strangers alike, and how a good vibe can multiply from one person and grow into a whole block party. We wanted to create an emotional thread between the visuals and how the characters were feeling, and how they imagined themselves." Gabriel Kuo, creative director at The House of Marley: "We wanted to create a cultural and artistic branch for The House of Marley brand, named 'The Get Together'. After brainstorming about the campaign ideation, we finally landed on the idea that it would not be a hard product campaign, but that it would make more sense to celebrate what The Get Together speaker actually encourages - people getting together. "That was the seed to what would become the overarching message. How do people get together, and how does one idea become infectious? The spirit of community and communication starts with just one idea, one message." GD: "When we first started to talk about this project, Gabe reached out to me and wanted to know how I would interpret the campaign idea - their main directive was to visually articulate the idea of how one becomes many, which they felt was the key conceptual imprint of The Get Together campaign. records.description: A solid idea from Mother London plus bang-on execution from MJZ director Juan Cabral and a crew of 15 VFX artists at the MPC London keeps IKEA's "The Wonderful Everyday" ad campaign going with this spectacular spot which gains even more altitude via Prunella Scales' reading from "The Tempest." The MPC team, led by 2D creative director Bill McNamara, spent their time "creating detailed matte paintings, adding CG beds and embellishments and compositing elements including the NASA rocket and plume. "A selection of the wide shots were created by filming a skydiver and removing the parachute pack, while many of the shots were filmed against greenscreen with the sky and various surroundings composited in the studio. "Juan Cabral's innovative storytelling approach saw the protagonist and many of the beds hung from cranes and suspended over buildings during the three-day shoot in Johannesburg. "One sequence used an 80-foot weighted crane and controlled drop to allow the actress to literally plummet from the sky – thereby perfectly capturing her emotion as she falls. "A selection of the wide shots were created by filming a skydiver and removing the parachute pack, while many of the shots were filmed against greenscreen with the sky and various surroundings composited in the studio. MPC global creative director of colour grading Jean-Clement Soret: "Most of the time colorists are asked to help structure a narrative spot, or give unity to a visual piece, and they know quite well what needs to be done. "This time was different because it is a dream and as in dreams your mind jumps from one thing to another, so we treated each sequence as individual to a certain degree to surprise the audience. Decisions can be quite subjective and a close collaboration with director Juan Cabral was necessary to translate the images he had in mind."

records.description: ManvsMachine in London: "Nike Football came to us with their radical new football boot inspired by Cristiano Ronaldo. Tasked with creating the centrepiece for the launch campaign for the Mercurial, also coinciding with the Football World Cup 2014, we were challenged with exploring the devastating speed and finesse of this unique boot. "Creatively we set out to create something that wasn't 'just another trainer/boot film'. Finding unique abstractions and interesting ways of eliciting tension to contrast and showcase speed in a new light took a lot of exploration. "We wanted to aggressively build momentum and force, whilst opening up room for ambience to really play off the contrast. "A large amount of R&D went into solving various aspects of the piece, from the flyknit knitting, to the complex shattering simulations. We also took to 3D scanning the boot and the players. Working with the fantastic folk at FBFX we scanned the players, capturing moments mid-action in their dynamic poses. "It was important for us to capture them in this way so that we could really see all of the detail in that precise moment: muscles engaging, postures tensing, faces contorting, cloth rippling and actively pulling, etc. in a true overly dramatic and high tension fashion. "Trivia: MvsM creative director Mike Alderson's perfectly sculpted classical beard lead him to being cast as one of the defenders scrambling to stop the Mercurial." Schedule: "It was an eight-week turnaround from creative development to grade, with R&D running throughout the whole process."

records.description: Pablo Tufaro, director at Laposta in Buenos Aires, Argentina: "The fact this client was very open minded was the most attractive part of this project. And they wanted to do some nasty humor with disgusting and disturbing trolls disturbing the owner of the garden because he has abandoned it." "The script was awesome, very good jokes all the time but the best part was when the actors that made the voices started to improvise. That was hilarious. "That's when we decided to do an extended version of the commercial with a couple more jokes than the original script. "There were many technical challenges: muscle systems, facial expression tracking, long hair with dynamics, three characters at the same time on a two-month deadline. records.description: MPC say they channeled Samuel L Jackson, John Travolta, Michael Jackson and Beyonce to choreograph the moves of this funky 15-foot African bull elephant strutting the streets of Vancouver. MPC 3D supervisor Fabian Frank: "The biggest challenge was creating an elephant that could pull out the moves with the best of them, yet was also believable and true to life. We solved this by ensuring his dance moves stayed within the realms of what a real elephant could do. "The second challenge came with integrating the elephant into the shot footage. Matching the interaction between the talent and the elephant were key, so the talent was tracked and rotoscoped back into the shots – using select takes to perfectly match the elephant's walk cycle." "MPC's 3D team began to concept their elephant two weeks prior to the shoot. A pre-vis laying out his size and basic flow of movement was then used as a guide for the rig on set. "Following the shoot, the team decided upon the look of the elephant and his subsequent texture. They settled on the male African elephant, embarking on the creation of an exact replica with added personality. "As part of this creative process, the intricacies of elephant mobility and human dance moves were studied. A number of dance variations and moves were tested in order to create his final choreographed routine. "A range of detailed matte paintings were also developed, adding skyscrapers and lights to emphasis the 'epic' feel of the backdrop for our VIP's."

records.description: Robert Sethi, director and creative director at the The Mill+: "We had the honour of collaborating with Wieden+Kennedy on Oregon Health & Science University's (OHSU) new campaign outlining how OHSU revolutionised the treatment of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, making a once lethal disease non-lethal for hundreds of thousands of people. "And having taken one cancer down, they're going after the rest. "This piece is inspired by reality without trying to replicate it. Whilst we did a lot of research to understand cells and cancer, we used it more for inspiration. "Instead of individually sculpting each cell we used a set of noise and rules to randomly generate them, giving us a lot more freedom. And the comp team, led by Martin Karlsson, did a really excellent job. They took our renders and really pushed the electro-microscope effect to the maximum." "Initially it's a darker world which progressively lightens as the cancer explodes and disappears. The colors shift and the camera goes from static to loose movements, all conveying this sense of hopefulness and victory. "It was an incredibly gratifying piece to work on not just from an artistic point of view; everyone has a loved one that's been affected by cancer, so working on a project that might help people in the future was a very rewarding thing."

records.description: Ilija Brunck, CG artist at Polynoid/Woodblock in Berlin: "We were contacted directly by Alexander Kalchev at DDB Paris to see if we would be interested in collaborating on a fake commercial to raise awareness of the growing disappearance of honeybees. "Alex had a very clear vision of the content of the film and asked us to realise it in our style. "Finding the right ironic/sarcastic tone for the film was a challenge since it should work as a realistic commercial that advertises robotic bees with all their advantages, and still picture a creepy dystopian future that nobody wants. "Getting a good track out of the live action plates was sometimes very tricky due to a lot of moving plants and flowers plus strong depth of field. Also, we needed quite a while to define the animation style of the bees so it's the right mixture of natural and robotic movement. The plates were shot on a RED Epic. In post production we used ZBrush, Mari and Softimage with Arnold for the 3D. Nuke was used for compositing and Premiere for the edit. "The schedule was kind of open because Greenpeace did not yet know when they'd use the film. After the shoot in late summer last year, we worked on the spot for a couple of months. It was quite refreshing to work without a fixed deadline since we could really bring everything to a good level."

raw_source.description: Ilija Brunck, CG artist at Polynoid/Woodblock in Berlin: "We were contacted directly by Alexander Kalchev at DDB Paris to see if we would be interested in collaborating on a fake commercial to raise awareness of the growing disappearance of honeybees. "Alex had a very clear vision of the content of the film and asked us to realise it in our style. "Finding the right ironic/sarcastic tone for the film was a challenge since it should work as a realistic commercial that advertises robotic bees with all their advantages, and still picture a creepy dystopian future that nobody wants. "Getting a good track out of the live action plates was sometimes very tricky due to a lot of moving plants and flowers plus strong depth of field. Also, we needed quite a while to define the animation style of the bees so it's the right mixture of natural and robotic movement. The plates were shot on a RED Epic. In post production we used ZBrush, Mari and Softimage with Arnold for the 3D. Nuke was used for compositing and Premiere for the edit. "The schedule was kind of open because Greenpeace did not yet know when they'd use the film. After the shoot in late summer last year, we worked on the spot for a couple of months. It was quite refreshing to work without a fixed deadline since we could really bring everything to a good level."

records.description: Method VFX supervisor Benjamin Walsh: "This VFX heavy spot was turned around in just two weeks by our artists in LA and New York. It launched on television during the opening ceremony of the 2014 Winter Olympics and will continue running throughout the year. "The commercial depicts a variety of scenes and environments, each resulting in their own unique VFX challenges. The underwater vignette involved CG water, bubbles, particulate matter, the large turbines and submarine itself. "Other CG components include a fantastical printer, planes with bird wings, birdcage, engine, train, trees and a paper hospital. In amongst each scene are matte painted environments and various dynamic elements such as dirt, dust and clouds. "With only 14 days to work on the shots after receiving plates, the Method team made use of the R&D from past feature film projects, specifically CG feathers and trees which are typically time consuming elements to produce. "Our New York team led by Doug Luka and Jason Hawkins took on the challenge of creating a full CG water environment populated with giant turbines, explored by the little girl in her submarine. Distributing the workload across Method's two studios was essential in order for us to meet the deadline."

records.description: Sheldon Gardner, VFX supervisor at Time Based Arts in London: "This project first crossed our path in the spring with a phone call from the director Sebastian Strasser. "What followed was a bizarre conversation about sim cards, eggs, cats, transformers, buffalos and rockets. Although we were left scratching our heads, it was immediately apparent that the film was going to be ambitious, bold and packed with creative VFX. "The film's premise is a simple (if crazy) one: that the new Vodafone sim card will, like some bizarre piece of modern day sorcery, 'power up' any object to a new form. "We were primarily tasked with problem solving at every level: during scripting and development, on set and through to the later post production stages. "Stylistically the director wanted to keep the camera off the tripod and hand held throughout, which added to the narrative flow of the spot overall, but of course increased the complexity of the VFX shots. "With each vignette lasting only a short duration of the overall edit it was also the case that there were enormous amounts of R&D for very short sections. The creature work and full fur on the buffalo, for example, taking many weeks to perfect for the completion of only three short shots."

records.description: Psyop director Fletcher Moules in New York: "We really embraced the bright, stylized and saturated look of the game. We wanted to fully conceptualize what the world would look like if we were running alongside the horde of barbarians, what would it feel like to be covered in their saliva. "The Psyop team worked closely with BFG to bring the mayhem to life, developing the characters and creating dynamic backgrounds and environments to keep the explosive and goofy nature of the spot intact while maintaining the game's intrigue. "The scene with the giants became a favorite; it added the heart and the warmth that was only achieved when we removed ourselves a little from the ruckus to enjoy it from their perspective. "We also worked to find the middle ground of the narrative - striking the right balance between action and comedy, determining where to use gags, feeling out how long to feature each character and determining how many explosions were necessary but not overwhelming. "In total the team created 88 shots during pre-vis which were ultimately cut down to the final, tumultuous 20."

records.description: We carry very few fashion films on Stash but this new spot from director/photographer Floria Sigismondi thru Quad with VFX by Digital District grabbed our attention for its reverential depiction of "a Solar Goddess awakening to the light" shot in the stunning Castello di Sammezzano in Tuscany and set to the music of "Brennisteinn" by Sigur Ros. The following in an excerpt from an interview with Floria Sigismondi by Christophe de Lataillade, creative director of Parfums Thierry Mugler: Christophe de Lataillade: We are very impressed with the work you have done on the Alien campaign. How do you select your projects? Floria Sigismondi: They need to have a message, something I can connect with, and with this one, I really love the idea of the goddess, capturing something from the universe, and transformation. Transformation is a recurrent theme in most of my work. CDL: What attracts you artistically speaking? FS: The unknown, the universe, the possibility of other dimensions, metamorphosis, and continuing to learn through creativity, through finding yourself, through exploration. CDL: It would seem, from the early stages of your treatment of the Alien campaign, that choreography, dance and body movement are essential elements in your work. Is it also a recurrent theme in your work? FS: For me, movement has always been a major part of the language. In the video clips I direct, besides the sound track, it's the only way to express things. So I've always used the body. It's a bit like silent movies, even if it's more of a caricature, movement can evoke certain emotions. CDL: Do you look back on your work? Some artists never do, others have a more analytical vision of their work. Do you look back on what you do and can you define your style? FS: I look back maybe every five years when someone has put together a body of work for a show or for a festival. It's quite emotional for me to do that; I experience two feelings. The first one is that it's as if I review my work through the perspective of a third person's point of view. And second, if there are emotional ties, I relive them again, so it's a bit too emotional for me to just view something. It's interesting, but I don't do it very often. CDL: When you look at your work with a certain distance, can you define it in terms of style, or is it something you just don't think about, or that you won't do? FS: I definitely don't consciously think about where I'm going with something, in terms of if I have a style to stick to. I'm always attracted to different things, but I love color, to what color can say emotionally, so I'm always drawn to playing with that. I think of myself as an experimentalist. Most of the time, I dabble in different sources of inspiration. To begin it was the opera. My parents are opera singers, I grew up in the theatre with its themes, its costumes. At one point I wanted to simplify, I stripped everything away to get to the emotion of things. CDL: What, in your eyes, is a good picture? FS: Composition is always very important, to get a good look at the subject and capture something evocative. Sometimes it's the transformational emotion rather than the final result. If the message expressed is too obvious, the result can be a bit flat rather than 'in the moment'. But it's very objective-subjective. CDL: I suppose the answer would be the same for a film. FS: When I started out as a photographer and a painter, one image had to tell a story. In a film, it's a completely different thing. There is time: I can use all the possible nuances and a hundred different ideas to take a person somewhere. CDL: When we received your mock-ups, I was very impressed. When we started working together, I could tell that the backbone of what you were going to do was there, but that you leave a lot of room for the unexpected. It's an element I always try to defend in Mugler projects, because I feel that it is essential, and I was very impressed by the way you left room for artistic surprises. FS: That's how I've always done my work, and I've always thought that in doing so I actually produce better work. I plan everything, everything is very organized; it's a backbone, as you've said. But you have to leave the door open to unexpected magical moments. I love to be on set, to bring all the elements together, people who don't know each other. That's what makes the whole process and the end result feel alive. I think that if it's too controlled, there's no emotion. CDL: What does the name Mugler evoke for you? Is there anything in his work that made you want to work for him? FS: I remember Mugler from the end of the eighties and nineties. The images were always very fantastical and striking, they definitely stood out. Coming from painting and a more artistic background, those images captured my imagination. So for me, it was like the perfect match. It's not as conventional as some other projects. And again, the inspiration takes your mind to a possible other reality, which I love, in the way that women are portrayed as goddesses. CDL: How did you work with the Mugler team, is our way of working different from yours? FS: Working with people who are confident with the brand and the project makes the experience more fluid. I felt a great sense of confidence in the Mugler team that really helped the creative process. It was a really beautiful experience. CDL : What inspired you for the project? FS: The idea of a woman who lays dormant...before something awakens her. It's a bit like these people who are just going through the motions of their everyday life, but in fact, they are dormant: they don't have any perspective on their life. And then, this inspiration comes from the universe, and the sun that gives life to everything on earth. I thought the idea was really beautiful, how the woman transforms, and especially her desire to share this renaissance with all of us. The concept and the way it can be portrayed were well thought out. CDL: The Castello di Sammezzano, what an amazing place! FS: Yes, and it brought me back to my home country! This castle is amazing. I had only seen a photo of it, and the experience of walking through it was incredible. Every room had a different theme, and you could feel the emotion and the huge work put into it, also the commitment of seeing an idea right through to the end. I guess that's why the Egyptians made their monuments out of stone, so they lasted for people to visit. It's the feeling it left me with. CDL : Spending a week in the castle was a truly amazing experience because most of the art that we see, the decor, is from the mid-19th century, but it's almost like a prophecy in art. There is something psychedelic before the hour, the colors, the glass, a bit like the embryo of many styles that appeared almost a hundred years after and you wonder where that comes from. FS: Yes, it is like a prophecy, you could see the generations to come and the movement of art within that, that's what I felt was so fantastic. A lot of styles mixed in, and for a fragrance named Alien, it's perfect! CDL: There is a would-be spiritual dimension in the idea of the film, this relationship between the goddess and the sun which is a kind of god. All this is in a poetic form of course, not actually religious. What do you think was so spiritual in the building? There is something very mysterious in the way it is designed to capture the light. FS: Thanks to the way the windows are situated, there is always light in the castle. The way the light bounces through the white room, at the beginning of the spot, is really magical. It gives the impression that all the elements are three-dimensional and carved out. You can really feel the three-dimensional aspect of the walls and the architecture. It is amazing to see that completely choreographed with the natural light. CDL: There is also a room with amazing colors and styles, almost religious, but without reflecting any particular religion, which is perfect for our project. When you are actually in there, the light is like you have described it, it's as if we were, without knowing it, in a sort of temple dedicated to the sun. FS: It took 40 years to build this castle. The owner must have calculated the way the sun comes in to light up the floor. There was probably some kind of spiritual or religious alignment with the sun and what was happening there in the way he designed it. CDL: What is the connection between the film and the photo work? Is there a particular essence that you transfer from the film into the photos? How does that work in your mind? FS: To link the print ad with the commercial you need to pick its key moment. In this case the key moment was to capture the light, and the goddess being the luminous point of the image with her desire to share, hence the body position that we chose. Those are the key moments in the commercial. The challenge is to put everything into one image rather than slowly tell the story, like you do in the clip. CDL: What is the "Floria Sigismondi touch" in this work? FS: It's hard to step outside yourself and analyze that, but maybe it's the movement and the wide shots. I truly believe that the environment can be like a character in a story. This small woman, so small in this huge environment, and the way she moves and receives this powerful solar force...I'm always drawn to that, through camera lenses, camera movement, and also her movements, and bringing all those things together and creating something more lyrical, musical. CDL: It's funny what you are saying about the proportions: "She is so small in this huge environment." Several decades ago, we did a photo shoot in the desert for an haute couture Thierry Mugler campaign, and there was a tiny person that you could hardly see in a huge landscape. FS: I remember that. CDL: People remember it. It's funny that you have the same connection to immensity and smallness of characters. FS: Yes, but the light remains the main character, before any other.

FS: I look back maybe every five years when someone has put together a body of work for a show or for a festival. It's quite emotional for me to do that; I experience two feelings. The first one is that it's as if I review my work through the perspective of a third person's point of view. And second, if there are emotional ties, I relive them again, so it's a bit too emotional for me to just view something. It's interesting, but I don't do it very often. CDL: When you look at your work with a certain distance, can you define it in terms of style, or is it something you just don't think about, or that you won't do? FS: I definitely don't consciously think about where I'm going with something, in terms of if I have a style to stick to. I'm always attracted to different things, but I love color, to what color can say emotionally, so I'm always drawn to playing with that. I think of myself as an experimentalist. Most of the time, I dabble in different sources of inspiration. To begin it was the opera. My parents are opera singers, I grew up in the theatre with its themes, its costumes. At one point I wanted to simplify, I stripped everything away to get to the emotion of things. CDL: What, in your eyes, is a good picture? FS: Composition is always very important, to get a good look at the subject and capture something evocative. Sometimes it's the transformational emotion rather than the final result. If the message expressed is too obvious, the result can be a bit flat rather than 'in the moment'. But it's very objective-subjective. CDL: I suppose the answer would be the same for a film. FS: When I started out as a photographer and a painter, one image had to tell a story. In a film, it's a completely different thing. There is time: I can use all the possible nuances and a hundred different ideas to take a person somewhere. CDL: When we received your mock-ups, I was very impressed. When we started working together, I could tell that the backbone of what you were going to do was there, but that you leave a lot of room for the unexpected. It's an element I always try to defend in Mugler projects, because I feel that it is essential, and I was very impressed by the way you left room for artistic surprises. FS: That's how I've always done my work, and I've always thought that in doing so I actually produce better work. I plan everything, everything is very organized; it's a backbone, as you've said. But you have to leave the door open to unexpected magical moments. I love to be on set, to bring all the elements together, people who don't know each other. That's what makes the whole process and the end result feel alive. I think that if it's too controlled, there's no emotion. CDL: What does the name Mugler evoke for you? Is there anything in his work that made you want to work for him? FS: I remember Mugler from the end of the eighties and nineties. The images were always very fantastical and striking, they definitely stood out. Coming from painting and a more artistic background, those images captured my imagination. So for me, it was like the perfect match. It's not as conventional as some other projects. And again, the inspiration takes your mind to a possible other reality, which I love, in the way that women are portrayed as goddesses. CDL: How did you work with the Mugler team, is our way of working different from yours? FS: Working with people who are confident with the brand and the project makes the experience more fluid. I felt a great sense of confidence in the Mugler team that really helped the creative process. It was a really beautiful experience. CDL : What inspired you for the project? FS: The idea of a woman who lays dormant...before something awakens her. It's a bit like these people who are just going through the motions of their everyday life, but in fact, they are dormant: they don't have any perspective on their life. And then, this inspiration comes from the universe, and the sun that gives life to everything on earth. I thought the idea was really beautiful, how the woman transforms, and especially her desire to share this renaissance with all of us. The concept and the way it can be portrayed were well thought out. CDL: The Castello di Sammezzano, what an amazing place! FS: Yes, and it brought me back to my home country! This castle is amazing. I had only seen a photo of it, and the experience of walking through it was incredible. Every room had a different theme, and you could feel the emotion and the huge work put into it, also the commitment of seeing an idea right through to the end. I guess that's why the Egyptians made their monuments out of stone, so they lasted for people to visit. It's the feeling it left me with. CDL : Spending a week in the castle was a truly amazing experience because most of the art that we see, the decor, is from the mid-19th century, but it's almost like a prophecy in art. There is something psychedelic before the hour, the colors, the glass, a bit like the embryo of many styles that appeared almost a hundred years after and you wonder where that comes from. FS: Yes, it is like a prophecy, you could see the generations to come and the movement of art within that, that's what I felt was so fantastic. A lot of styles mixed in, and for a fragrance named Alien, it's perfect! CDL: There is a would-be spiritual dimension in the idea of the film, this relationship between the goddess and the sun which is a kind of god. All this is in a poetic form of course, not actually religious. What do you think was so spiritual in the building? There is something very mysterious in the way it is designed to capture the light. FS: Thanks to the way the windows are situated, there is always light in the castle. The way the light bounces through the white room, at the beginning of the spot, is really magical. It gives the impression that all the elements are three-dimensional and carved out. You can really feel the three-dimensional aspect of the walls and the architecture. It is amazing to see that completely choreographed with the natural light. CDL: There is also a room with amazing colors and styles, almost religious, but without reflecting any particular religion, which is perfect for our project. When you are actually in there, the light is like you have described it, it's as if we were, without knowing it, in a sort of temple dedicated to the sun. FS: It took 40 years to build this castle. The owner must have calculated the way the sun comes in to light up the floor. There was probably some kind of spiritual or religious alignment with the sun and what was happening there in the way he designed it. CDL: What is the connection between the film and the photo work? Is there a particular essence that you transfer from the film into the photos? How does that work in your mind? FS: To link the print ad with the commercial you need to pick its key moment. In this case the key moment was to capture the light, and the goddess being the luminous point of the image with her desire to share, hence the body position that we chose. Those are the key moments in the commercial. The challenge is to put everything into one image rather than slowly tell the story, like you do in the clip. CDL: What is the "Floria Sigismondi touch" in this work? FS: It's hard to step outside yourself and analyze that, but maybe it's the movement and the wide shots. I truly believe that the environment can be like a character in a story. This small woman, so small in this huge environment, and the way she moves and receives this powerful solar force...I'm always drawn to that, through camera lenses, camera movement, and also her movements, and bringing all those things together and creating something more lyrical, musical. CDL: It's funny what you are saying about the proportions: "She is so small in this huge environment." Several decades ago, we did a photo shoot in the desert for an haute couture Thierry Mugler campaign, and there was a tiny person that you could hardly see in a huge landscape. FS: I remember that. CDL: People remember it. It's funny that you have the same connection to immensity and smallness of characters. FS: Yes, but the light remains the main character, before any other.

records.description: Olivier Pinol, CEO/Cinematographer/VFX super at Dwarf Labs in Perols, France: "The Initial brief from the agency and Cartier was to reach the level of animation in Bibo Bergeron's 2011 feature film 'Monster in Paris', but in a Christmas fashion. "First, we developed a storyboard which quickly turned into an animated storyboard that served as a pre-visualisation tool. Hundreds of drawings and concepts were developed to set the mood, color and lighting design. "Meanwhile our R&D department was working hard in developing shaders and tools to answer the needs of the artistic vision. "Bibo wanted the characters to have a strong stylized look but with the surfaces and materials interacting naturally with the environment lighting. "To get this we used our in-house color, lighting and rendering tools, which allowed our artists to develop very complex lighting setups using high end algorithms like spherical harmonics, point cloud-based lighting, color bleeding, deep and soft shadows, sub-surface scattering, procedural shaders and so on.

records.description: Producer Chris Batten at The Mill: "Working closely with Sam Brown from the concept stage, we were heavily influenced by the Lexus design aesthetics in the design of the hero characters. "Parallel to this, we pre-vized the animations for all shots. These 3D pre-vis coordinates were then sent to an electronics company called Kmel whose bespoke software then interpreted this data to control the quadrotors. "Filmed in Vancouver at multiple city locations, motion capture environments were created on all sets, in which computers controlled each of the hero characters individually, all flying perfectly in formation, in and around the various setup's throughout the commercial. "This unique technological and client workflow solution was an important practical solution to the brief, and with our lead 3D CG artist Mike Chapman and a large team of CG artists, we were able to augment a lot of in-camera shots and indeed develop others entirely in CG. "What we end up with 'Swarm' is a world first. The spot takes existing quadrotor or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) technology out of its typical engineering environment and flies them in real locations. The result is a playful story of quads exploring the city at night. Jorge Montiel, head of animation: "Even though most of the shots had been done with real quads in motion, the animation team had to work on animating all the quads for every shot beforehand. "The reason behind this was to add personality and character to these little quadrotors which were something Sam had wanted from the very beginning of the project. "Their movements were choreographed in 3D and then transferred by Kmel. It has been a huge challenge bringing these little guys to life. "The huge amount of technical detail was crucial to be able to animate these devices properly without having crashes or strange behaviors. Distance, acceleration, speed, and the physics behind the helices were the main parameters we had to keep in mind whilst animating them. "The way the quadrotors move is very agile but they also have a lot of limitations, which caused a higher level of difficulty when trying to make them expressive."

records.description: Director Dougal Wilson: "MPC tackled the Herculean post-production task of this commercial with incredible assurance. There were an enormous amount of rigs to remove, plates to rotoscope, backgrounds to paint and layers to composite, and an alarmingly short space of time to do it in. "However, they still had time to humor my usual last minute tinkering." Tom Harding, MPC VFX team lead: "It quickly became apparent how challenging the spot would be due to the sheer amount of intricate clean up and rig removal involved. Hundreds of objects were hand rotoscoped and cleaned, frame by frame, by our teams in London and Bangalore. "Then we had to piece together all the elements created on the various different formats, from digital stills to 35mm film, and ensure it felt seamless. "MPC assisted the production team in planning the two-week shoot. They began by creating a full 3D pre-vis in pre-production, enabling different lenses to be tested. They also tested the angles, framing and composition of each shot at the same time. "It was imperative to present the pre-vis as an offline so that signoff could be given before animation commenced as re-shooting scenes later was not possible. "The shot of the stairwell was created by compositing together multiple plates and removing puppeteers and rigs. The lighting was controlled in the final wide outdoor shot by erecting an enormous tent around the entire house."

records.description: Producer Nikki Kefford-White at Studio aka in London: "In seeking to craft a film which celebrated the combination of traditional ideas with contemporary application, Marc chose to combine the hand-crafted artistry of 2D hand-drawn character animation within 3D CGI sets. Marc's use of a constantly circling camera provides the momentum and sense of optimism that drives the piece throughout the build of the story. "The film is full of wonderful nuances and details complimented by an uplifting score composed by Anne Dudley and recorded with the Chamber Orchestra of London. With subtle sound design from Anthony Moore and Tom Joyce at Factory. "A 90-second version of the film will screen in cinemas nationally with the full 2.5-minute version debuting on the web."
