records.description: Director Damon Duncan at Assembly in Auckland, New Zealand: "The brief came to us from Draft FCB who had the idea of a possessed chair wreaking havoc on a small port town. The challenge was imparting the chair with a malevolence without anthropomorphizing it or bringing it to life. "We also wanted to create an entire town that was recognizable to all New Zealanders, one that would hold up to scrutiny, and would be a rich environment with which to continue telling stories in and around for years to come. "One thing we were keen to achieve in this commercial is a natural cinematic lighting style. We wanted bright things to feel really bright and dark areas to feel properly dark. "We weren't worried about having things like blown-out skies in the frame. These are phenomena that happen within shot footage so we let that happen with the CG lighting as well. "We could have used the infinite control the artist has of the CG scene to artificially bring down the brightness levels of very bright parts of the scene. Instead we just let them blow out like they would in a real camera. "Because we chose a naturalistic render style, we were faced with some long render times. With our detailed interior shots containing many props, the way that light bounces and interacts in the scene is very complicated, which in turn results in a LOT of rays shot by the ray tracing software to get a smooth final image. "Some of our final render times ended up taking up to 20 hours per frame. It's possible that these could have been optimized, but sometimes during a project, artist hours are more valuable than computer rendering hours and it is not worth the time to spend days optimizing a scene. "V-Ray was a real workhorse on the project. It ate up everything we threw at it and produced pretty pictures reliably. "Another challenge we faced was modeling and rigging all the characters within the timeline. There were upwards of 20 characters of different builds and looks to sculpt and rig. "There wasn't time to make mistakes. The character modelers did an amazing job of turning out model after model that were rapidly approved. "We had 2.5 months of full-on production. We were lucky to have a very comprehensive animatic to work to. This was created in-house by one of our talented Maya animators. "Our hardware is pretty un-exotic. We use custom-made Windows PC's for workstations. Our render farm is 70 1U rack-mounted machines all managed by Thinkbox Deadline. "Our main applications are 3ds Max, Maya, Nuke and V-Ray. We used Mari for texture painting and Hiero for maintaining a live cut of the final commercial throughout the whole project."

records.description: Helmed by Platige director Damian Nenow and narrated by Dakota Fanning, this powerful spot leads off the UN-sponsored Hunger Personified campaign designed "to highlight the dangers of being apathetic to hunger and accepting it as a necessary evil." records.description: Andy Hall, director at Elastic in Santa Monica: "The agency asked us to conceive of an animation style or identity that could be owned by the brand while conveying a clear and concise fable-genre based story. "Finding a unique look for anything these days is a challenge. Most of what we see being done is referential to a degree. So we spent some time developing that look so that it could be our own. "As a studio, we're not necessarily known for doing traditional 2D animation but we pride ourselves on pushing our limits and always reinventing our style. So we worked from within, using our talents and applying what we know about animation to the 2D execution. "Also, we had to find a way to retain the very graphic look of the concept art within the animation while taking it to another level. There were a lot of mediums that we worked across and they all had to live within the same graphic language. "In developing the look we had to keep in mind it needed to translate into print, point of sale, posters, and a graphic novel that was printed for use by their sales force. The graphic novel is designed and the story told in the true style of the genre. All of the artwork and storytelling was designed by our team at Elastic." Schedule: six weeks.

records.description: Director Ryan Dunn at CHRLX in NY: "It's always been a goal of mine to effectively emulate the analog world in a digital space. Many have tried it, myself included, but I think we've gotten really close here. "Suspending viewer disbelief was the key to the campaign, so we put a lot of effort into creating a seamless experience without the distraction of the technique itself. "Whether or not it could be done the way I pictured it in my head was another story. I had a full stop-motion team on standby up until our CG crew showed me a proof of concept that blew us all away. "The Jarritos scripts were inspired by the miniatures and dioramas created by artist Tamra Kohl, and the agency wanted to match the original look. They also wanted the flexibility of revisions, something for which full stop-motion was not very amenable. "After I saw what our CG team could do, I knew that our process needed to combine digital characters with analog sets, and it turned out to be the perfect choice for our client's needs and the end product. "Our characters had to look, feel, and act the part so we focused heavily on the performance of our digital actors and made sure that the spaces they occupied held up to the curiosity of the campaign's overall concept."

records.description: Creative team at Mainframe in London: "The client came to us with a fairly open concept: a nest of ants work together to create the Harrods logo using parts from watch movements. "Mainframe was responsible for creating the flow and narrative of the spot, concentrating on camera moves and set-ups, trying to create shots that would draw the viewer into the story and emphasize the macro scale of the scenes. "We were lucky to find some amazing ant reference footage from a BBC documentary. This proved vital for the last two shots where they interact in the piles or 'death spiral', as it is known in ant circles. "We predominantly use Maya but the ant pile shot required more complicated dynamic simulations, which was taken care of with PFlow in 3ds Max. The rest of the ant flocking animation was made using nParticles, curve flow and instanced geometry with walk cycles in Maya. "We rendered using V-Ray in Maya and used Nuke to composite, then added Video Copilot optical flares for some finishing touches. "The most demanding technical aspect of this project surrounded the scale of the piece. Starting in macro before pulling out and revealing the enormity of the swarm, thousands of ants, all working together. This was achieved using a V-Ray proxy/Maya particle combo. "The proxies in V-Ray allow a huge number of objects to be in a scene, whilst only displaying a fraction of the faces actually present. This makes moving around the viewport and generally working with the scene bearable, without which it would be chug central. "Our workflow involved a generic walk-cycle instanced as a V-Ray proxy in the particle system with tweaks to the movement so the pace of the ants matched the cycle. " We used the same technique for the cogs in the logo, which was modeled then converted after animation and reimported into the scene as a proxy."

records.description: The Mill, working with adam&eveDDB, director Simon McQuoid and Gorgeous, bring the 300-year old brand Smithwick's company returns to TV after seven-years with the masterful insertion of a photo-real CG red squirrel into live action that took five months of post. Leonardo Costa, 2D lead artist at The Mill in London: "We comped numerous assets, including the CG squirrel itself, fire (matches), dust, flares, light rays and so on. "The close-up of the squirrel's eye took more than two months to get right. We added every single layer possible to make the eye as photo real as possible." Tom Bussell, head of 3D: "From the moment Simon talked us through his vision we saw the potential of this project as it challenged us in every way, both technically and creatively with the whole team working incredibly hard to make sure the vision and potential were met. "We used Houdini to generate the fur and developed a whole new workflow within the software to enable us to update animation and simulation painlessly. "It takes a leap of faith for creatives and directors to take on a project like this, as for a long time they don't get to see anything close to finished results, with it really all coming down to the final weeks when everything starts coming together."

records.description: MPC VFX team lead Anthony Bloor in London: "Creating a CG platypus with such a unique character was a fantastic challenge. Barry (the platypus) is a cheeky individual with very distinct movements. "We've worked on many CG characters in the past and making sure that all movements are photo-realistic is our absolute focus and commitment. Working with Dom and Nic is always the greatest pleasure as they have such a clear and strong vision for their films. This helps our work enormously." "As with any MPC animated character development, extensive research was carried out into both animal behavior and physical attributes - from anatomical, skeletal and muscle structure, through to surface texture. We developed a 3D model using ZBrush. After a few tweaks to Barry's weight and height, the team got to work animating him in CG. "Once the CG model was built, the team created a skeleton and muscle rigging system to create realistic movements. "Animating the platypus required a large amount of creative vision as he behaves in ways never seen in real-life: sitting at a bar, rifling through records and riding on a motorized scooter. "Right from the outset it was important that we focused on his walk cycle. It needed to be individual, to suit his character, but also realistic so the audience almost believes he is a real platypus. "As the team were creating expressions within the limits of platypus' features, the acting focus was on the body mechanics and head and hand movements. "MPC's in-house fur grooming system Furtility was utilized, originally developed for MPC's film pipeline and has been used in films including 'Narnia' and 'X-Men: First Class'. "After being applied, it was combed in different directions. This lengthy process allows the fur to curl and curve, creating very complex patterns."

"Special attention was paid to ensuring realism for the hamsters' look; MPC artists implemented a custom fur and physically-based shader setup to create photo-real characters in live-action environments. "We really wanted to bring the personality out of the hamsters so we built advanced facial and body muscle rigs to achieve fluid integration with the live action. "The result needed to be unnoticeable – like you've seen a giant hamster in a Speedo and goggles before, and we happened to get some nice shots of it."

records.description: 2D lead artist Andy Dill at the Mill in London: "We wanted to create a new benchmark for achieving the most realistic and seamless head replacement shots ever used on a commercial to date so we decided not to use the traditional method of motion capture and all of the facial CG was created through hand animation. "We began by reviewing hours and hours of Bruce's archive footage, pulling out as many images from as many different angles as possible. Each new angle brought the team closer to the most realistic 3D face. "The team used the Bruce Lee footage as reference, and hundreds of Bruce head models were created with every single feature meticulously modeled to get the exact nuances and facial expressions absolutely right. What everyone wanted to achieve was a seamless performance, so convincing that when you watch Bruce you can see his real emotions and believe that you are watching Bruce Lee the man, not a model, pixels or wireframes, which is why it was so important to create the animation by hand. "The challenges and level of detail involved on this project are something we are all hugely proud of. "We were very lucky to have incredible input and feedback from Shannon Lee from the Bruce Lee Estate, which was invaluable in creating the true emotions of Bruce, which was a great experience with both of them providing support and direction through the entire project." Resurrecting legends for advertising is a touchy business, mostly because fans consider it blasphemy when you screw with their perceptions of their beloved hero. "In this case, resurrecting a martial arts master known for his teetotaling ways to sell Johnny Walker Blue Label in China. Not surprisingly 'Change the Game' polarized fans and the media. Director Joseph Kahn made this response: "This spot isn't about drinking, nor does Bruce Lee ever pitch, hold, talk about it. It's a short inspirational film sponsored by Johnnie Walker. Those making comparisons of 'water' to 'alcohol' are literalists and wrong. "Last thing alcohol wants to be is water. It's a metaphor for life. It's his metaphor in his actual words. I spent a year living and breathing this man, thinking about him every day. For me, it's not an ad. It's an exploration and celebration of him. This is a sculpture in a different medium, paid for by a different church. I stand behind it."

records.description: "Imagine" is the inauguration of Sony's yearlong Visionaries campaign, which aims to pair creative innovators together with new Sony technology to unleash their unbounded potential. Directed by and featuring RESET's Garth Davis (co-director of "Top of the Lake") and shot by Academy Award winning cinematographer Claudio Miranda ("Life of Pi"), the spot imagines the limitless potential of Davis' vision, as realized through the new 4K Ultra High Definition TV. The spot sets several important milestones, as it is among the first commercials to embrace true 4K both in production and delivery (with a companion piece being shown in 4K at retail locations), utilizing the technology that raises definition by four times that of your standard HD television. Additionally, the spaceship created by MPC is the largest asset ever created for TV. Garth Davis: "The Sony 4K Ultra HD TV really is a new way of looking at things, a new visual language. It's almost like you can walk into the picture. One of the things unique to the TV is color. And the story we've been creating for this project is about celebrating color in lots of ways." The commercial was shot on location in New Zealand with the Sony Cine-Alta F65 and F55 professional 4K cameras.

records.description: Stephanie Gilgar, EP at Method Studios in Los Angeles: "The production of 'Troll' employed an extensive list of visual effects techniques. Aside from the computer-generated creature himself, the artists were tasked with matte painted backdrops, fluid and cloth simulations, set extensions, atmospheric FX elements such as dust and mist, CG animals and of course compositing everything together. "The biggest challenge involved creating and animating the giant Troll. To begin with, a highly detailed 3D model was sculpted based on signed off concept art. "Particular attention was paid to rigging complex facial muscles which ensured that the Troll's emotions were conveyed by his expressions - a requirement essential to the storytelling. While his face was animated by hand, the rest of his body was animated using finely tuned motion capture data. "Firstly his walk cycle was established during a motion capture session using an actor wearing a weighted body suit. "The backgrounds were shot at four different locations: Disney's Golden Oak Ranch; Universal's European Village; Universal's Stage 20; and helicopter plates shot with a Long Line camera rig over Tejon Ranch. "This edited footage was then used as a guide for the actor performing moves during a second motion capture session. This mocap data was then taken by the animators at Method who crafted the final movements of the Troll. "Another challenge to the VFX crew was depicting the magical countryside environments. The village scenes were captured at night, while the expansive countryside had to be shot with a traditional day-for-night approach, requiring the team to adapt daylight plates to match the nighttime look. "Layers of CG mist, a moon and even 3D ducks and a cow enhance the scenes. "One shot of particular interest is the opener which is in fact entirely computer generated. Lighting of the water, the Troll and his reflections throughout the spot was of the upmost importance and helped give the commercial its fairytale feel. "Overall, a team of 50+ CG artists, compositors, and matte painters utilized a complex tool set from programs such as Maya, ZBrush, Mari, and Houdini to execute this largescale VFX project."

records.description: Mike Merron, VFX supervisor at Analog in London: "Oscar-nominated directors Smith & Foulkes and Nexus Productions were commissioned by Wieden+Kennedy to create Channel 4 idents for Honda UK which take viewers on a journey through Honda's rich heritage and engineering advancements. "The campaign includes groundbreaking historical and concept products as well as current machinery - all reflecting Honda's passion for friendly technology, useful design and ultimately, 'The Power of Dreams'. "Analog was a driving force from the very beginning of the project, with our VFX supervisors providing the methodology of shooting articulated props and the accurate geometry tracking of the hands, using witness cameras. "Working closely with Nexus' animation team, who provided the character and transformation animation, we began to assemble the multiple shots, remove props, track and bring photorealism to the many products. "The props were scaled models of Honda products with some of them even having opening doors, rotating components and pipes to funnel water. This kept the Analog team busy tracking but it also meant we had to all pitch in with some tedious paint work. "Hands are notoriously difficult to draw, and it turns out that getting this many animated objects to sit in the hands is quite difficult too. Our initial tests showed the directors and animators at Nexus just how important this element of the production was. "We knew from the outset that it was hugely important for the hands to physically hold, grip and inspect 'something' as it would immediately ground the spot in reality." Schedule: eight weeks.

records.description: Directors/animators Polynoid in Berlin: "We needed to design a creature that gave us everything we needed to tell the story and then generate the overall tone for the spot, all while highlighting the product. "The scale changes from wide angle shots to close-ups were a challenge as they made it obvious we needed a fully functioning environment for both of these scenarios. We had to make sure that we maintained all the detail in the textures across the changing point of view, too. "So a fair amount of time went into the shading and surfacing. To have the materials behave properly and look as real as possible for all angles was also a challenge. "The product had to look perfect, so we approached the shoe itself on 'physical basics', making sure we built it as it is in real life regarding modeling, texturing as well as the materials. "Looking at it, not with our bare eyes but with macro lenses, helped us see the physical details and apply them in CG. "The rigs also had to deliver nice deformations of a high quality and dense representation of the shoe. We had to make sure that the animators would be able to hit the desired poses easily while the deformations stayed nice and solid. "On top of that the shoe had to look alive and menacing! We had to build in extra controls and shapes to support a believable transition from a static object to a living and venomous creature. "We had five weeks to complete the spot. Luckily, we already built some of the assets during the pitch, so we didn't have to start from zero when the job was awarded. "At Polynoid, we work on i7- six core, 32GB RAM workstations, and render with Royal Render on our in-house render farm with a total of 336 real XEON cpu cores. Software-wise we used Softimage and ZBrush for 3D and rendered with Arnold. "All the compositing work was done in Nuke, and we used Photoshop for texturing and After Effects for the edit and additional effects."

records.description: The Mill+ animation director Angus Kneale: "'98% Human' is part of PETA's commitment to stop primates being used within the entertainment industries as actors. We embarked on an incredibly ambitious journey to create a truly photo-real 100 percent CGI chimpanzee. "This was one of the most exciting and challenging projects I've ever worked on. Crafting PETA '98% Human' was more than about creating a totally believable, CG chimp. It was about establishing an emotional connection and empathy with the audience. "In the past we would have used motion capture and mapped a human actor's performance directly onto the CG character. But we wanted to approach this project in a different way, so we decided to rely on the skill of our animators for the final chimp performances, only using an actor for pre-vis. "We pushed computer graphics imagery to a new level creating bespoke technology in muscle and skin simulation, higher than any other project or film to date. "We achieved this by developing new techniques from simulated bloodstreams, skin tension and even individual pores at the base of every hair on the chimpanzee, all with the aim to create a creature that is practically indistinguishable from his flesh and blood counterpart. The spot demonstrates the partnership between creativity and technology by delivering on PETA's powerful message that you do not need to use live primates as actors, now that we can create fully life-like, photo-real primates."

"To keep the project streamlined and cost efficient, Yoho created the entire project in After Effects, adding textures to the final piece. "We wanted a very tactile feel, which we would have done in camera if the budget and timeline allowed. The end result was very close to that and allowed for a lot of flexibility."

records.description: Jean-Sebastien Guillemette, 3D artist at Shed in Montreal: "We had to create the concepts, storyboard, animatic and final rendered animation from a scenario the agency Sid Lee wrote. The story followed a client asking an IGA employee what he could do with an eggplant. "The character designs were of great concern to the clients because even though the goal was to deliver a cartoonish animation, the character couldn't look too funny. The whole project had to be balanced between cartoon and realism. "The quantity of detail in the environment and the quantity of characters to create from scratch were definitely a challenge in the time we had. "We used Softimage as our primary 3D software. Everything was rendered in Arnold and composited in Nuke. We have our own in-house renderfarm to process the whole thing." Schedule: "We had a little bit more than two months from the time we received the brief and delivered the project."

records.description: MCDONALD'S MYBURGER NAM'S Pinata animator Mikko in Helsinki, Finland: "The team wanted to mix different techniques and see how far they can push when combining totally different styles and still pull it off. The film combines 2D animated effects, 3D elements, some compositing magic and particle simulation. "The challenge was to blend all techniques seamlessly together. However that is what usually makes the project most interesting, developing a visual key for the animation and see how creative people can go, still following that same idea." MCDONALD'S MYBURGER HEVIKANA Pinata compositor Mika: "The goal was to show some really heavy machinery and instruments and still keep the look fresh and vibrant. That's one of the reasons we chose an organic painterly style for this animation. And to keep things interesting we introduced this little robot fellow to better show the scale of things during camera movement. "We aimed for a look that mixes different techniques so seamlessly together it's hard to say if something is crafted in 3D, hand painted 2D animation or a careful simulation." MCDONALD'S MYBURGER MCSMOKEY CHILI Pinata artist Jonna: "Competition winner Tero Halonen put together an inspired burger full of intriguing flavors and our job was to visualize them in an exciting way. McSmokey Chili is a combination of hot and mild ingredients: desert heat and the calmness of space. "The film's look started to fall into place after designing the little chihuahua character. After that, all rolled on pretty smoothly and I didn't have any problems creating stuff. Actually I ended up creating way too many elements than necessary. Maybe there will be a sequel one day!"

records.description: Bryan Shrednick, director of business development for Royale in LA: "Nike came to Royale with a very simple request, to create a film that showcases the flexibility of the Nike Free 5.0 Running shoe. "Ten days later, Royale had created five independently unique concepts that showcased the flexibility of the shoe. Nike immediately selected the Kaleidoscope option, and Royale went back to the drawing board to flesh out production style frames, and later, a completely CG pre-vis. "One technical challenge was shooting the shoes live action rather than using CG. We felt this method allowed us to remain true to the original creative request from Nike. "For the live-action shoot, physically rigging the shoes to contort to the movements we desired was also a challenge. Timing the motion rig and camera movements became exponentially more difficult as the rig melted under the extremely hot studio lights. "Our main creative challenge was keeping the Kaleidoscope imagery engaging and beautiful while remaining uncluttered. When you're duplicating/reflecting the shoes, things get chaotic very quickly. Royale also produced a print campaign that has seen heavy OOH rotation. The campaign can be seen on billboards, displays at Nike stores, and displays at Nike retailers including Foot Locker and Sports Authority. Schedule: 1/31/13: Live Action Shoot 2/1/12: Editorial Prep and Rotoscoping 2/13/13: Animation 3/7/13: Final Cleanup and Color Grading 3/14/13: Final Rendering 3/21/13: Complete and Deliver Finals "Nike distributed the videos around the web, including their social media platforms, the nike.com US homepage, and various international Nike web properties. "Our favorite fan comment from YouTube has been 'I had total mindfuck after watching this commercial.' Thanks man, that's usually what we're going for. The videos can also be seen in stores as part of an interactive display and on video billboards around the world." Hardware: RED Epic, turntable rig, fishing line. Software: After Effects, Cinema 4D, REDCINE-X Pro After Effects: compositing, editing, color grading REDCINE: transcoding and color correction Cinema 4D: Match move cg shoes to the live plates to generate accurate shadows

records.description: MPC helps Adam Berg show off the features of a Samsung television which can be controlled with voice recognition and motion sensors, starting with a ten-day shoot in Cape Town. MPC VFX supervisor Franck Lambertz in London: "We shot a herd of wildebeest on a massive green screen, working in a safari park just out of Cape Town. "This was challenging to say the least, as wildebeest aren't exactly the most co-operative animals. Once shot, we utilized MPC's proprietary crowd replication software to build the scene. "MPC's team of concept artists designed the suitably terrifying tyrannosaurus rex, which was then sculpted in 3D using ZBrush. Following the sculpt in ZBrush, we extracted vector displacement, which allowed us to keep the rig geometry nice and light, in turn making the animators' lives easier. "The T-rex had an automatic tail system, muscles and proprietary jiggle deformers, which was originally developed for MPC's film pipeline. The compositing team added debris and saliva to the dinosaur, further adding to the realism. "The racing car shot was captured in camera and driven by real-life racing drivers. The team added the wind effects and composited our protagonist, who was shot on greenscreen. The bear was a puppet, whose rig was removed and had his eyes animated. "The final, epic scene showing a space age assault was a combination of live action and CG magic. Referencing films such as 'Indendepence Day' and 'Alien', the concept artists turned their hand to designing the mothership and UFO crafts. "These were then fully produced in 2D and Maya. As the crafts start to shoot fireballs, MPC's extensive element library was utilized to add to the flame and smoke effects. "The car flipping onto its side during the action was captured in camera, as were a great deal of the explosions and fireballs, then further enhanced in Maya. Five cameras were used, mounted on buildings and cars, to help capture the epic scene. "MPC's Motion Design studio was enlisted to create the television interface and end shot. The interface was created in After Effects, then composited into the TV itself in Flame."

records.description: MPC VFX producer Chris Allen in London: "MPC's team of concept artists developed an extensive series of exploratory sketches using films such as 'Wrath of the Titans' as reference. The team researched volcanic behavior, as well as ice cracks and rocks to create the monster, affectionately nicknamed James. "The next step was to create a 3D model of the selected character. The team took special care to define James' personality, using human expressions and applying them to the 3D model. This allows a high level of anthropomorphism, and shows James both angrily destroying the city, then in shock as he is vaporized. "The next step was to determine the texture of his body. The team constructed a shader in Maya that could dynamically change its apparent temperature to vary between volatile fiery lava, all the way down to icy frozen rock. "The opening scene was built up using stock footage and built-up still frames. MPC's extensive element library was used to add smoke effects while the team of matte painters added a menacing feel to the sky. The helicopters were created in-house and are completely CG. "As James gets to work destroying the city, his touch on the buildings around him blackens them - this effect was added by the matte painting team. "A great deal of the fire and flames were captured in camera and were embellished with CG elements."

records.description: Method VFX supervisor Andy Boyd in New York: "As if making a CG rhino in a spacesuit wasn't cool enough, we got to animate him screaming and praying for his life as he re-entered the atmosphere in a rocket pod. "Realizing the baby planet and populating it with CG animals required a concerted effort during pre-production to prep the assets ahead of the shoot. CG supervisor Brian Burke led a creature team that involved the creation of over ten different types of CG animals as well as their customized spacesuits. "We were able to take tools from prior jobs and make it modular in a way that allowed individual artists to use them across different characters. The work done by one artist on previous jobs could be shared across the whole team. "For outer space, director Jake Scott wanted an ethereal look similar to the formation sequence from the film 'The Tree of Life'. Scott consulted with 'Tree of Life' VFX supervisor and Method senior creative director Dan Glass about his approach to capturing these elements in-camera. "Production built two large liquid containers that were shot as a B-unit during the shoot. Method used this footage as a basis for the space environments and added detail in matte painting and compositing. "All of the animal assets were deep into development ahead of principal photography. As plates were coming back from production, the lighting team would have first pass renders in the scenes within days. The instantaneous workflow allowed clients very early access to animation and look development as they edited the piece. "The Babylandia planet's lush landscapes were based on conceptual renderings from Method London and derived from aerial footage shot in Kauai, Hawaii by Method VFX producer Mike Wigart. The Los Angeles team, led by artists Chris Sanchez and Zach Christian, executed matte painted backgrounds for Babylandia and Earth. Schedule: three months.

records.description: Damon Duncan, director at Assembly in Aukland, NZ: "Colenso BBDO came to Assembly with a fantastic concept for their client Anchor – the concept was based around a new package that protects the milk from being exposed to light. "The concept was to create a glass cow, desperate to keep its precious cargo away from the light. Assembly leapt at the chance to create a test to prove the concept. "This was a little less polished than the final results but gave Colenso and the team at Anchor the confidence that the idea would could work in the real world. "There were a few sleepless nights leading up to the filming as we were shooting this spot in the depths of a New Zealand winter, famous for its long, rainy days. "We were lucky enough to have good weather on the shoot days however, a blessing as the entire concept hinged on the interplay of shadows and the sun, both extremely important characters in the scripts. "We used full size cutouts of cows on the shoot so we could frame up on the correct scale within our scenes. "Ultimately we relied on cinematographer Ian McCarrol's feel for the motion we were trying to express when we were capturing our clean plates, leading the viewers to the action and endeavoring to follow the protagonists on the screen. "We made the decision very early on to keep the camera very naturalistic with a softened handheld feel, utilizing a bungee rig on the camera to achieve this. "The animation of the cows was extremely important to achieve the subtlety that we were after, injecting the right amount of character into the cows without losing their bovine qualities. "The extremely talented animation department at Assembly tackled the job with an eye to weight and gravity to ensure the large amount of volume that the cows were moving around inside them felt believable and true to the real world. "Technically this job was an enormous challenge. From the rendering of the glass to the simulation of the milk there were numerous issues to overcome. "Our pipeline started with Maya where the cow modeling, rigging and animation was done. The animation was all keyframe. Maya Muscle was used to achieve convincing skin sliding and jiggle effects while maintaining volume. "Despite the cows being made of glass, it turned out that these effects were an important part of getting the cows to appear lifelike and full of bovine character. We then used the built-in point caching to transfer the completed animation to 3ds Max. "Once inside Max, we used Thinkbox Frost to calculate the mesh from our fluid particle files that we generated in a proprietary fluid simulator. We cached the fluid meshes to the network with Thinkbox XMesh to give us fast scene interactivity. "On top of this mesh we used some custom modifiers made in Thinkbox Genome to get smooth sides and sharp edges where the milk hits the glass. "Once we had a nice milk mesh, we cached the subsurface light scattering (SSS) contribution on the milk. This means we could re-render without having to wait for the time consuming SSS calculations. It also meant that the milk surface stayed smooth and flicker free despite being refracted through the glass. "All the rendering was done using V-Ray and we used Thinkbox Deadline to manage simulation, caching, and 2D and 3D rendering tasks on our render farm. "The bird was all made in Maya with individual feather geometry. Because of the bird's rapid movement, it was animated with subframe animation so that the motion blur would reveal all the action. "All the comp work was completed in Nuke 7 using deep compositing for some of the crowd shots. Having deep renders meant we could render all the cows in one pass and then insert grass mattes in between individual cows for the grass/ground integration. "We used The Foundry Hiero to maintain a current cut of each commercial, ready for review at any time. As each shot was updated and finished, they seamlessly updated in context of the full edit. We also found it great for making tweaks to the cut right up to the deadline."

"We made the decision very early on to keep the camera very naturalistic with a softened handheld feel, utilizing a bungee rig on the camera to achieve this. "The animation of the cows was extremely important to achieve the subtlety that we were after, injecting the right amount of character into the cows without losing their bovine qualities. "The extremely talented animation department at Assembly tackled the job with an eye to weight and gravity to ensure the large amount of volume that the cows were moving around inside them felt believable and true to the real world. "Technically this job was an enormous challenge. From the rendering of the glass to the simulation of the milk there were numerous issues to overcome. "Our pipeline started with Maya where the cow modeling, rigging and animation was done. The animation was all keyframe. Maya Muscle was used to achieve convincing skin sliding and jiggle effects while maintaining volume. "Despite the cows being made of glass, it turned out that these effects were an important part of getting the cows to appear lifelike and full of bovine character. We then used the built-in point caching to transfer the completed animation to 3ds Max. "Once inside Max, we used Thinkbox Frost to calculate the mesh from our fluid particle files that we generated in a proprietary fluid simulator. We cached the fluid meshes to the network with Thinkbox XMesh to give us fast scene interactivity. "On top of this mesh we used some custom modifiers made in Thinkbox Genome to get smooth sides and sharp edges where the milk hits the glass. "Once we had a nice milk mesh, we cached the subsurface light scattering (SSS) contribution on the milk. This means we could re-render without having to wait for the time consuming SSS calculations. It also meant that the milk surface stayed smooth and flicker free despite being refracted through the glass. "All the rendering was done using V-Ray and we used Thinkbox Deadline to manage simulation, caching, and 2D and 3D rendering tasks on our render farm. "The bird was all made in Maya with individual feather geometry. Because of the bird's rapid movement, it was animated with subframe animation so that the motion blur would reveal all the action. "All the comp work was completed in Nuke 7 using deep compositing for some of the crowd shots. Having deep renders meant we could render all the cows in one pass and then insert grass mattes in between individual cows for the grass/ground integration. "We used The Foundry Hiero to maintain a current cut of each commercial, ready for review at any time. As each shot was updated and finished, they seamlessly updated in context of the full edit. We also found it great for making tweaks to the cut right up to the deadline."

records.description: Project lead, Chris Johnson at Topix in Toronto: "First we built a fairly exhaustive library of reference material. This allowed us to determine, on paper, which attributes would best fit our ideal TELUS spokes-critter, in collaboration with the agency and client. "We gathered numerous video clips to provide the animators with behavior and motion references. We also developed a customized production pipeline integrating the steps needed to build and rig the assets, animate them, apply textures, fur, skin and muscle dynamics, and finally render our images photo-realistically, using a carefully selected collection of both available software and our own proprietary tools. "While the design and build of the models, rigs and furring routines were time-consuming tasks, the assets are now built and available for an entire campaign and beyond. "The other great benefit is that the pipeline, documented expertise and toolsets are all in place so that we can quickly and efficiently adapt them to other new critters as they are added to the line-up." Topix animation supervisor, Marcus Alqueres: "We were constantly walking this fine line between cartoony and realistic performances, so every time we had a very specific direction, we had to stop and think about how a real animal would perform that action." Topix senior producer Cathy Jefferies: "Starting with our own core group of in-house designers, animators and project leads, we were able to assemble a dream team of very specialized talent from all over the world, most of whom have worked on large scale feature projects. At its peak, the team was up to 20 people. "Marcus is from Brazil, one of our lighters is located in Australia, one of our modelers was working remotely from Paris and New York. We also had a couple of people working out of Montreal and some animators were re-located to Toronto from Vancouver."

records.description: Wolf & Crow visualize the power of sound for the new Skullcandy Crusher headphones in this new spot starring NBA superstar Kevin Durant and Grammy-nominated rapper Wale, featuring a Wale and French Montana remix of "We Back 2 Ballin." The scope of the project, from concept to storyboard, live-action shoot to VFX, and final Flame finishing, was completed entirely by the team at Wolf & Crow at their Los Angeles studio. Skullcandy approached Wolf & Crow with the challenge of visualizing sound in a way that hadn't been seen before. Skullcandy Crushers are bass-driven headphones that physically vibrate when they are used, which the Wolf & Crow team interpreted in different manifestations throughout the spot. The ripples through Durant's skin were created by modeling Durant's head, texturing the skin on it and matching the lighting, then layering in some compositing magic to finish. Once Wale's track really kicks in, the physicality of the audio explodes out of the headphones into the environment. The VFX elements are glossy and clean, representing the aesthetic of the Crusher headphones, as well as rough and aggressive to highlight the audio power that the user experiences when wearing the headphones.

records.description: MPC NY managing director Justin Lane: "The key to a spot like this is to capture the whimsical qualities of the animated pieces and connect those to the real world. "The team worked painstakingly at designing and expressing personality in all of the characters and it truly shows - you really want to learn more about each of them. "The most important personality trait of the toad is that he is a bit grumpy and irritable. We tried to accentuate this with his mouth line by making it more prominent, but with a subtle frown. We also emphasized how his eyes furrow and are never really open wide. He's never curious, but always suspicious. "By contrast, the rabbit character is always wide-eyed and alert." MPC CG lead Bill Dorais: "Our priority was also researching anatomy to capture a perfect, believable look. For the toad we were trying to get the blinks to look correct, giving him a nictitating membrane, a thin skin that covers the eye. "Our philosophy going into this was that the more details we added, the more believable the piece would be. "Over the years we've researched and developed quite a bit of software for our feature film side and have been able to utilize and apply these technological advances to commercials. Without the use of Furtility, I don't think we would have captured the nuances of these characters as easily."

records.description: The Mission creative director Rob Trent in LA: "We shot in Madrid, Spain with Phantom cameras and utilized two sets for the surreal 'diorama' field: both were the same size, but one was flat and the other was pitched 20 degrees to put all the action on a decline. The entire stage was bluescreen. "For the speed vortex, confetti, smoke, water, glass and other debris with wind were shot separately to be composited with athletes later. Stunt men and fence pieces were flying continuously during the shoot to create the desired effect. "The platform was Astroturf, which The Mission enhanced and extended, then added the earthen cross-section. Additional confetti and smoke were created in Maya with the 'glitchy' perimeter board designed and fabricated in Flame. "Ronaldo's skill was amazing. The coach quickly broke down the desired blocking for him and he just took the footwork to a new level when the cameras rolled. "We had just watched him at his home stadium the night before against Germany and he really brought the electricity from there to our set. "Back at The Mission's studio in Venice, Wieden+Kennedy creatives and director Mark Zibert worked closely with the VFX team to help fine-tune the images."

records.description: Jane Bakx, EP at Glassworks Amsterdam: "The G-Star RAW creative team created the concept for a macro-level journey through the denim-making process. "While the brief was to create a dramatic animation film, it was still very important to remain faithful to the core processes involved in creating their famous RAW denim. "We wanted to create an original and magical world, to take the viewer from the untreated cotton burs all the way to the final denim object. Denim, especially G-Star's RAW denim is very iconic. "First of all you have the denim material itself, with its distinct woven pattern, and its use of indigo-dyed and natural cotton, then you have the typical yellow double stitching and rivets, elements that everyone will instantly recognize. "Right from the beginning, my idea was to focus on these elements and to present the beauty of the materials - soft natural cotton, the slightly shiny surface unique to RAW denim, metallic rivets. "I wanted the images to focus on each specific part of the denim-making process without distracting background or environments. To support this I opted for a toned down color pallet: dark blue, whites and black, with a splash of warm color coming from the cotton leaves, the orange thread and the rivet. "To get an interesting contrast to the realism of the materials, I wanted to create a clean graphic layout for the shots, a very coordinated and choreographed animation style, whilst also highlighting all of the little detail that makes it look like macro photography. "Our goal was to create the feeling of a journey, with a naturally flowing edit from one sequence to the next. "During storyboarding and 3D layout, we were in close contact with G-Star's denim specialists to make sure that our film remained true to the processes of denim-making. "We actually changed the dying sequence completely at the layout stage because it was too far away from the real dying procedure. "It was crucial to achieve a super photo-realistic look that would stand up to the critical eyes of the denim experts. As we figured every sequence needed its own approach, we decided to split the job up into sequences rather than departments (e.g. animation, rigging, etc.). "So every sequence was handled by a different artist who would then take care of their whole shot, from the models and rigging all the way to texturing and rendering. "This led to many different ways of setting up the ropes and threads, each meeting the needs of that specific shot. "To make sure there was a clear continuity throughout the film, every artist always referred back to our own real macro photography of the G-Star RAW denim, rather than trying to match what another artist had made. "We started concepting and storyboarding at the beginning of June, and we completed the 3D animatic and color boards by the end of July. "Then we had three months until beginning of December to produce the shots. During the main production period we had a team of four-five 3D artists working simultaneously on the different sequences. "The film will play in their stores and also be released for cinemas worldwide, as the original 60 sec version as well as a 30 sec cut-down. "All the CG was done in Softimage using the Arnold renderer, and the film was composited in Nuke. Additional 2D elements were added in Flame, and the grading was done in-house on Baselight. "The detailed images needed quite some time to render, so we were more than happy to be connected to our London office via our extremely fast glassfibre connection. This enabled us to make full use of their additional 60 node renderfarm."

records.description: Christopher Vulpi, EP at Trizz in Barcelona: "For Galicia Distillery and their internationally acclaimed brandy, Renuage, Trizz were invited to create an exquisite journey of tastes. The concept stems from the experience you have during the first sip. "Learning about the distillers unique process and flavor, Trizz co-founder and director, Oriol Puig developed a poetic treatment. records.description: Danny Robashkin, creative director at MAKE in Minneapolis: "The two spots were made completely in-house, the idea started with the desire to do a 2D animation interaction with real actors in an interview setting. "Using the infamous anti-smoking slogan, 'Monkey on your back' as a base, we went on to write the two spots. It was important to keep them fun with splashes of humor, yet still hit the mark that smoking will kill. "Visualizing and directing not only the actors, but the monkeys that weren't there was definitely a challenge. Thank goodness for storyboards and animators who volunteered to be puppeteers. Even though we were on a greenscreen, there was a lot going on. Making the performance of the actor and monkey feel cohesive was key. Figuring out all the exact moves with the animators prior to shooting was extremely helpful. "Designing the monkeys so they would work with the actors, but still be fun to look at was also a hurdle. "We asked a lot of questions like, 'When the monkey gets shot, what should the blood look like?' 'How stylized do we want the cartoon gun?' 'How gross should the turkey be?' "Not to mention the animation supervisor left part way into the project to go to Disney. "Integrating live action with 2D animation and CG elements was a huge challenge. In terms of the animation, there were strict rules to follow because the monkeys had to feel like they were on the actors. If the actor shifted, you had to make the anticipation of the monkey's movement feel right. "We animated on 'ones' so there were a lot of frames, plus we were doing all this as 4K files. On top of that, each monkey was broken into several layers. So between the large file sizes and communication to the compositors about all the different layers, there were a lot of details that couldn't be overlooked. "We also had to do a lot of puppeteering tests with clothing, fishing line, and stand-in objects to know what was working performance-wise and what could be roto'ed or covered with the animation." Schedule: "Shooting was only two and a half days, but we had several days of prep and tests. Animation and finishing took several weeks."

records.description: Darren Jaffe, executive producer at Superfad in LA: "The client came to us to visualize the concept of 'No Dream Limit'. "As this piece would be seen at the 2012 SEMA automotive specialty products tradeshow, they needed to find a way to explain that the Fiat 500 is like a blank canvas. Fiat owners should feel completely uninhibited by what they can do with their car through aftermarket vendors. "We were tasked with creating a piece that would inspire the SEMA audience to look at their Fiat in a completely new way. "This was done by complimenting the internal monologue of the designer with a visual stream of consciousness that takes the viewer through the inspiration and conceptualization behind two of the new custom Fiat 500's that were unveiled at the show in Vegas: The Beach Cruiser Car and The Cafe Racer. "We had a very aggressive two-week schedule for this project so from the start, we had to have a strong game plan. First and most importantly, we constructed an imaginative story that visualized the inspirations the designer looked to when realizing the new 500 models. "We then drew up storyboards to help illustrate the whole story. Once approved, we went into a full pre-vis, blocking out each shot and car animation. When we had a good idea of how we were connecting each section, it was full-on production mode. "Designers, 2D/3D and cel animators went to work creating every element, being careful to keep the design aesthetic cohesive in each section. Because of the accelerated schedule, we worked with compositors early on to put together each scene. "This helped us see the bigger picture and helped to problem solve some of the tougher scenes right away. It is a great credit to the awesome team on the job that we were able to pull off such a strong piece in such a limited time. "We knew from the beginning that the car was going to be in 3D, but we didn't have the schedule to make everything fully realized. Our process started by first planning out what elements and shots would best be created in 3D and what things we could create using other methods. "Our team of cel animators created beautiful animations and transitions that we used in conjunction with the 3D car and 2D design elements. It was really great to work with traditional cel animators as their medium really spoke well to the dream concept. "We could block out concepts quickly and fluidly, using our initial pre-vis and all the way into final production. "The end of the piece features the stylized cars tearing away their skin to reveal the photo-real versions underneath and cel animation was the perfect technique to achieve the effect. "On the 3D side, we worked hard to develop three different rendering styles for the three cars in the environments. A toon-shaded line art look worked perfectly for the Beach Cruiser model, while a more aggressive high contrast graphic chrome look felt more appropriate for the Cafe Racer. "In the last scene, we employed a graphic flat look to the cars so that there would be enough contrast when they transitioned to photo real cars." Schedule: 2.5 weeks.

records.description: Pablo Tufaro, CG head at La Posta in Buenos Aires, Argentina: "We were asked to create a rapper pigeon. I mean, a real pigeon, with some rapper accessories like sunglasses, hat, and gold chains, singing a rap song along Sao Paulo streets. "The most difficult creative part of the job was that the director (Jonathan Gurvit) asked us to make the pigeon sing and dance like a rapper-singer but with real pigeon movements. "We only made a little joke on the breakdance section, but this was totally accepted by the director, at the moment he saw it he exploded in laughs. "For sure this was the most difficult technical job we have done. The rig was the most challenging part. We hired a couple of riggers that were experienced in birds to allow us to animate the wings in this particular dancing way. "The other big thing was the feathers, not only the setup but the look development too. Render times were pretty crazy. "We used Softimage running on Windows for the CG and Arnold for the render. We comped in Nuke and After Effects and the color correction was done in our color room with Scratch running on a Mac pro." Schedule: "One month to do the entire spot. Luckily we finished one week earlier and we had that time that you never count on, to look after every detail, to make the CG look perfect.

records.description: Director Pete Circuitt, Auckland, NZ: "My brief was to create an upbeat, vibrant and energetic animation technique to reflect the life that happens within the walls of our homes. "The ad was to feature a cast of characters sliding along the walls in heavily stylized, painted silhouettes, leaving behind a trail of colorful destruction that only a paint like Dulux Wash and Wear could withstand. "It was important to remain honest to the tools available for interior painting. So all the artwork is painted predominantly with a roller, with a little detail work done with a four-inch brush. We created natural digital brushes directly from what we observed when we painted on actual walls during pre-production. "Initially to limit our toolset to big rollers and broad four-inch brushes seemed like a big task but when I did the initial style frames, I found I could get a tremendous amount of detail from your average roller, and it could be made to look very cool. "We didn't paint the animation on set because it was not practical to secure any residential location for the many weeks required to do it. The action is instead painted digitally, and because it's done in computers, the real achievement lies in the trail technique. "When a character moves it leaves a history behind it. And it is this quality which was terrifically difficult to execute with tracked cameras. "Originally a story was written that observed a battle between two brother and sister 'monsters'. I was really excited to use my son's drawings as a base for the creature designs. "Although the final script changed significantly, the original monster style frames I painted informed me how to approach the project creatively. I have included a few of these for fun and because I am very fond of them. "Finally, credit must be given to the amazing animated graffiti work of BLU. His incredible work was a constant inspiration. Thank-you." Schedule: "All told we had six weeks, but only two weeks after we shot the live-action to digitally paint all the action on the walls."

records.description: Blacklist directing collective Polynoid deploy a mix of procedural animation and photo-real rendering in this thinly disguised jab at Apple while introducing the Lenovo Thinkpad laptop aimed at the no-nonsense power user. Ilija Brunck: "The Woo Agency had the idea to establish an Apple-like world and get it swallowed by our hero, the carbon fiber. What we really liked about the brief is that we could destroy something white and slick and by that making the world a darker place. "Because of the long pack shots we were left with only 15 seconds for the actual storytelling. It was quite challenging to establish the setting and tell the story of the carbon take over in this short amount of time. "The carbon fibers are created in Softimage ICE using strands. We use those strands in a lot of our productions and built a production pipeline for using it in all kind of situations. "The wonderful thing about strands is that it gives you the opportunity to procedurally create something very detailed and still design and render it quickly. Schedule: "The spot was produced in six weeks from concept to final product. In the first weeks we worked on basic animatics to nail the pacing and edit of the clip. After that we went through several rounds of redefining all the elements."

Cullen worked with Target's in-house team to develop concepts for each spot based on the tracks themselves, together with subtle visual nods to Target's branding. "The performance sequence was captured in Los Angeles on a set adorned with reflective orbs.

records.description: French directing duo ROJO teams with Prague studio Eallin Motion Art to help mark the 170th anniversary of the creation of the Czech beer Pilsner Urquell by enhancing high-speed macro live action footage with CGI. "The challenge was to fit the idea within a budget. We did this by not creating the film fully in 3D but by shooting elements of the universe on table top then combining the 3D with the live action footage in the most believable and organic way. "The most difficult part was dynamic simulation of a rotating galaxy and fire elements. Even with the most high end technology behind you, simulating such complex phenomena is a very hard task. Especially when you require the maximum level of creative freedom and visual control which you cannot achieve during real shooting. Schedule: Six weeks.

records.description: Clementine Buren at Wanda in Plaine Saint Denis, France: "On the 4th of August 2006, 17 aid workers from Action Contre la Faim were murdered in Muttur, southeastern Sri Lanka. "For the past six years, Action Contre la Faim has fought for the opening of an international investigation supervised by the United Nations to finally shed light on the circumstances and on those who are guilty of this massacre. "Our idea was to use blood to tell the story without falling into the free violence pitfall; the film manages to express the terrible reality with astuteness and poetry. "Symbolically playing with the white NGO's T-shirt and the victims' blood shed on it, the film gives a voice to a fictitious last witnesses of this horrible day. The talent of the director Luis Nieto, who mixes realism and metaphor, makes this testimony visually both powerful and striking. "The challenges were to find the right mix between something violent yet poetic and to make the symbolic feel as real as possible." Schedule: six weeks.

records.description: Vidya Thomas, director/founder at Rocketscience Lab in Mumbai, India: "The agency's brief was to design a series of films imitating the real tests Samsonite suitcases are put through while simultaneously showcasing the craftsmanship behind their products. "The goal was to produce hyper-realistic CG films that not only highlighted the strength and durability of the products but also transformed the manufacturing process into an aesthetically striking experience. "One of the primary creative challenges was ensuring that each sequence maintained the visual integrity and precision of a high-end print advertisement. "Every frame had to be meticulously composed, with a strong emphasis on aesthetic framing, lighting, and surface detailing. "A unique constraint given to the team was to avoid using depth of field in the renderings, a common technique for guiding focus and masking imperfections. "This meant that every inch of the environment, from foreground to background, needed to be crafted with equal care. "We had to ensure every corner of the set was rich in detail, employing high-resolution textures and procedural materials to achieve an uncompromising level of hyper-realism. "The greatest technical challenge lay in achieving an extraordinary level of realism, ensuring every simulation and surface detail precisely mirrored the actual Samsonite product. "From the tactile qualities of the materials to the way the suitcases responded to physical forces during testing, every element had to be meticulously recreated in CG. "This demanded not only high-fidelity texturing and material accuracy but also complex simulations that captured real-world physics with precision." Schedule: Four months.
